Drone hits another Wildberries warehouse near Moscow
A drone has hit a warehouse of Russian e-commerce company Wildberries near Moscow and caused a fire at the site, regional governor Andrei Vorobyov said.
He said the fire has now been extinguished but the drone attack damaged other buildings, including private houses, apartment buildings, shops and a power station.
At least three people were injured in the attack, he said.
In the past month, Ukraine has hit at least seven of the 10 largest Wildberries warehouses, which it says is complicit in Moscow’s war against Kyiv.
UK says it stands ‘shoulder to shoulder’ with Ukraine after Russia fumes over British drones
Britain has said it stands united with Ukraine against Russia’s aggression after Moscow fumed over British-made drones being used in strikes on Russia.
The Russian embassy in the UK on Monday accused London of complicity in aiding Ukraine with drones that are hitting targets deep inside Russian territory.
The UK, it said, is “deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis”.
"In doing so, the United Kingdom is acting as an accomplice and co-perpetrator of the bloody crimes and terrorist attacks," the Russian Embassy to the UK said.
It added: "London's actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer," and the deeper its involvement in the conflict, "the higher the price it will pay".
A spokesperson for the Ministry of Defence (MoD) told BBC News that Britain stands “shoulder to shoulder” with Ukraine.
"Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this Government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies," the spokesperson said.
The UK was "committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against [Russian president Vladimir] Putin's illegal invasion," they said.
Russia tells North Korea they are making 'new and righteous world order'
Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov has hailed North Korea's role in fighting to eject Ukrainian forces from the Kursk region, writing in a letter that they succeeded in driving out a "Ukrainian Nazi clique".
North Korea and Russia are working to establish a "new and righteous world order," Lavrov wrote in a letter to North Korean foreign minister Choe Son Hui, according to the North's state news agency KCNA this morning.
Pyongyang has deployed troops to Russia since late 2024, when it helped Moscow retake a portion of Kursk that had been captured by a Ukrainian counteroffensive.
Vladimir Putin's regime routinely calls the Ukrainian administration “neo-Nazis,” even though the country has a Jewish president who lost relatives in the Holocaust and who heads a Western-backed, democratically elected government.
Putin has vowed to fight on in Ukraine until Moscow secures the country's "demilitarisation", "denazification" and neutrality, unless Kyiv accepts a deal that achieves those goals.
Russia fires top economist after he compares Putin’s economy to 1917 revolution
The chief economist of a Russian state development bank has been fired after reportedly drawing comparisons between Russia’s present day economy and the 1917 revolution.
Andrei Klepach, one of Russia's most prominent macroeconomists who worked for VEB, made the remarks to a financial forum in May. They were reported by Russian media only last week.
He warned that the country was falling behind the West and China and suffering mounting economic damage from the war in Ukraine, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Russian forces have downed at least 180 drones in the Moscow region overnight, the capital's mayor Sergei Sobyanin said in the early hours today.
Overall, 620 drones were heading for the region surrounding the Russian capital between Monday evening and 5am, he said.

Somewhere along the county road between Independence and Manchester, I lost Rob Sand.
This had been a distinct possibility when I agreed to join the 44-year-old Democratic candidate for governor on a segment of a weeklong bike ride across Iowa. Unlike Sand, I am not a biker—merely a leisurely walker and, like any good Millennial woman, an occasional Pilates-doer. Which is why, on a long, low-grade hill dotted with Queen Anne’s lace, my quads began to burn, my pace slowed, and the subject of my story disappeared into a rainbow river of helmets. A minute later, the sag wagon overtook me. Soon so did a 9-year-old boy.
Thankfully, my humiliation was short-lived. These days in Iowa, one can never truly be without Rob Sand. Even as I panted alone at the back of the peloton, I could hear people chattering about the man who would be governor. “Was that who I think it was?” they said. And, “Oh, I just love him!” At one point, a fit-looking cyclist who turned out to be the former NFL wide receiver Tim Dwight pulled up beside me to lament Iowa’s unfulfilled economic potential. “This is why,” he said, “we need Rob.”
Sand, the state auditor, is ubiquitous in Iowa. On any given day, one might encounter him in a TV ad, promising jail time for corrupt politicians; on Instagram, talking through a mouthful of Casey’s breakfast pizza; and at a town hall singing “America the Beautiful” with a bipartisan crowd of gray hairs. Sand is something rarely found in nature: a successful Iowa Democrat. Which is perhaps why his presence generates such mania. Biking with him across the state felt a little like showing up to a middle-school slumber party with Taylor Swift—or riding shotgun in the popemobile. Despite Sand’s bike helmet and lack of signage, hundreds of people recognized him and begged for selfies. “I nearly killed Iowa’s next governor!” yelled a man in Winthrop who bumped into Sand’s bike. People often used both his first and last name, running them together into a single word. “I lent my bike pump to Robsand!” another man declared in Independence.
Sand’s party has struggled to gain purchase in Iowa since the dawn of the Trump era, and a Democrat hasn’t been elected governor since 2006. The funny thing is, Sand is not a particularly proud Democrat. He tends to refer to the party as “the lesser of two evils” and made a face when I asked whether he enjoyed being in it. “I can’t imagine saying I like being in any political party,” he told me. “I love being a dad.” Before addressing a crowd in Des Moines County last year, Sand’s staff asked for party insignia to be removed from the walls to make the space more inclusive.
The auditor obviously wants to steer clear of the national party’s noxious fumes. But whereas his progressive contemporaries distance themselves by railing against the establishment, Sand’s campaign approach has been different: Quietly, and with an easygoing optimism that Fred Rogers would envy, Sand questions the concept of partisanship itself. “Our political system is broken, and it’s broken mostly because it’s run by two private clubs” that make voters “feel trapped” into making a binary choice, he told a crowd last month in Newton. “The good news is that Iowa is a place where we have typically said we are going to make politics work for ordinary people.”
National Democrats like what they see—even if they find it tough to describe. Sand “is doing the opposite of what almost every other politician is doing,” the strategist and former Pete Buttigieg adviser Lis Smith told me. He isn’t a loud progressive, but he also doesn’t sound like a corporate moderate, Adam Carlson, a pollster, agreed. “Sand is doing a third thing.”
In November, Sand will be up against a potentially strong GOP candidate. But his most daunting adversary will be the math: Registered Republicans outnumber Democrats by almost 200,000 in Iowa. Which means that Sand plans to spend the next 11 weeks telling Iowans that he can be trusted, in spite of the D behind his name. Will enough of them believe it?
Sand had been annoyed the last time I wrote about him. I’d included all of the relevant background details in my story: that he grew up in Decorah, a town near the Minnesota border, which explains his long vowels (Sand pronounces it “Dee-corah”); that he went to Brown University and worked a few modeling jobs in Europe before attending law school and working for seven years as a prosecutor. I’d explained that, like any good red-state Democrat, Sand loves to hunt and spends Sunday morning in church—and that his wife’s brothers called him “Baby Jesus” for his tendency toward self-righteousness.
But Sand was concerned about something else: that I had not fully captured his frustration with America’s two-party political system. “I was hoping you’d get more into election reform,” he texted me—a sentence that, I am confident, no one has ever said before or since. At the time, I did not imagine that many readers were pining to hear a state auditor’s thoughts on the decline of bipartisanship. But here we are, three summers later, and Sand is still talking about the same ideas: moving to an open-primary system and implementing “approval voting,” which would allow Iowans to support more than one candidate. More remarkable, voters are listening.
Sand is a Democrat because “Jesus is for the little guy, and the Democratic Party, at its best, is for the little guy.” But his more inclusive vision wouldn’t require party affiliation. The scramble to replace Graham Platner in Maine, for example, wouldn’t have happened under Sand’s system, he said. Or, “if a really old candidate, hypothetically, had a bad debate experience, and everyone was like, Um, maybe this person is too old to do this, it wouldn’t be a crisis.” The reforms would reward civility, Sand added, and prevent one-party domination of a state.
Republicans have had total control over Iowa for a decade. In that time, they’ve dramatically cut income taxes, redirected hundreds of millions of public dollars toward private schools, and restricted abortion after six weeks. Right now, the state is facing a $1 billion budget shortfall and the second-highest cancer rate in the country.
But Sand does not harp on Republicans. Actually, a Sand political event doesn’t really feel like one: Each town hall begins with a round of applause for the Republicans, independents, and Democrats (for good measure) who showed up, then transitions into a group rendition of “America the Beautiful.” Sand speaks for a while about his policy priorities (corruption, public education, affordability) before opening the floor to questions, some friendly and others confrontational. The event I attended in Newton concluded with a resounding cheer for—you guessed it!—a return to divided government in Iowa.
An observer might fairly describe all of this as just a tad cringe. But one person’s cringe is another’s stirring call for unity. “There’s a movement afoot for change, and he comes along at a good time,” Steve Mullen, a retired teacher, told me in Newton.
It helps that Sand does not behave like most Democrats. He is not, for example, easily drawn into culture-war debates or bandwagon slogans. Early in his campaign when a radio host asked him whether biological males should be allowed to play in women’s sports, Sand answered succinctly, “No.” In January, after federal officers killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, Sand did not join in the calls to abolish ICE. “He’s taken some of the cultural issues that dog Democrats in red states off the table,” Adam Jentleson, the founder of the center-left think tank Searchlight, told me.
The progressive left, as you might imagine, is not wild about Sand. Some were disgusted, for example, that the Democrat did not release a statement denouncing ICE after Good’s and Pretti’s deaths. Others see Sand’s comments on trans athletes as a betrayal of the LGBTQ community. Still, most seem to find the state auditor tolerable. “He’s a happy warrior for nonpartisan technocratic efficiency and anti-corruption,” Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, told me. Sand might slap that on a billboard.
Iowa’s state auditor can seem a little naive. Even if he becomes governor, Sand would almost certainly be working with a Republican state legislature that won’t be eager to hand him any wins. But Sand says he isn’t worried. “There’s still a lot of people of good faith in that caucus,” Sand told me at a deli in Manchester after we’d finished our bike ride. State GOP lawmakers know that they’ll need to have something to show for their public service when they “reach the pearly gates.” Had Sand met a politician recently? I thought. When I voiced my doubts out loud, Sand looked stricken. “I am really hopeful,” he said.
Meanwhile, Republicans are busy trying to convince Iowa voters that the auditor is more extreme than his kumbaya suggests. “It’s like The Truman Show,” Zach Lahn, Sand’s GOP opponent, says in one campaign video. “He’s not a moderate.” In another, Lahn pledges to take back Iowa’s public-school curriculum “from the Marxists who hijacked it.”
Lahn, a former Republican operative, seemed to come out of nowhere in June when he defeated incumbent Representative Randy Feenstra for the GOP nomination. More specifically, Lahn came from Kansas. Although he was born and raised in Iowa, he has lived in Wichita, where he founded a private school, for much of the past decade. The Des Moines Register reported that Lahn splits his time between Iowa and his second home in Kansas, where some of his children live, although Lahn reassured Iowans that if he is elected governor, he will be in the state “as much as humanly possible.” (Lahn did not respond to my requests for comment.)
But Lahn’s outsider status might help him. He has no elected-office experience and is not yet a known quantity in Iowa, which means that he does not wear the albatross of incumbency. So far, he’s campaigned on protecting small farms from corporate agriculture, an unusual Republican position in the state. For this, as well as his pledge to ban mRNA vaccines and improve the state’s water quality, Lahn has also received the MAHA stamp of approval. Several conservative Iowans along the bike route told me that they wouldn’t have voted for Feenstra, but they were considering Lahn’s “new ideas.”
Lately, Republicans have accused Sand of doing too much stumping and not enough of his day job; they’ve also drawn attention to the significant campaign donations from his wife and her wealthy family. But Lahn’s main project ahead of November will be to remind Iowans that Sand, regardless of his rhetoric, is running as a Democrat. At Sand’s Newton town hall, a Lahn supporter named Carrie Atkinson asked the auditor to declare the number of weeks at which he would support a ban on abortion. Sand answered that he thought Roe v. Wade was a reasonable decision. “He didn’t answer my question!” Atkinson told me later. At another event, a local Republican activist named Gary Loeffler asked Sand to justify his support for abortion as a Christian. There are “many verses in the Bible that say life begins at breath,” Sand said, an answer that enraged some religious conservatives.
Republicans believe, or say they believe, that Sand, a wealthy guy with an Ivy League education, is far more liberal than he lets on. Loeffler offered a disturbing visual: Like an infested cob of sweet corn, Sand might look normal on the outside, but inside, he’s “full of worms.”
Luckily, I was able to test Loeffler’s hypothesis—by traveling to Sand’s hometown and peering into the proverbial husk. In Decorah, along the Upper Iowa River, I attended Nordic Fest, a celebration of Scandinavian heritage that included Viking battle reenactments, Nordic dancers, and a parade featuring Sand in the back of a convertible. It felt a little like visiting Bedford Falls with George Bailey. “This is Rob Sand; he’s a good friend of my eldest son!” the announcer said as the auditor drove by. Sand’s aunt, who ran the lefse stand, trotted into the street to give him a package of fresh Norwegian flatbread. Sand’s father asked me in Norwegian if I spoke the language of my ancestors. (I do not.)
After the parade, Sand offered a wry tour of his hometown. Walking down the main drag, he pointed out the old teen center. “Can you guess how many times we went?” Near a statue of a long-snouted woodland creature, he explained: “Trolls are out in the world and can be dangerous.” Quickly, we were overwhelmed by friends and well-wishers. Among them was Andy Rasmussen, Sand’s best friend from high school. Sand was always smart and ambitious, Rasmussen, who does autobody work in Decorah, told me later. He liked to skateboard and bowhunt. He didn’t drink, but he’d give friends rides to parties. “The running joke was that someday Rob’s gonna be president,” Rasmussen said. But what were Sand’s politics back then? I wanted to know. Is he a Trojan horse of socialist corn worms? Rasmussen basically shrugged. “He will generally talk to and listen to anybody that’s out there.”
Others who knew Sand during college and law school similarly described a man committed to listening. At Brown in the early 2000s, Sand frequently criticized the Bush administration in his column in the school paper. Still, he recruited Stephen Beale, a conservative columnist at the paper, to start a new class on conservative thought, featuring readings from Edmund Burke, Barry Goldwater, and Pat Buchanan. Sand is still “being his authentic self,” Beale, who now works as a freelance writer, told me. “He really does care about hearing the other side.”
I thought about Sand’s cheering section at the Nordic Fest parade. “Light ’em up, Rob!” one man had shouted. But Sand had waved him off. “No, no, no,” he’d said.
The next two months may not be so friendly. So far, Sand has outraised Lahn, but Republicans are pouring millions into the state, partly thanks to a high-profile Senate bid from Democrat Josh Turek and three surprisingly competitive House races. Expect ads from both parties to be vicious—and pervasive. On Thursday, screaming activists for Turning Point Action chased Sand around the Iowa State Fair.
Right now, Sand looks reasonably well positioned for victory. The Cook Political Report has changed its analysis of the race from “lean Republican” to “toss up,” and new polling shows Sand leading Lahn by five points. If he succeeds, Democrats might finally be able to say out loud what many have believed for years: that Iowa still defies partisan categorization.
Many Iowans are only now starting to pay attention. Before I lost Sand on the bike ride, a middle-aged man named Ethan Vaas had rolled up next to us. “Are you who I think you are?” he asked Sand, sounding more suspicious than excited. The two chatted for a moment, but Vaas soon pedaled away, looking unimpressed. An hour later, though, he was back, this time to talk with Sand about his job and his kids. Vaas wasn’t sure how he’d vote this year, he told me later. He typically “leans right.” But there was something different about Sand.

The Best Budget Laptops to Get Your Money’s Worth
Featured in this article
Computers have put people on the moon. You'd think that given the miraculous technological utopia of our age, we’d also be able to get decently cheap laptops. For so long, that felt like a hopeless case. More recently, many budget laptops have become quite good. Chromebooks are more modern, and budget Windows laptops now offer strong battery life. There’s even a MacBook affordable enough to earn the “cheap” designation. If your budget for a computer is tight, I have you covered with my recommendations for the best affordable laptops.

Updated August 2026: I've added the Dell XPS 13, HP OmniBook 3, and MSI Cyborg A15. I’ve also confirmed accuracy and up-to-date pricing throughout.

Other Budget Laptops to Consider
Here at WIRED, we never recommend products we haven't tested ourselves—and I’ve tried hundreds of laptops over the years. I left many laptops off this list due to price, quality, or both. While I stand by my top-pick recommendations above, there are a few additional laptops I've tested that are still worth buying for a particular use case.
Lenovo LOQ 15 for $1,400: This fantastic gaming laptop used to sell for $900, despite coming with an RTX 5060. And unlike so many other affordable gaming laptops, this one comes with a solid IPS panel that has not only a fast refresh rate but also great image quality. So no, it's not extremely cheap, but it's worth considering because it remains the best value in gaming laptops right now.
Acer Chromebook Plus 516 for $479: Chromebooks are really at their best when they cost less than $500. They thrive as cheap laptops that don't feel cheap. The Acer Chromebook Plus 516 has one primary advantage over other laptops around this price: its touchpad. I care a lot about touchpad quality, as it's an area where budget laptops tend to make compromises despite being a component that can impact day-to-day laptop use. Poor touchpad quality can make simple things like drag-and-drop or text selection frustrating. The Acer Chromebook Plus 516 has a really nice touchpad with a smooth surface for your finger to swipe or drag across. It makes a huge difference.
Acer Nitro V 16 for $900: No gaming laptop selling for this price is going to be perfect. Far from it. The Acer Nitro V 16 (7/10, WIRED Recommends) has a big compromise that I need to warn you about up front: its 135-watt power adapter. It's just not enough to keep the Nitro V 16 fully powered during many of the GPU-heavy games I tested, such as Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong. That means even if the laptop is plugged in, it'll start to drain the battery when you tax the GPU hard enough. That sounds awful, and it is. Acer could have easily sold the Nitro V 16 with a larger adapter. But the battery only drains in certain games and only when playing in Turbo or Performance modes. Stick to Balanced mode, and you'll be fine, as it only drops performance by around 5 percent. All said, I still think the MSI Cyborg A15 is the better laptop for this reason.
Lenovo Chromebook Duet Gen 9 for $379: Lenovo’s Chromebook Duet Gen 9 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) quickly became one of my favorite gadgets of 2024, despite its small size. That’s the whole point of this 11-inch detachable laptop, which is incredibly fun to use around the house and throw in a bag when it’s time to go. The keyboard detaches from the screen, so it makes for a nice tablet when paired with ChromeOS's Android apps. With the keyboard attached, you can get some work done. At nearly 10 hours on average, its battery life will easily get you through the day, too.
Cheap Laptops to Avoid
Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1: 16-inch laptops tend to be more expensive than smaller options, making them hard to find at a cheap price. The Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1 (6/10, WIRED Recommends) is a 16-inch laptop that tried to squeeze out just enough quality to make it worth the price. While the display has typical deficiencies (such as poor color coverage), I do appreciate that it doesn't have a matte finish, which brings out more clarity in the panel. I also found the keyboard tiresome to type on, and ultimately feel the OmniBook 3 is the better laptop for the price.
Asus Vivobook 14: As one of the first cheap laptops to use the Snapdragon X, I praised this laptop through 2025 for its excellent battery life. But once the OmniBook 5 and OmniBook 3 came along, I stopped recommending the Vivobook 14. That's primarily because of how much better the OLED screens are on the OmniBook devices compared to the washed-out display that comes on the Vivobook 14. But if you ever see this drop to below the price of the OmniBook 3 and want the cheapest Windows laptop possible, it might be worth considering.
What Are Important Specs in a Cheap Laptop?
Read our guide on How to Choose the Right Laptop if you want all the details on specs and what to look for. In short, your budget is the most important factor, as it determines what you can expect out of the device you're purchasing. Next, you should consider display size, chassis thickness, CPU, memory, storage, and port selection. While appropriate specs can vary wildly when you're considering laptops ranging from $200 to around $1,000, there are a few hard lines I don't recommend crossing.
For example, don't buy a laptop if it doesn't have a display resolution of at least 1920 x 1080. In 2025, there's just no excuse for anything less than that. You should also never buy a laptop without at least 8 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage. Even in Chromebooks, these specs are becoming the new standard. You're selling yourself short by getting anything less. Another rule is to avoid a Windows laptop with an Intel Celeron processor—leave those for Chromebooks only.
Specs are only half the battle, though. Based on our years of testing, laptop manufacturers tend to make compromises in display quality and touchpad quality. You can't tell from the photos or listed specs online, but once you get the laptop in your hands, you may notice that the colors of the screen look a bit off or that the touchpad feels choppy to use. It's nearly impossible to find laptops under $500 that don't compromise in these areas, but this is where our reviewers and testers can help.
How Much RAM Do You Need in a Cheap Laptop?
The simple answer? You need at least 8 GB of RAM, but you'll likely want at least 16 GB. These days, lots of Windows laptops that fall into the “budget” category come with 16 GB of RAM standard t, as part of the Copilot+ PC marketing push. That's a great value that ensures you'll get the best performance out of your laptop, especially when running heavier applications or multitasking. Either way, it's important to factor in the price of the RAM because manufacturers will often charge $100 or even $200 to double the memory.
On Chromebooks, there are some rare occasions where 4 GB of RAM is acceptable, but only on the very cheapest models that are less than $200. Even budget Chromebooks like the Asus Chromebook CX15 now start with 8 GB of RAM.
Prices are constantly shifting, however, largely because of the ongoing memory shortage. We are starting to see the return of 8 GB in laptops like the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13, but I recommend opting for 16 GB if at all possible.
Are There Any Good Laptops Under $300?
Yes, but you need to be careful. Don't just go buy a random laptop on Amazon for less than $300, as you'll likely end up with an outdated, slow device you'll regret having purchased. You might be tempted by something like this or this, but trust me—there are better options, some of which you'll find in this guide.
For starters, you shouldn't buy a Windows laptop for less than $300. That price puts you solidly in cheap Chromebook territory. These Chromebooks are budget-level in terms of quality, but they're still better in almost every way than their Windows counterparts of a similar price. A good example is the Asus Chromebook CX15.
If you want a Windows laptop that won't give you instant buyer's remorse, you'll need to spend at least a few hundred more. Once you hit $500 or $600, there are some more solid Windows laptops available, such as the HP OmniBook 3. Even in that case, though, you're making some compromises in features like touchpad quality and chassis thickness. But as a general principle, Windows laptops only start to become worth buying in the $500-plus range.
Should You Get a Cheap Windows Laptop or Chromebook?
The eternal question. If you're looking for a laptop for less than $500, I highly recommend that you opt for a Chromebook. I know that won't be a possibility for everyone, as some people require certain applications that require a Windows laptop or a MacBook. If you do decide to get a Chromebook, make sure all of your connected accessories and other devices are compatible.
Chromebooks give you access to a full desktop Chrome browser, as well as Android apps. While that leaves some gaps for apps that some may need, you might be surprised by how much you can get done without the need to install any software. Most applications have web versions that are every bit as useful.
While Chromebooks are most well-known as junky student laptops, the “Chromebook Plus” designation has filled in the gap between dirt-cheap Chromebooks and $800 Windows laptops. You'll find some great Chromebook Plus options in the $400 to $600 range that have better performance and displays and look a bit more like a modern laptop. The Acer Chromebook Plus 514 is a great example of this. You can read more about the differences between Windows laptops and Chromebooks here.

The Supreme Court on Thursday (August 13, 2026) criticised the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), the country’s food regulator, for not introducing front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food products indicating sugar, salt and saturated fat levels.
A Bench headed by Justice J.B. Pardiwala asked the FSSAI whether it did not want children to grow up healthy.
The hearing was based on a petition filed by the Kerala-based NGO, 3S and Our Health Society, seeking directions from the Centre to introduce front-of-pack warning labels.
“Are you taking the court for a toss?” Justice Pardiwala asked Additional Solicitor General Brijender Chahar on learning that nothing much had moved in the FSSAI on the issue of labelling.
“We are doing this in public interest. Keep it in mind. We are not doing it for ourselves. Why are you not abiding by our order? We know the pressure on you. Will you do it on your own or should we pass an order?” Justice Pardiwala asked the government side.
Mr. Chahar said one-third of enterprises were based on traditional food, exposing items like ‘namkeen’ to be categorised as unhealthy.
“You should be concerned about the health of young children. They are addicted,” Justice Pardiwala said.
An FSSAI affidavit had earlier said the front-of-pack labelling was in format with global practices and provided consumers with simplified information on nutritional content.

Dearborn had a documented local dispute over mosque loudspeakers used for the Islamic call to prayer in 2025. But local reporting described complaints about those broadcasts, not Muslims demanding that churches stop ringing bells.
In August 2026, a rumor recirculated on social media that Muslims in Dearborn, Michigan, demanded that churches stop ringing bells on Sundays.
One X post (archived) spreading the claim started:
In Dearborn Michigan: Muslims DEMAND submission!!
In Dearborn Michigan, Muslims are now demanding that CHRISTIAN CHURCHES stop ringing their bells on Sundays. This is real and their reasoning should terrify every Christian American.
Muslims are saying "According to Sharia Law, church bells cannot be louder than our Islamic call to prayer. We are the majority in this city and you HAVE TO respect us, our laws, and our religion."
Versions of the rumor spread across multiple social media platforms, including X, LinkedIn and Threads.
However, the rumor appeared to spread only through social media posts, which did not identify who allegedly made the demand, which church or churches were targeted, when it happened or where the quoted statement came from. We found 
We contacted the city of Dearborn for comment and asked whether it was aware of any incident matching the claim. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Complaints about mosque loudspeakers
The rumor may have grown out of a real, but different, noise dispute in Dearborn. Local reporting showed the city had recently dealt with complaints from some residents about mosque loudspeakers used to broadcast the Islamic call to prayer. In October 2025, Detroit-area news outlet WXYZ reported that some Dearborn residents had complained about outdoor calls to prayer that could be heard on loudspeakers throughout the city.
According to WXYZ, the Islamic Institute of Knowledge on Schaefer Road broadcast the call to prayer by loudspeaker twice a day for about two minutes. The outlet reported that Dearborn resident Andrea Unger had raised concerns at City Council meetings, saying she did not want to hear the loudspeakers in her yard or home.
The same report quoted Fouad Berry, a board member at the Islamic Institute of Knowledge, saying the mosque had stopped broadcasting the early-morning prayer after complaints came in "just to be respectful to the community." Also according to the report, Dearborn police Chief Issa Shahin said at an Oct. 7, 2025, City Council meeting that mosques could be cited if they used loudspeakers before 7 a.m. or exceeded permitted decibel levels.
Detroit news station WKBD also reported on the mosque loudspeaker complaints. According to that report, Unger presented a signed petition at a City Council meeting concerning the use of an outdoor loudspeaker at the Dearborn Community Center, one of several mosques in Dearborn that had received noise complaints.
WKBD reported that Dearborn officials conducted decibel tests at some mosques and found instances of a mosque violating the city ordinance. The outlet also reported that Nabeel Bahalwan, director of the Dearborn Community Center, said the mosque was within allowable noise limits and did not want to bother neighbors.
None of that reporting described Muslims demanding that church bells be silenced. Rather, it described residents' complaints about mosque loudspeakers and city officials' efforts to enforce Dearborn's secular noise rules.
Dearborn's noise rules
Dearborn's code also does not support the post's framing. The city's general noise regulation prohibits "unreasonably loud, disturbing, unusual or unnecessary noise" that disturbs or endangers the comfort, peace, health or safety of others. The provision does not mention Shariah, Islam, mosques, churches or church bells.
A separate section restricts the use of loudspeakers or similar devices between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. when the sound creates a noise disturbance across a residential property line. That rule applies to loudspeakers "for any purpose," rather than to one religion or type of house of worship.
What we know about Dearborn's demographics
The post's description of Dearborn as a "Muslim-majority town" was not supported by an official religious count.
Dearborn is known for its large Muslim and Arab American communities. However, the census-related figure often cited in coverage of the city concerns ancestry, not religion. Detroit news station WDIV reported that U.S. Census Bureau data showed people of Middle Eastern or North African ancestry made up 54.5% of the city's population. In other words, the 54.5% figure measured Middle Eastern or North African ancestry, not Muslim identity.
The federal government does not have an official count of Dearborn residents by religion. Pew Research Center has reported that U.S. census forms do not ask about religion, and that the decennial census has never directly asked Americans about their religion. The Census Bureau also has said (Page 22) it does not collect data on religious affiliation in its demographic surveys or the decennial census.
Some nongovernmental groups compile religious-demographic estimates. For example, the Association of Religion Data Archives' 2020 U.S. Religion Census includes data for the Detroit-Warren-Dearborn metropolitan area, but not a city-level count for Dearborn itself.
Snopes has previously fact-checked similar false claims tying Dearborn or Michigan communities to Islamic law, which is commonly referred to as Shariah. In 2017, we found that a viral image did not show a KFC in Dearborn using separate lines for men and women, but the photo was actually taken at a KFC in Saudi Arabia. In 2018, we investigated a claim from a satirical website that a so-called Shariah zone in Michigan had banned bacon and required women to wear burqas in public.

Nvidia to provide up to US$105 billion guarantee for OpenAI’s Ohio data centre
Leading technology firms are increasingly tying together chips, power and data centre development as they race to meet soaring AI demand
Nvidia has agreed to guarantee as much as US$105 billion in lease payments to help OpenAI secure a sprawling data centre in Ohio being developed by SoftBank-backed SB Energy, in one of the chipmaker’s largest infrastructure financing commitments.
The chip giant will also invest US$1.5 billion in SB Energy and secure up to 8 gigawatts of AI computing capacity at the site, where the data centre developer will build, own and operate a campus for OpenAI under a 20-year lease, the companies said on Monday.
The deal is the latest example of Nvidia financing the infrastructure built around its chips, a strategy that helps drive demand but has also raised questions about circular funding flows between the chip giant and its customers.
Nvidia has secured land and power for the facility in Pike County, Ohio, for an AI data centre with an initial capacity of 4.25GW, expected to come online in phases beginning in 2028. One gigawatt is enough electricity to power roughly 750,000 US homes.
The chip giant will exclusively provide AI compute infrastructure at the site and is providing credit support for land, power and shell construction tied to the initial capacity. It also has an option to secure the remaining 3.75GW.
Leading technology firms are increasingly tying together chips, power and data centre development as they race to meet soaring AI demand, while ageing grids, lengthy approval processes and scarce land and power capacity constrain new projects.

Nearly 6 in 10 professionals in India say their job title does not reflect their compensation, revealing a growing disconnect between recognition and reward in India’s workplaces, according to the latest quarterly hiring tracker of Indeed, a global hiring platform.
According to the survey, nearly 80% of professionalsbelieve title inflation, a practice where grand job titles are awarded without a corresponding increase in pay, has become common across industries.
Prefer compensation over title
The survey, conducted by Valuvox on behalf of Indeed in May and June 2026, reached 1,211 employers and 2,533 employees representing a mix of industries, organisation sizes, age groups, career stages, and locations across tier 1, tier 2, tier 3 cities, and rural India.
Nearly 1 in 3 professionals, who received a title change over the past two years, says it came with either no salary increase or an increment of less than 5%. Around 52% of professionals said they would choose a higher salary over a better designation when considering a new opportunity.
Interestingly, the survey shows that professionals are not dismissing titles altogether. Nearly 70% believe their designation plays an important role in shaping future career opportunities, while almost 73% feel a stronger title improves how potential employers perceive them. Around 57% also say their designation has a significant impact on their overall job satisfaction.
According to Indeed, these findings suggest that employees continue to value titles, but increasingly expect them to be backed by meaningful compensation and genuine career progression.
A strategic tool for employers
Around 57%of employers said their organisation uses senior-sounding or enhanced job titles to some or a great extent to attract or retain talent, signalling that designations are increasingly being used as a strategic talent tool, alongside compensation, especially when salary budgets remain constrained. Employers cite evolving market expectations and changing organisational structures as factors driving the use of more senior titles.
The findings suggest that while organisations view titles as one of several ways to recognise talent, employees continue to associate career progression most strongly with financial advancement.
“A job title has always carried professional identity. Titles remain meaningful because they signal opportunity and capability, but they are most effective when they reflect genuine career progression rather than becoming a substitute for it. Building that alignment will be increasingly important for organisations looking to attract and retain talent in a competitive market,“ said Sashi Kumar, Managing Director, Indeed India.

People are betting on wildfires on Polymarket. What could go wrong?
Lawmakers are warning that predictions markets could make a bad wildfire season worse.
The 2026 wildfire season on the West Coast is shaping up to be an especially bad one: In Oregon, more than 2 million acres have already burned, breaking a record set just a few years ago, in 2024. In neighboring Washington state, suburbs around the city of Spokane recently burned in an increasingly common example of fires reaching urban and suburban areas (as my colleague Caitlin Dewey covered recently). And the consequences are spreading far beyond where the fires are burning, with hazardous smoke from the Pacific Northwest drifting as far away as New England.
Much of this is a story about climate change, as increasingly dry, hot summers provide ample fuel for fires. But the crisis is also being made worse by the Trump administration: Staff cuts to the US Forest Service have left the agency stretched thin and unable to respond as effectively to fires, while a planned reorganization is also set to shutter Forest Service labs researching and tracking wildfires. EPA research into wildfires and wildfire smoke has also been slashed.
All of this — plus a Trump administration shift away from letting some fires burn themselves out, which has further increased the workload on wildland firefighters — has also resulted in a more dangerous fire season for firefighters; Reuters reported this week that firefighters are “being overrun by wildfires at the highest rate in two decades” — with months still to go until the end of the season.
Go a little deeper
As if the above weren’t enough to worry about, lawmakers are also raising a brand-new fire season concern: prediction markets. Specifically, the possibility that bettors could turn to arson in order to manipulate prediction markets — and earn themselves some money.
Polymarket, on its international platform, has offered users the chance to bet on everything from when and where a fire might spread to when it could be contained or extinguished, which resulted in more than $1 million in bets on major fires in California last year. High Country News reported in June that a new prediction market, called Wyldfyre, had launched specifically for betting on wildfires.
Legislators like Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR) have pointed out that, unlike most other natural disasters, fires are easily started or spread by humans, creating a real risk that people could attempt to manipulate markets.
“Offering bets on destructive wildfires threatens to minimize communities’ suffering all so the rich and powerful can profit,” Merkley and eight other Democratic senators wrote in a letter to the head of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission last week. “There’s also the heightened risk—according to state and local fire officials—that individuals could be tempted to commit arson in order to make sure their bets are successful. By offering contracts on fires, prediction market sites run the risk of encouraging people to influence fires that have already started, creating additional concerns around public safety and insider trading.
One link for later
➨ Build (your attention span) back better. Beset as we are by short-form video and tweets, it can often feel like our attention spans are slipping unavoidably away. The good news, it turns out, is that decline doesn’t have to be permanent — there are ways to rebuild attention, including by simply letting your brain rest more.

After a tweet about “30 to 50 feral hogs” went viral in August 2019, my former colleague Dylan Matthews embarked on a serious consideration of how the pigs impact the US — and how we impact them in turn. It’s still one of my favorite articles on the Vox site.

Flavorful, filling, actually delicious prepared meals delivered to your home. Meals designed by restaurant chefs. No microwave required. Wide variety of cuisines represented. Many meals delivered the same day they're packed.
TIRED
Quality and selection may differ depending on region and chef. Not all areas served. Must enter contact information before seeing the week’s menu.
My lunch felt impossible. Was my fried chicken actually … crispy and moist?
This result was by no means likely. After all, I'd received this chicken in a sealed microwavable tray three days ago, by courier from Seattle to Portland, Oregon. It seemed unlikely that my Night Market Chicken from meal delivery service CookUnity would stand up to the harsh light of day when reheated.
And yet, here we were. When heated in an air fryer, the chicken's breading was nicely crisp. The meat was tender, juicy even. The Asian-influenced sesame-soy glaze was pleasantly sweet and tangy, paired with a heaping portion of egg fried rice. If this had been takeout food from a restaurant down the street, I would have accepted it gladly.
In fact, a number of the meals I've tasted from CookUnity over the past two years have rivaled restaurant takeout—a genuine rarity among prepared delivery meals. Most of the big meal delivery services have branched out into ready-to-heat prepared meals, and I've tried most of them. CookUnity is the best I've tried by a pretty long margin, while maintaining similar prices: $12 to $13 a meal on the most common plans.
CookUnity stands out for two reasons. One is that it's less reliant on the microwave—offering alternate instructions that still usually only take five or 10 minutes. The other is that the meals are prepared in kitchens run by actual restaurant chefs, who each put their name and face on the box.
My tasty Night Market Chicken came from the Seattle commissary of Michelin-decorated LA chef Kevin Meehan. And while I doubt Michelin will come calling this time, it was a genuine prize winner among work lunches hoovered over my laptop. And while last year I worried that veggies were a rarity, this year CookUnity's meals have expanded in both quantity and variety.
Here's how it works, and my (quite good) results.
Specs
Cost per meal
$12 to $16 per meal, variable shipping depending on distance from hub
Meal plan options
Choose anywhere from four to 16 meals a week
Lowest-cost plan at full price
$74; four meals plus shipping
Size of weekly menu
Varies by hub; even small hubs offer 200+ meals.
Gluten-free meals?
On some weeks, half of meals might be listed as gluten-free
Plant-based meals?
About a fifth of meals are vegetarian or vegan
Other dietary plans or restrictions
Meal filters include high protein, low carb, keto, and GLP-1 balance
Prep time
A few minutes in the microwave, or maybe 15 minutes in an oven or on the stovetop
The Chef-Centric Delivery Model
The reason CookUnity is not like other prepared meal services is that, quite frankly, it's not like other prepared meal services. CookUnity is a singular model, something like a cross between a meal service and DoorDash.
Rather than make recipes in a top-down corporate kitchen, CookUnity is regional. The service enlists local and national chefs and promises to bring restaurant-quality meals to the home—prepared according to recipes from occasionally quite big names. (Hello, Jose Garces. Hello, Esther Choi.)
Like a lot of meal kits, CookUnity is a subscription service. You choose the number of prepared meals that you want delivered each week—and then pick out your meals from that week's menu. It's around $12 a meal if you get 10 portions a week—or more than $15 if you only want four meals. This is more than scratch cooking or a frozen dinner, but less than restaurant delivery or takeout.
The meal service is run out of eight regional commissary hubs around the United States and Canada: Seattle, LA, Austin, Chicago, New York, Atlanta, Miami, and Toronto. Each hub has its own stable of chefs: Some are local. Some are kitchens operated by national chefs. This does have the side effect of leaving out most of West Virginia and a good swath of the Plains states.
If your zip code is covered, it goes like this: You sign up for a certain number of single-serve meals per week, which arrive in heatable trays in a big, cold-packed box. A representative menu for each region is available here, but you won't see any given week's menu where you live till you've entered your zip code and handed out your email address. (I know, I don't love this either.)
Generally, if you order by Thursday, you can have delivery of your week's meals by Monday. Meals can be filtered for meal type (salad, meats and twos, pasta, et al.), vegan, vegetarian, GLP-1, fiber-rich, precise calorie counts (whether high or low), and a whole host of allergens. They can also be sorted by chef, and range from dainty 500-calorie lunches to 1,200-calorie feasts like that Night Market Chicken.
Each meal arrives in a tray that looks like a TV dinner, and I can microwave it in three minutes if I want. I usually don't, because each meal also has “chef-recommended” heating methods for optimal results. Maybe this involves a 10-minute turn in a toaster oven or a five-minute sauté. (Often, I sub in an air fryer where toaster ovens are suggested, with excellent results.)
Local Chefs, Local Menus
One of the most interesting things about CookUnity is that chefs and menus are different for each region. My hub, in Seattle, is among the smallest with only a dozen chefs. But because each chef offers anywhere from eight to 20 meals, my weekly menu in Seattle still ranged above 200 dishes. This is a far greater variety than when I first tried the service last year.
Many chefs expand nationally to multiple hubs. In Seattle, I can order sweet-sauced barbecue chicken herbed up with Haitian epis from Texas West-Indian chef Nahika Hillery, chicken adobo from Los Angeles chef Stacy Baraeng, or a summery udon from Esther Choi.
But my favorite dishes didn't come from the national chefs and celebrities—and indeed, the meat in a pork adobo from Baraeng came out a bit tough. What I loved best were the flavorful Indian gravies from Odisha-born Seattle chef Gaurav Raj, whether a lightly fiery chicken lababdar or a smooth and rich butter chicken.
At a lower cost, each of Raj's delivery meals consistently tastes better than the (admittedly not great) Punjabi restaurant down the street from me—less sugary, more rich, with saffron-tinged basmati and chicken that remains juicy and plump, not overcooked. Raj's Indian gravies offer the most compelling argument for me to order CookUnity, in a city (Portland) where the best Indian food is often a half-hour drive into the suburbs.
But, of course, Raj's meals are available only to those served by the Seattle hub. Others, near Los Angeles or Atlanta, may have other local chefs who offer similarly compelling arguments. I wouldn't know.
Local Mileage May Differ
The strength of CookUnity is that each regional hub is basically local. But this is also a potential weakness: Each regional hub is different. Each hub has greater or lesser variety. Each also has a different selection of chefs and meals.
But my good experience with the Seattle hub might translate to what you'll find in a different kitchen, with different cooks. This may be true even if the same chef's name and face are on your meal box. Some chefs operate four or five kitchens at different hubs, and different kitchens may have different results, even with the same recipes. And heck, I've had different results even from the same chefs. I can only speak to my own good experience and the good experience of my colleague Louryn Strampe, who ordered out of the Chicago hub.
Note that while CookUnity offers a much bigger caloric range than most prepared meal kits, usually the big feasts are heavily carb-loaded: rice, noodles, pasta. Those looking for a focus on proteins and veggies can find them easily, but usually in more moderate portions. Food cost is food cost. Starches are cheap.
But I have reason to believe that CookUnity's other hubs also offer good cooking—and that has a lot to do with CookUnity's business model. The overall factor that I think makes CookUnity work is healthy competition.
Each CookUnity chef making prepared meals is, essentially, a competing food business within the same big commissary kitchen. Their name is on each box, and a good number of the chefs have restaurants and reputations to protect. There are many incentives to make each meal interesting and delicious. My experience bears this out.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has approved 31 new applications under the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS), amounting to a cumulative ₹6,844 Cr. MeitY also cleared a further ₹1,033 Cr capacity expansion to existing beneficiary Wipro Global, taking the fresh clearance amount to ₹7,877 Cr. With this, MeitY has now approved 106 applications over the lifetime of the scheme. Capital goods led the allocation with five approved applications seeking ₹1,451 Cr in total. Optical transceivers and connectors followed suit in volume terms with three applications approved each. In terms of value, the second-largest application approved was one for manufacturing camera modules worth ₹740 Cr. Other high-value categories approved for investment included display modules (₹717 Cr), anode materials (₹582 Cr), and enclosures (₹565 Cr). The fresh approvals aim to create 9,588 jobs in the component manufacturing space across 10 Indian states. Out of 31 projects, Tamil Nadu leads the pack in terms of number of projects approved at seven. Maharashtra and Haryana accounted for six projects each, followed by Karnataka with five. Furthermore, the project pipeline is expected to generate ₹82,243 Cr worth of components in total production value. Some of the beneficiaries of the scheme include Kaynes Technology, Dixon Technologies, Wipro, and Tata Electronics. The scheme was launched in April 2025 and bids to build the country’s electronics component manufacturing ecosystem to a $500 Bn industry by FY32. Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman launched the scheme in April 2025 with an outlay of ₹22,919 Cr. The scheme offers a mix of incentives, including those linked to turnover and capital expenditure. Notably, the latest series of approvals has also enabled the ECMS programme to surpass its target metrics. While the scheme’s initial target in terms of approved investments was ₹59,350 Cr, this figure has now crossed ₹69,548 Cr. The Centre has also exceeded the cumulative production value target as of now, with the current projection surpassing ₹5.3 Lakh Cr as against the erstwhile target of ₹4.6 Lakh Cr. In terms of generating employment opportunities, the scheme has created 74,628 jobs against a target of 91,600 thus far. Union IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the scheme is accelerating the development of a robust localised electronics value chain and going beyond mere assembly into domestic manufacturing of critical components The approval of the previous batch of proposals under ECMS was announced back in March.

It was a busy first day at D23: The Ultimate Disney Fan Event, in Anaheim, California, with Marvel Studios releasing the first trailer for VisionQuest. We also got the first teaser for Ahsoka S2; the public release of the Avengers: Doomsday special footage featured last month for attendees only at San Diego Comic-Con; a special sneak peek (for attendees only) for Star Wars: Starfighter; casting news for the MCU’s X-Men movie; and a trailer for an animated special, LEGO Star Wars: The Mandalorian, coming to Disney+ next month.
(Some spoilers below. One MAJOR spoiler for Spider-Man: Brand New Day; we’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)
VisionQuest
Marvel’s streaming TV portfolio has kind of been all over the place: a handful of hits, a few misses, and a bunch of middling offerings. One of the standout hits was WandaVision, followed by an excellent sequel (of sorts), Agatha All Along. VisionQuest will complete the trilogy. Yes, Vision (Paul Bettany) died in Infinity War, but WandaVision resurrected an all-white version whose memories were restored in the finale. We finally get to learn what happened afterward.
Per the official premise:
Vision, rebooted and having escaped from those who sought to weaponize him, has been in hiding. Searching for new meaning, he consults the AI personas embedded in his programming, including F.R.I.D.A.Y., E.D.I.T.H., J.A.R.V.I.S., and the infamous Ultron. His discreet existence ends when a bounty placed on his head thrusts him on the run with Thomas Shepard, a mysterious boy who may be Vision’s son, reincarnate. As Vision evades capture, he must confront his nature, resist Ultron’s influence, and unravel the enigma that is his young companion if he’s to survive.
Naturally Bettany is returning as Vision, along with James Spader as Ultron. Agatha All Along gave us a new Billy Maximoff, whose soul took over the dying body of another teen as Wanda’s spell unraveled at the end of WandaVision. Fans may recall that Agatha helped Bill track down the soul of his twin, Tommy (aka Speed), and place him into the body of a teen boy who drowned, Thomas Shepherd. That storyline is clearly getting picked up in VisionQuest, since Ruaridh Mollica has been cast as Tommy/Thomas Shepherd. Bettany said last year that the series would explore “intergenerational trauma” with fathers and sons.

Trump envoy Kushner meets Hamas leader to push Gaza peace plan
- Published
US President Donald Trump's Middle East envoy Jared Kushner has held rare talks with Hamas to discuss the implementation of the US-backed Gaza peace plan.
A Palestinian official told the BBC Trump's son-in-law met a delegation led by Hamas's new leader Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt on Sunday.
Last month, Trump's Board of Peace said it had reached agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed group in Gaza. Last week, Israel rejected Trump's 15-point plan which also calls for Israeli troops to withdraw and for Gaza to be rebuilt under a new civilian Palestinian administration.
Eight Muslim countries issued a statement on Sunday condemning Israel's rejection.
Trump leads the Board of Peace - created as an international organisation originally intended to bring peace to Gaza, but later expanded to include conflicts worldwide.
Kushner's meeting with Hayya is said to be the first at this level since last year's agreement of a ceasefire for the Gaza Strip.
According to reports, Board of Peace envoys Nickolai Mladenov and UK ex-Prime Minister Tony Blair were also part of the meeting - alongside representatives of Egypt, Qatar and Turkey, which have mediated in the peace efforts.
No official statement has been released of the talks reportedly focusing on concrete actions to decommission Hamas's weapons - as well as the withdrawal of Israeli troops and humanitarian efforts.
Whilst in Egypt, Kushner also met Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi. According to Israeli media reports, Kushner, Mladenov and Blair will meet Netanyahu on Monday with the aim of advancing Trump's plan.
The Israeli prime minister has said he wants a full Hamas disarmament first in order to implement the deal.
"Israel rejects the Board of Peace's 15-point document on Gaza. The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed," Netanyahu said last week defying Israel's closest ally.
In a joint statement on Sunday, Egypt, UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Turkey, Pakistan and Indonesia said Israel's rejection of the US plan threatened Trump's efforts for peace.
The ceasefire, which came into effect on 10 October last year, remains in place.
However, the Israel Defense Forces have carried out several strikes in Gaza since then - the latest on "terrorists" in Khan Yunis and Nuseirat areas of Gaza - accusing Hamas of breaking the truce.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The UN estimates that about 1.9 million people - 90% of Gaza's population - have been displaced since the war started.

Uber aims for 1 million daily drone deliveries with Zipline partnership
The first Zipline drone deliveries for Uber Eats orders will start later this year.
You could soon get your Uber Eats order delivered by a Zipline drone thanks to the latest partnership between the two companies. As detailed in an Uber press release, the company is targeting a goal of one million drone deliveries each day by end of 2029. The partnering companies also announced that the first deployments are scheduled for later this year, with drone deliveries first becoming available in Zipline's existing US markets, including Pea Ridge, Ark. and the Dallas-Fort Worth metro, before expanding to dozens of more cities.
On top of the combination of Uber's network and Zipline's drone fleet, Uber made a strategic investment into Zipline but didn't disclose the financial details. Before this partnership, Zipline teamed up with Walmart and Chipotle to make food and retail deliveries. On its own, Zipline has delivered more than 2.7 million deliveries ranging from healthcare products to food.
It's not the first major investment Uber has made into drone deliveries, having partnered with Flytrex for Uber Eats in 2025. Beyond drones, Uber has partnered with companies Lucid and Momenta to offer robotaxis for autonomous ride-hailing services. However, Uber and Zipline will be directly competing with DoorDash and Wing, who kicked off their drone delivery partnership in 2022 and recently expanded their drone delivery service footprint to the metro Atlanta area.

Are some soldiers colluding with Nigeria's criminal gangs? A recent arrest prompts questions
- Published
A Nigerian soldier has been arrested over allegations he supplied military uniforms to "terrorist" and "criminal" groups, the army says.
Private Mohammed Yusuf was caught on Saturday evening at a bus stop in the north-eastern city of Maiduguri, military spokesperson Mohammed Goni said the following day.
The soldier, who was previously stationed at a factory for army equipment, was allegedly attempting to flee across the border into neighbouring Cameroon.
He deserted his unit earlier this month, Goni said, before relocating to Maiduguri, where he went into hiding with the help of an "associate".
Yusuf has not publicly commented on the case against him, but the arrest has reignited speculation that collusion could be the reason behind rampant insecurity in the country.
A variety of armed groups - including militant Islamists, separatists and gangs who kidnap civilians for ransom - have been causing problems for the authorities, and some of them deceptively wear military uniforms.
Now, in a nation that for over a decade has been blighted by armed attacks on civilians, people are wondering whether these assaults are failing to subside because criminal elements and security personnel are working together.
It is not unreasonable to believe some of these groups are being assisted by military personnel, Bashir Galma, a security analyst and retired army major, told the BBC.
"I know there have been instances where plans are made for an attack on a location and the information finds its way to either [militant Islamist group] Boko Haram or another criminal gang," he said, suggesting an insider tip-off.
At least 3,000 kidnappings and 3,580 killings by armed groups took place between January 2024 and April 2025 alone, data from Nigeria's National Human Rights Commission records
The alarming surge in mass abductions has been attributed to gunmen known locally as bandits, as well as insurgent attacks from Boko Haram and its offshoot, Iswap.
Attacks on schools have also been making the headlines, although this has been a problem for years. Between April 2014 and May 2026, there were 26 major school attacks with at least 2,416 students abducted, the International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) says.
Ransom payments are estimated to run into millions of dollars annually, according to official data.
In April 2025, the governor of Nigeria's embattled Borno state, Babagana Zulum, alleged that informants and collaborators for Boko Haram insurgents were operating within the country's armed forces, political class and local communities.
"What we need to do is to strengthen our intelligence and to deal with them ruthlessly," he said during a security meeting.
Months later, a special court-martial sentenced three Nigerian soldiers to life imprisonment for their involvement in a major arms and ammunition racketeering scheme. The army said they were guilty of theft, unlawful dealing in ammunition, and "aiding the enemy".
Security analyst Galma told the BBC he believes poor pay breeds such corruption within soldiers. There is also the "issue of ideology" - some personnel might hold a secret allegiance to other groups, he said.
A current serving soldier, who spoke to the BBC on the condition of anonymity, admitted that there have been instances of soldiers "caught dealing with the other side" but said such matters are often "hushed and dealt with internally".
One man, freed after his family paid a 57m naira ($42,000; £31,000) ransom, described a disturbing scene upon his release.
"They dropped us off in one location and there were security personnel who they shook hands and laughed with," he told the BBC, asking not to be named.
He believes the security forces he saw may have received a portion of the ransom, though he has no proof that this was the case.
Farmer Yahuza Isa, who was kidnapped in Zamfara state, expressed the frustration shared by many victims.
"I myself know where these criminals are," he said. "So why not deal with them completely?"
Another survivor, who endured a 30-day ordeal in late 2024, said he suspected collusion "at a much higher level".
He described hearing a helicopter landing very close to the hidden camp where he was held blindfolded.
"The first time I heard it I was expecting that the Nigerian Air Force... had come to rescue us," he said. "But we could hear the helicopter leaving afterwards."
He heard it several more times, leading him to believe the gangs had some form of high-level logistical cooperation.
Security expert Abdullahi Abdullahi said he believed armed groups are not just getting help from security forces, but from civilian informants.
"And that is why the issue is continuing after all these years," he said.
The persistent security challenges point to a failing system, but the arrest of Yusuf shows the military is – at the very least – acknowledging that the problem exists within its own ranks.
Whether that acknowledgment will translate into meaningful action remains to be seen.
Yusuf remains in custody, and investigations are continuing to determine the full extent of his alleged operation and whether others were involved.
The military's director of media operations, Maj Gen Markus Kangye, did not respond to a BBC request for comment.
