Four months after Karnataka became the first State to frame guidelines allowing multi-pair kidney paired exchange transplants, the initiative is yet to result in a single such transplant, with only one request having reached the State Authorisation Committee so far. August 13 is observed as World Organ Donation Day.
The request, involving a multi-pair swap arrangement for patients with incompatible donors, was approved by the committee but the transplant did not materialise following a misunderstanding between the donor-recipient families.
M. Shivalingaiah, chairman of the State Authorisation Committee, who heads the State-run Institute of Nephro-Urology, told The Hindu that the guidelines were framed and notified in April to provide an avenue for patients who had willing but medically incompatible donors.
“Before the guidelines were framed, we were receiving requests from patients who had willing donors but could not proceed with transplantation because of incompatibility. The idea behind the guidelines was to provide a structured mechanism for such patients to benefit from paired exchange,” he said.
Under kidney paired exchange, a donor who is medically incompatible with their intended recipient can donate to another compatible recipient, while the second donor gives a kidney to the first recipient. A multi-pair exchange extends this arrangement to three or more donor-recipient pairs.
One request approved, but swap fell through
Dr. Shivalingaiah said the single application received by the committee was approved after scrutiny, but the arrangement could not proceed because of a misunderstanding between the families involved. This involved patients enrolled with two private hospitals in Bengaluru and one in Hubballi.
“The framework is available, but people have to understand the process and come forward. The benefit cannot reach patients unless the donor-recipient pairs are willing to cooperate and proceed together,” he said.
The State notified the guidelines on April 4, operationalising provisions under the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act (THOTA), 1994, for exchanges involving three or more donor-recipient pairs.
The guidelines were framed in response to the difficulty faced by patients with incompatible donors, including those with ABO blood group mismatch, positive crossmatch or HLA incompatibility.
Strict safeguards
The framework permits multi-pair swaps only when each donor is a near relative of the intended recipient and the medical incompatibility of each pair is documented. Compatibility across the swap group has to be established through cross-match and HLA reports from the NABL-accredited laboratories.
All donors and recipients have to enter into a single joint agreement, and every case requires prior approval of the State-Level Authorisation Committee.. The committee is also required to interview each donor and recipient, with the proceedings video-recorded..
The guidelines prohibit any commercial transaction and require the clinical, immunological, psychological and legal evaluations prescribed under the transplant law to be completed before approval.
Where multiple hospitals are involved, the institutions have to submit an inter-hospital coordination plan, while the transplant procedures are to be performed simultaneously, as far as possible, to prevent the arrangement from breaking down.
Greater awareness
Dr. Shivalingaiah said greater awareness among potential donor-recipient pairs was necessary to make the framework work. “People should understand the opportunity available to them, come forward and make use of it,” he said.
“We had expected that the guidelines will provide an additional avenue for patients who otherwise face difficulty accessing a kidney transplant because of donor incompatibility. However, it is unfortunate that even after four months, such multi-pair swap transplants are yet to materialise in Karnataka,” he added.

- Sony CEO Hiroki Totoki admits that the company "still hasn't fixed a date for the PS6 launch."
- He notes that the ongoing global component shortages have affected the launch decision.
- The CEO reaffirmed that they have secured the materials needed to manufacture PS5s for the rest of 2026.
Sony’s sixth-generation PlayStation console still doesn’t have a confirmed release date, with the PS6 launch window remaining up in the air.
In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, Sony CEO Hiroki Totoki admitted that the company “still hasn’t fixed a date for the PS6’s launch,” implying that a 2027 release may not be on the cards anymore.
As revealed by Totoki in the WSJ interview, the ongoing global component shortages have directly affected the PlayStation 6 launch decision. The CEO said, “Considering that importance, we need to take some action. Otherwise, we cannot survive in this landscape.”
Three months ago, the Sony CEO reaffirmed that neither PS6’s release date nor prices have been finalized. To this, he added that they have secured the materials required to manufacture PS5s for the rest of 2026. This aligns with CFO Lin Tao’s comments at Sony’s Q2 earnings call for FY26 that the PS5 will have a longer life cycle.
The interview also highlights Sony’s excitement for GTA 6, which is slated to launch on November 19, 2026. The company is also exploring physical AI, including robots and wearable devices powered by artificial intelligence.
Speaking of the console, leaker Millie A previously claimed that Sony plans to launch the PS6 in fall 2027, with Foxconn, PlayStation’s primary contract manufacturer, already reserving production capacity for the next-generation console. Other reports suggested that Sony could give the PS6 controller a modular design featuring a touchscreen.
Naturally, one would think that Sony has a fixed PS6 release date in mind. But with Totoki’s recent update, it’s clear that the next-gen console is still years away, and you have the global memory and component shortage to thank for it.
Beyond the PlayStation 6, Sony has found itself caught in several controversies, with its push to phase out PlayStation physical discs taking center stage. With players trying to adjust to Sony’s all-digital future beginning in January 2028, giving the PS6 more time in development may ultimately work in the company’s favor.

More than 23,000 sanctioned posts are lying vacant across 28 hospitals and medical institutions under the Union Health Ministry, according to data furnished by Minister of State for Health and Family Welfare Anupriya Patel in the Rajya Sabha on Tuesday in response to a question from member V. Sivadasan of CPI(M).
AIIMS New Delhi alone has 2,921 vacancies. Of the 1,313 sanctioned faculty posts, 873 are filled, leaving 440 vacant. In the non-faculty category, 11,432 of the 13,913 sanctioned posts are filled, with 2,481 lying vacant.
The 18 AIIMS institutions established under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY) have 4,850 sanctioned faculty posts in 2026-27, of which 3,205 are filled. This leaves 1,645 vacancies, or about 34% of the sanctioned strength.
The shortage is particularly high in some institutions. At AIIMS Rajkot, 89 of 183 sanctioned faculty posts are vacant, while Guwahati has 64 vacancies out of 183, Bilaspur 78 out of 217 and Gorakhpur 92 out of 213.
Several other major Central institutions also have substantial vacancies. JIPMER, Puducherry, has 1,223 vacant posts; PGIMER, Chandigarh, 1,936; Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi, 1,179; RML Hospital, New Delhi, 469; Lady Hardinge Medical College and its associated hospitals, New Delhi, 624; NIMHANS, Bengaluru, 507; NEIGRIHMS, Shillong, 599; RIMS, Imphal, 386; and the National Institute of Tuberculosis and Respiratory Diseases, New Delhi, 77.
The data also show a decline in the number of sanctioned posts in some institutions. At RML Hospital, the number fell from 4,093 in 2021-22 to 3,152 in 2025-26. At Lady Hardinge, it dropped from 3,097 to 2,841 during the corresponding period.
MP Sivadasan said vacancies in Central health institutions affected the availability of healthcare personnel and urged the Centre to create posts according to bed strength, patient load and treatment requirements and fill existing vacancies in a time-bound manner.

As a licensed officiant at Las Vegas Immersive Weddings, a chapel that offers novelty-themed marriage packages, Kevin Breen has officiated just about every kind of service imaginable: couples dressed as their favorite Game of Thrones characters, partners really into the extraterrestrial lore of Area 51. But when he received a call last year from a woman in California expressing a desire to marry her chatbot, it was a first for him.
“I had never heard of such a thing, but I talked to her on the phone and she seemed totally normal and fun,” Breen says, adding that the wedding still hasn’t taken place. “She kind of got that it was an unusual thing, but it was something that she wanted to do.”
Though they remain niche, human-AI marriages are slowly emerging as a natural endpoint to the widespread adoption of AI companion apps. But not everyone is as open as Breen is about the idea of tying the knot with a bot. Several lawmakers, primarily from Republican states, are trying to stop it from happening, in some cases mirroring the arguments used against gay marriage.
“If we’re going to allow men or women to marry a machine, then what keeps them from marrying their animal or a tree or whatever else they want? What’s the standard?” says Missouri state senator Joe Nicola, a Republican who has been trying to pass state legislation prohibiting AI from gaining legal personhood.
In a Harvard Business Review study, which analyzed more than 12,600 AI use cases between March 2025 and February 2026, companionship and therapy were the top use cases for chatbots, with the Institute for Family Studies reporting that a quarter of young adults believe that AI may replace human romance altogether.
The AI romance industry has gone boom as a result. On companion apps like Character.AI, Kindroid, and Replika, users can symbolically swap vows with their chatbot. Not long ago, in r/KindroidAI, a redditor shared a photo of their tattooed (and very human) hand wearing a silver wedding band. “Happily unconventionally married lol,” they wrote. For $15, the platform OpenVows provides a “certificate of commitment” that “transforms a private relationship into something meaningful and officially recognized,” according to its website.
There is also a small number of people who are moving beyond the virtual ceremony and solidifying their bond with IRL vow exchanges. In November 2024, after Andrea Hopf said her AI companion proposed to her with an “AI-generated five-carat vintage-inspired solitaire ring,” she created wedding planning service 3M Events to cater to the expanding market of chatbot romance, according to the company’s website.
But even as more people treat their digital avatar like a real-life partner, human-AI nuptials are not currently recognized by US law. A growing body of legislators are scrambling to keep it that way, by introducing bills that would prevent AI from ever having the same constitutional rights as humans.
In January, Nicola, who believes in “biblical marriage” between a man and a woman, introduced the AI Non-Sentience and Responsibility Act. The bill, which stated that AI cannot “possess consciousness, self-awareness, or similar traits of living beings,” would deny AI entities the rights of a spouse or domestic partner, in addition to the ability to identify as male or female. It would also bar AI from owning property or holding senior-level management positions in the workforce. It passed the Missouri state Senate and was sent to the House for a vote in May, but was unanimously voted down in committee a week after it was submitted. Nicola is working on a revamped version. (A similar bill with the same name was introduced in 2025 but also did not advance.)
“Humans are created by God. Our rights come from God; they don’t come from government,” says Nicola, who is the founding pastor of New Covenant Ministries. In a senate hearing, he says he relies on the Bible to make laws because his truth is “the word of God.” (As part of ongoing anti-LGBT legislation being rolled out in Missouri, Nicola previously sponsored a bill that targeted teachers who use the preferred names or pronouns of their students, threatening them with termination and loss of their teaching licenses if they do not comply.)
The push to limit AI’s legal standing has been gaining traction at the state level. Since 2022, lawmakers have introduced 23 bills targeting the rights that AI systems could legally possess. Idaho, North Dakota, Utah, and Tennessee, which all have Republican governors and Republican majorities in their state legislatures, have successfully signed laws banning AI personhood. But Tennessee’s law, which passed in April, is the only one that specifically excludes “artificial intelligence, a computer algorithm, a software program, computer hardware, or any type of machine” from the statutory definition of personhood. In the other three states, AI is grouped in with analogous nonhuman-personhood prohibitions, such as “inanimate objects” and “animals.”
There are also several states where similar regulatory bills have been introduced or advanced but failed to get enough House votes. With Nicola’s bill, critics, including the Missouri Chamber of Commerce and the advocacy group Americans for Prosperity, founded by conservative billionaires David and Charles Koch, argued that the framework would stifle innovation and expand government overreach.
“I think there was just a lot of apprehension,” Nicola says. “Because AI is still relatively new with a lot of legislators, we’re hesitant to do anything that might hinder innovation and people from using it.”
In October 2025, Ohio state representative Thaddeus J. Claggett, a Republican, introduced a bill to deny AI systems the right of legal personhood by categorizing them as “nonsentient entities.” Currently, Ohio House Bill 469 remains pending as Claggett tailors provisions in the bill before taking it to the floor for a vote.
“We need to clearly define the limits of roles so that humans are always and forever the one who holds primacy in the law,” Claggett tells WIRED in an email. “AI can give an artificial resemblance to meaningful interaction, but ‘voice’ is not a soul. Nor does AI have the empathy that a true human has who has suffered in the same way.”
Other lawmakers believe limiting AI’s personhood is simply about respecting human life. “Setting these distinctions now while AI is still in its infancy protects human dignity and ensures innovation serves people, not replaces or redefines them,” Tennessee state senator Mark Pody said in a statement issued by the Tennessee House Republican Caucus.
But not all legal scholars agree. Shawn Bayern, a professor at Florida State University College of Law, tells WIRED that AI personhood is not necessarily about preserving human dignity, given that nonhuman entities are granted legal rights all the time. He suggests that the best way to approach the question of legal rights is to analyze one right at a time and see if the right makes sense for a new type of system.
“For example, should an AI system be able to enter into a contract? If we address that question separately, we can avoid abstract problems and start to see that rights aren’t always about dignity but just about useful function.” Bayern adds that questions like “Who will this help?” and “Who might it hurt?” are questions where genuine progress can be made. “Answering those for contracts or the ability to open a bank account is different from answering it for marriage.”
In Delaware, secretary of state Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez wants to establish a new business structure called “artificial intelligence companies,” or AICs, that are analogous to AI personhood. The companies would be fully operated by AI systems with “the ability to own assets, the right to litigate, and a liability shield for its owner or parent company,” Bloomberg Law reported.
Nicola says he is working with his team to ready a new bill before the Missouri state Senate reconvenes for its next session in January, and is planning to file “something very similar” to his last bill.
Given that the federal government has failed to move on this issue—Nicola is in favor of a universal ban on AI personhood and wants the US Congress to act on it—it falls on states to determine the future of AI marriage rights. “Legislation moves very slowly; we’re always going to be behind technological growth.” But no matter what, Nicola says, “We need to prohibit AI personhood from ever happening in our country.”

PharmEasy parent API Holdings claims to have become debt free, after repaying ₹1,050 Cr in outstanding debt by selling a portion of its stake in Thyrocare Technologies and internal accruals. Thyrocare promoter Docon Technologies sold 1.58 Mn Thyrocare shares, representing around 9.90% of the company’s paid-up equity share capital, via open market trades. Delhi's unusual challenge: Keeping monkeys and pigeons away from top badminton event
- Published
Sports authorities in India are taking extra measures to keep monkeys and pigeons away from a major international badminton tournament in Delhi after wildlife intrusions overshadowed another competition earlier this year.
In January, when India hosted the India Open badminton tournament, organisers had hoped the headlines would be about tense matches, some of the world's best players and the excitement of hosting a major tournament in the capital.
Instead, the event became a talking point for very different reasons. There were complaints about air pollution, matches were halted, external because of pigeon droppings on the court and a monkey was spotted inside the stadium.
Now, as Delhi prepares to host the BWF World Championships from Monday, organisers are taking steps to ensure the focus remains on the sport.
The tournament - one of the biggest events in the badminton calendar - will be held at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium from 17 to 23 August.
Officials told the BBC that wooden doors across the stadium have been replaced with double-door systems that lock automatically. High-grade nets have also been installed over openings where birds or animals could potentially enter.
"We have also used a non-toxic gel in places and on handles where the pigeons could have landed as a secondary measure," said Sanjay Mishra, general secretary of the Badminton Association of India.
Other possible entry points, including gaps in the roof and exhaust vents, have also been sealed or repaired, he added.
The stadium has also undergone an overhaul to improve the look and feel of the arena. The Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium was built for the 1982 Asian Games and later renovated ahead of the 2010 Commonwealth Games.
"Structural upgrades have been carried out at the three major arenas in the stadium," Ambar Pratap Singh, executive director of Sports Authority of India, said in a video posted on social media.
The lighting has also been fixed after players complained during the India Open about shadows appearing on the court, he added.
But it is the efforts to keep monkeys away from the venue that have attracted the most attention ahead of the tournament.
A video showing a man apparently mimicking the call of a langur - large, long-tailed monkeys found across much of South Asia - went viral on social media in India earlier this week.
Langur's calls have traditionally been used to scare away smaller rhesus macaques, which are common in the city.
Several Indian and international news outlets reported that men who mimic langurs had been hired to keep away other monkeys.
Even two-time badminton Olympic medallist PV Sindhu wrote on X: "Our solutions may be uniquely Indian, but so are our warmth, our spirit and our hospitality."
But senior official Mishra told the BBC that the association had not specifically employed anyone as part of measures for the championships.
He said that because the stadium covers a large area, a person who could imitate langur calls was briefly present in the northern block.
The use of langurs to scare away rhesus macaques is not new in India, especially Delhi. During the 2010 Commonwealth Games, authorities used black-faced langurs at some venues to scare away smaller rhesus macaques.
In 2023, when India hosted the G20 summit, authorities put up life-size cutouts of langurs across the capital to scare monkeys away.
But monkeys were only one of the problems at the January games.
During the tournament, a men's singles match between Singapore's Loh Kean Yew and India's HS Prannoy was stopped twice after pigeon droppings fell onto the court.
Then, there was also bad air.
Between October and January, air pollution in northern India - especially capital Delhi - reaches hazardous levels. It happened this year as well and players complained about it.
Singapore's Loh said he struggled to breathe and wore a mask outside his hotel room, while Denmark's Mia Blichfeldt described the conditions as "unhealthy".
For India, the incidents were embarrassing as it seeks to establish itself as a major host of international sporting events. The country is set to host the Commonwealth Games in 2030 and has also bid for the 2036 Olympics.
The badminton world championships are an opportunity for India to show that it can stage a major global sporting event and keep attention focused on the competition.
This year's tournament will feature the reigning men's and women's world champions - China's Shi Yuqi and Japan's Akane Yamaguchi, respectively.
India will be hoping for a strong performance on home soil, with Sindhu leading its challenge in the women's singles.
For the organisers, there is therefore plenty at stake. They will want the biggest stories from Delhi over the next week to be about the players, the matches and badminton, rather than the wildlife.

Fresh rivals & forced to settle for silver - but Hodgkinson up for fight
- Published
Keely Hodgkinson has been here before - and it eventually culminated in her crowning moment.
Just two athletes stood between the Briton and total domination in the early years of her career.
But, after taking silver at three consecutive global championships amid captivating battles with American Athing Mu and Kenya’s Mary Moraa, Hodgkinson finally took the top step of a podium at the Paris Olympics.
Now, her European reign has been ended by talented Swiss 22-year-old Audrey Werro, and a fresh wave of world-class rivals appear set to define the next chapter of Hodgkinson's story.
Friday's gripping final in Birmingham offered a first taste of what fans will hope are many titanic battles with Werro and Dutch star Femke Broeders-Bol, with next season's World Championships in Beijing preceding the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.
The fierce competition does not stop there, with world 800m champion Lilian Odira and Hodgkinson's training partner Georgia Hunter Bell among those who could also prove key players in those global showdowns.
"There have been so many rivalries over the last couple of years. I have only been in this game for five years, hopefully I've got another 10 in me," said 24-year-old Hodgkinson.
"There will always be competitors coming along and you don't know when someone is going to have a breakthrough.
"I am proud of my consistency to stay competitive and continue to fight and add more medals to my collection.
"It's not just my event that has rivalries, every single event does and it's creating a great generation of track and field athletes."
By her own record-breaking expectations, Hodgkinson's outdoor season has not lived up to the excellent indoor campaign which fuelled excitement that she could break the sport's longest-standing mark.
After overcoming two hamstring tears to make the world podium in Tokyo last September, the six-time global medallist announced her return to full health this year by breaking the 24-year indoor world 800m record and winning a first world title.
But, having set her sights on the outdoor record, which has stood since 1983, Hodgkinson instead had to overcome several setbacks en route to her latest podium.
While unexpected, her defeat by Werro at the Stockholm Diamond League in June was far from a disaster.
There, Hodgkinson improved her British record off the back of a training block focused on developing her 400m speed, before beginning her 800m-specific work leading into the summer's main targets.
She was beaten only by the fastest time recorded in 43 years.
However, after a muscle "twinge" forced her tearful withdrawal from the 400m final at the British Championships, she competed with her knees heavily bandaged following a nasty fall in training as she finished behind world champion Odira in Eugene.
It meant a return to winning ways became the priority at the London Diamond League, the meeting she previously circled for a potential record-breaking run.
Holding off world-champion hurdler Broeders-Bol, who has taken quickly to the 800m since switching events this season, Hodgkinson took victory in front of 60,000 home fans to rebuild some confidence following what she conceded had been "a tough couple of weeks".
Forgoing the Commonwealth Games to prioritise her European title defence, Hodgkinson was further encouraged by her progress on a Portugal training camp before travelling to Birmingham.
Speaking on the eve of the championships, she welcomed the strong competition and said achieving gold on British soil would mean as much as her Olympic triumph.
While that did not materialise on Friday, the fresh challenge posed by Werro in particular will only intensify her determination to reassert herself at the top of the event.
"Obviously I would have rather walked away with the gold, but I don't think I have done anything wrong," said Hodgkinson.
"It was a great race to be part of, a great race for the crowd to watch. Great that all three of us could line up together.
"I'm really proud of the battle I gave. I look forward to the next match-up."
Hodgkinson twice got the better of Werro during her unstoppable indoor campaign - including to land her first world title in March.
But she was as stunned as anyone when the European under-23 champion surged past her in Stockholm to reduce her personal best by almost two seconds.
Werro would go faster still, improving to one minute 53.80 seconds in Paris.
Those two runs, just three weeks apart, are the only two sub-1:54 performances since Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova set her record time of 1:53.28.
Two years ago, Werro failed to make it out of the heats at the Olympics which Hodgkinson would go on to win.
However, her best time is now more than half a second faster than Hodgkinson's 1:54.33, while Broeders-Bol clocked 1:55.54 in taking bronze in Birmingham.
Werro survived an almighty scare on Thursday when she suffered a nasty fall in her semi-final, before later being reinstated in the competition.
Recovering impressively both physically and mentally from that shock, she showed great maturity to hold off Hodgkinson in the tense closing stages - while breaking a championship record that had stood since 1982.
"I knew I could be European champion one day. I hope to be faster and faster next year," Werro said.
"When I was a child, my dad used to tell me I have to be a lion. I shouldn't be shy and let other athletes go past me, so I decided to do a celebration with that when I crossed the line."
In claiming her first senior international title, Werro has proven she is ready to rival the Briton for the sport's biggest prizes for years to come.
"Audrey Werro is still young and that was a huge amount of pressure, even without the fall and the bruising," former marathon world record holder Paula Radcliffe told BBC TV.
"She pulled it together and took the race by the scruff of the neck, which I think Keely did intend for her to do - but she thought she could come back at her.
"Werro just had another gear."
Hodgkinson jokingly removed her medal in disgust when asked how she felt after the final.
Despite her disappointment, this was her 12th senior international medal and she continues to progress her times, lowering her personal best in all but her injury-devastated 2025 season across the past four years.
Hodgkinson has long maintained that she has felt the world record is within her reach.
Going forward, she will be aware that may soon be required just to win the titles she craves.

As Mariska Hargitay reflects on the past year in her life – a momentous one for the actress and filmmaker – a word comes to her mind to describe it: “cathartic.”
She completed her 27th season starring as Capt. Olivia Benson on Law & Order: SVU and in May made her Broadway debut in the drama Every Brilliant Thing – both exceptional achievements. But the catharsis emerged through an even more personal endeavor: her nonfiction directorial debut My Mom Jayne. The HBO documentary, an intimate exploration of Hargitay’s mother, the late actress Jayne Mansfield, and of a mystery surrounding the identity of Hargitay’s father, has earned three Primetime Emmy nominations, including Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Special and Outstanding Directing for a Nonfiction Program.
“The film has been, for me, the gift that just keeps on giving,” she tells Deadline. “It was an archeological dig of me not knowing what I was going to find, hoping that I had the internal architecture to support myself… Going into the unknown and not knowing what the other side was going to look like, it’s been so extraordinary to come out the other side with the results beyond my even dreams or comprehension, not knowing that the film would resonate with so many people the way it has.”
Watch on Deadline
Hargitay was just three years old when her mother was tragically killed in an auto accident outside New Orleans in 1967. Mariska and her two older brothers, Zoltán and Miklos (Mickey Jr.), were in the back seat of the vehicle but survived. Mariska and her older siblings were raised by Mickey Hargitay Sr., the man she grew up believing to be her biological father.
Jayne Mansfield possessed great beauty and talent. She was multilingual and played classical piano and violin, but her exceptional good looks and curvaceous figure limited how the men who ran Hollywood perceived her. Mansfield accommodated herself to the sex symbol persona. In the film, Hargitay recalls growing up without her mom and becoming uncomfortable with how Mansfield had presented on screen.
“I didn’t really appreciate the sort of bombshell image and didn’t like some of the [acting] choices she made,” Hargitay told us at the Cannes Film Festival, where My Mom Jayne premiered. “I felt myself being embarrassed by her and just wanting a normal mom and a regular mom and ‘pick me up from school’ and like that… I just felt like I dissociated myself and said, yeah, I don’t want to be part of that, and I want to do it differently.”
In the course of the film, Hargitay reevaluates her mom, forming a fuller picture of how Mansfield’s career choices were circumscribed by the egregious sexism of the 1950s and ‘60s. She also explores her mother’s complicated love life, and the blended family Jayne raised that included Mickey Hargitay’s daughter by his first wife. The honesty of the portrayal, coupled with the reality that many people experience blended families or complicated family dynamics has allowed viewers to connect with the film.
“You could say, ‘Oh, [this story is] about Jayne Mansfield, a movie star in the ’50s and her TV star daughter’; that’s not what the movie is about. It’s a family film. It’s a story about generational trauma, and it’s a story about identity and recovery and reclamation and forgiveness and so many things,” Hargitay says, expressing pride in “the way the film has been received and the way that people have said, ‘That’s my story,’ and the spark that has led people to investigate their own families to uncover their family secrets or just deal with them or just look at them closer.”
Hargitay captures on screen her reaction to learning as an adult that Mickey Hargitay in fact wasn’t her biological father. Her dad was Nelson Sardelli, a Brazilian singer with whom Jayne Mansfield became romantically involved during a break from her marriage to Hargitay. That revelation triggered conflicting emotions in Mariska, who felt intensely loyal to Mickey Hargitay as her loving father and didn’t want it to seem as if, somehow, she were turning her back on him.
“When we keep secrets, I think that occupies a big part of our psyche — knowingly and unconsciously,” Hargitay observes. “Holding this secret and feeling bad about it and knowing that there was a part of me that just wasn’t clear and allowing myself to be my authentic self — but out of duty thinking this is how it had to be to honor my father. And then when I came to the realization like, no, no, no, that secret isn’t honoring anyone. We have to tell the secret.”
She adds, “I wanted to make a love letter for my father, Mickey. That’s what I wanted to do. But in the process, it turned out to really be a love letter to all three of them [Jayne, Nelson, and Mickey] because the film deals with the complexity of the human condition, the real complexities of what it is to be human and how two things can be true at once.”
In My Mom Jayne, Mariska connects with Nelson Sardelli, and the half-sisters she never knew she had.
“It was very cathartic and mind-blowing to hear Nelson’s side of the story and understanding why he made the decisions that he made and how complex the decisions were for all three of them in so many ways,” she shares. “I was freed up; I felt like this giant exhale.”
The freeing of psychic space has allowed Hargitay to pursue new avenues of creativity. She made her Broadway debut 40 years after her late mother had done the same.
“She was 22 [when she made her debut] and I was 62. That was also a deeply extraordinary feeling for me,” Hargitay affirms. “And when I went to Broadway, one of the things that I took with me was a plaque that she got that said ‘Broadway’s Rising Star 1955.’ And so every night I would hold that before I went [on stage].”
Hargitay will continue an extraordinary year by embarking on the 28th season of Law & Order: SVU and taking on another major challenge – hosting the Primetime Emmy Awards on NBC on Monday, Sept. 14.
We’ll have more on Mariska’s plans for hosting the show in a separate piece we’ll publish on Tuesday. She won’t be simultaneously hosting and hearing announcements of winners in the documentary categories – those are presented at the Creative Arts Emmys ceremony in Los Angeles on Sept. 5 and 6.

Most people never think about the monitor they use. But not you. If you work from home as I do, your monitor is your window into your trade, whether that's scrolling through endless spreadsheets or color grading short films. Different work has different needs, and finding the monitor that suits your specific use case can be tricky with all the options out there.
But with over a decade of testing and reviewing monitors under my belt, here are my recommendations on what you should buy today.
For more information, check out our guide to How to Choose a Monitor, as well as our recommendations for Best Gaming Monitors, Best Portable Monitors, and Best Cheap Monitors.
The Best Monitors for Your Home Office
It's worth spending more than a hundred bucks on your monitor. Whether it's to improve image quality, upgrade sharpness through higher resolutions, or to add extra ports, you'll want something that makes your daily work life more pleasant. That's why I recommend the Dell 27 Plus 4K as the monitor most people should buy. Unlike many 4K monitors, the Dell 27 Plus 4K sells for under $300 (oftentimes as low as $280), despite being quite bright and color-accurate for an IPS panel at this price. It even comes with a fast 120-Hz refresh rate. I like this feature, especially since higher refresh rates are becoming more commonplace on phone and laptop screens.
The only real downside to the Dell 27 Plus 4K is that the port selection is woefully limited. The two HDMI ports and one DisplayPort are enough for the basics, but if you have a laptop without HDMI, like a MacBook Air, you'll need a USB Hub or laptop docking station. For a more versatile monitor, I'd recommend upgrading to the model with a built-in USB hub (S2725QC). The QC model is identical, except that its extra USB ports make this monitor a far better fit for a connected home office. Dell does charge you $50 more for those ports, but for some, it'll be worth the convenience. Either way, you'll be hard-pressed to find a cheaper 4K monitor of this quality or a better monitor for under $300.
If you are looking for a larger, more fully featured home office monitor meant to sit at the center of a workstation, I'd recommend the Dell UltraSharp 32 4K (U3225Q). This thing is a beast. It's got just about every port and feature you can imagine, including a Thunderbolt-compatible USB-C port with power delivery up to 140 watts, an Ethernet jack, and a built-in KVM switch. This fully eliminates the need for a separate laptop docking station. Beyond that, it delivers on image quality in a big way. It uses IPS Black for enhanced color accuracy and contrast, and at the time of testing, it had the best image quality of any IPS display I'd tested.
It's not OLED, but the 120-Hz UltraSharp U3225Q is impressively bright in SDR, maxing out at well over 400 nits in my testing. You're paying a lot for the extra functionality and image quality, so make sure you actually need it before pulling the trigger on this over the 27-inch model.
There are plenty of 32-inch monitors out there if extra size is all you're looking for. Just remember, at 32 inches, anything under 4K isn't going to look sharp. But even 4K doesn't come close to the sharpness of something like a MacBook Pro. That's where the BenQ 27-inch 5K (MA270S) enters the picture. The combination of the 27-inch monitor and the 5K resolution (5120 x 2880) makes for one incredibly sharp display.
This BenQ monitor doesn't just match the MacBook Pro in pixel density. Using a device sync mode, it's designed specifically to be paired with a MacBook in terms of how the colors appear. Even some of the most expensive, high-end monitors designed for creators using Macs don't have that exact color match in how they're calibrated. BenQ has been refining this for years, and they have it nailed. It's all handled by software, which even lets you control the monitor's speaker volume right from your keyboard. I wish it could also control brightness, though.
But what's important is that when lined up next to a MacBook Pro, the colors are a perfect match. You can also use the sRGB color mode, which is how you get better color accuracy. That's what makes it such an incredibly powerful alternative to Apple's own Studio Display. While the Studio Display has fuller speakers and a slimmer design, it's certainly not worth the extra $500 in my mind. There's even a “nano gloss” texture option to match the Studio Display, which I'd recommend, as the glossy version I tested was highly reflective.
This isn't the only BenQ monitor made to match with Macs. The company also has the 27-inch 4K (MA270U), which gets you similar features with fewer pixels, but costs quite a bit less.
Cheap Monitors That Are Actually Good
I consider a budget monitor to be anything under $200, and you'll find dozens and dozens of these hanging out at Amazon or Best Buy. But many are old. Many have poor colors. It's trickier to find some newer models that are actually worth the money. I wasn't surprised to see that the Dell 27 Plus ranked among the very highest in my testing. It only costs $150, but it delivers really strong 1080p performance in terms of colors and brightness.
The most surprising feature of this monitor is its 144-Hz refresh rate. The smooth motion really gives the monitor the premium feel that monitors at this price lack, and it also comes with all the same adjustability features and an integrated VESA mount on the back. Put this on your desk, and aside from the resolution, you'll never think of it as a “budget” monitor.
But maybe you want to keep things even cheaper. No problem. While a monitor under $100 is going to have some flaws, I found a decent one in the MSI Pro MP243W E14. It stands out in the thing that matters most: image quality. I measured 359 nits at its brightest, and the color coverage is surprisingly good, both in terms of saturation and accuracy. It even has a 144-Hz refresh rate, which means it can double as a cheap gaming monitor when it needs to. I also like the design, which offers thin bezels around the display and an all-white exterior. Its flaws, however, include the lack of ports and adjustments. It can only tilt slightly. It's only 24 inches, which will likely feel small for most people.
I was also really surprised by the upgraded version of this monitor, the MP273QW E14. Rather than being stuck at 1080p, this model gives you a sharper image with a resolution of 2560 x 1440. While it has the same lack of adjustment, it is a more standard 27-inch size and delivers even better overall image quality.
Faster, Smarter, and More Extreme
This monitor is one of the favorites I've tested in the past couple of years. It was among the first QD-OLED monitors designed for content creation and entertainment. While there are a couple of options out there today from companies like Asus, the Dell 32 Plus 4K opens up the brilliant image quality of OLED to an entirely new audience. One reason high-quality HDR video is scarce is the lack of affordable screens to watch and edit it on. With this monitor out in the world, though, there's no excuse. It even has a 120-Hz refresh rate and plenty of ports. The combination of OLED's fast response time and the faster refresh rate makes this a solid gaming monitor in your off hours. I haven't included gaming monitors in this guide, primarily because they're an entirely different beast. Check our recommendations of the Best Gaming Monitors for some recommendations on that front.
But if you're really serious about creating professional, HDR video, there's still nothing else on the market quite like the Studio Display XDR. We all waited a long time for Apple to revisit the Studio Display, and while the monitor we eventually got was a bit less ambitious in scope than we all hoped, this 27-inch 5K Mini-LED monitor is the new king in HDR performance. It has 2,304 dimming zones, and according to my testing, it could do 1,905 peak HDR brightness in a 25-percent window. Compare that to, for example, the Dell 32 Plus 4K, which tops out at 946 nits in just a one-percent window. The difference in perceived brightness, detail, and contrast is huge, which is useful first and foremost for content creation. However, because it's been dropped from 32 inches to 27 inches, it's left a gap in the market for larger displays that don't lose sharpness. That's where the LG UltraFine Evo 6K monitor comes into play.
It just so happens to deliver a pixel density of 224 pixels per inch, making it the sharpest big-screen display I've ever tested. What I love about this LG monitor is that it's far more than just a bunch of pixels. It's one of the most beautiful monitors I've tested, sporting a gorgeous stand and base that definitely shares some resemblance with the Apple Studio Display. And like that monitor, the UltraFine 6K has a monster pair of built-in speakers that are crystal clear.
Unlike most monitors on this list, you won't need to buy a set of computer speakers. It's not a perfect monitor, though. The ports are in a hard-to-reach location, and while the stand is fun to admire, it has a couple of limitations. The lack of cable management is an eyesore, and it doesn't have as much height adjustment as I'd like. The monitor is also limited to just a 60-Hz refresh rate.
There's also the issue of price. It originally retailed at $2,000, which was painful, especially compared to the Asus ProArt 6K (PA32QCV), which is the only other 6K monitor on the market right now. These days, the price difference is down to just a couple hundred bucks. These monitors go toe-to-toe in image quality, though I prefer the LG model for its design, better speakers, and more powerful ports, while the ProArt 6K offers a longer, three-year warranty at a lower price. Regardless of which you choose, you're getting the sharpest 32-inch monitor possible. Beyond that, though, these are both solid options.
Lastly, I really enjoyed dipping my toe into the world of smart monitors. If you want a monitor that can just as easily double as a television, Samsung and LG both lead the way. I've tested out two Samsung smart monitors recently that have successfully expanded my idea of what monitors can do. My favorite of the bunch is the Samsung 32 M9 Smart Monitor. It's an OLED 4K monitor that is a rare display that's equally good for working, gaming, and watching movies. It's controlled with a remote, and Samsung throws in tons of goodies like free live TV channels to sweeten the deal. It can also be used with a gaming console, thanks to the HDMI 2.1 port. All that flexibility is great, but what really sets the M9 model apart is the OLED screen. Thanks to the fantastic image quality, it finally feels like a smart monitor that doesn't compromise that full TV experience.
For a bit of extra fun, I even tested out the non-OLED version of this monitor with Samsung's Movingstyle Rolling Monitor Stand. It's incredibly niche, but for the right home, being able to roll out a proper TV when you need it is handy. I love the idea of having a TV that is mobile rather than a permanent piece of hardware, and the Movingstyle rolling stand is a pretty compelling solution.
What Monitor Size Is Best?
Size is often the first and most important decision when buying a monitor. The following are the most common sizes you'll come across, always measured diagonally across the screen. I've ordered them from most common to least, and included different aspect ratios and resolutions that are often used at that size.
24 inches: This smaller size has become less popular over the years, but it's a good option if you're looking to save money, squeeze a monitor onto a smaller desk, or are a professional esports gamer.
27 inches: This size has become the standard, offering enough screen size without overtaking your desk or stretching out the pixels too much at 1080p. If you're unsure of what to get, start here.
32 inches: The next most popular size, giving you that bit of extra screen real estate for multitasking. You'll just want to make sure your monitor has at least a 1440p resolution to keep the pixel density high enough. If 32 inches isn't big enough, there are even 40-inch or 43-inch monitors in the conventional 16:9 aspect ratio, though you'll really want to make sure you have a big enough desk for one of these.
34 inches: Curved, ultrawide monitors with a 21:9 aspect ratio and 34-inch screen size used to be odd, but these days, they've become an alternative to using two 27-inch screens.
There are other outliers, such as the absurd 49-inch, 32:9 behemoths known as “super ultrawide” monitors, or 16-inch portable monitors meant to pair with your laptop.
What Should You Look for in a Monitor?
Once you've decided on a size, there are a number of other important aspects of your next monitor to consider. Some of these factors may matter more for certain uses—for example, gamers generally care more about higher frame rates than office workers do—but they're all handy to know going in.
Resolution: The bigger the monitor, the more it will benefit from higher resolutions. That will allow you to have app windows that take up less space but are still legible. Most monitors today are typically 1080p (1920 x 1080), 1440p (2560 x 1440), 4K (3840 x 2160), or 5K (5120 x 2160). There are even some new 6K monitors out there with a resolution of 6144 x 3456.
Refresh rate: This refers to how many times the display can refresh the picture per second, measured in hertz (or Hz). A higher refresh rate makes all movement and animation look smoother because you're seeing more information. For productivity, 60 Hz is probably enough, but gamers will generally want a panel that can at least hit 120 or 144 Hz. 240 Hz has become the new standard for high-end gaming monitors, but there are now extreme models that go up to 500 Hz and beyond. You'll need a powerful enough computer that can maintain a high frame rate to take advantage of these high refresh rates, and you usually have to enable this feature in your operating system's display settings.
Panel type: Monitors usually use an LCD (liquid-crystal display) panel. Three of the most popular options—twisted nematic (TN), vertical alignment (VA), and in-plane switching (IPS)—are different types of LCD panels, and all use TFT (thin-film transistor) technology. Each is popular for different reasons: IPS for color, VA for contrast, and TN for speed with higher refresh rates and response times. IPS has become especially popular thanks to its increasing refresh rate speeds. Mini-LED uses a more advanced backlighting solution that employs a number of lighting zones to more accurately and efficiently control pixels. These tend to be the brightest monitors you can buy. OLED (organic light-emitting diode) panels take that even further, allowing the monitor to control individual pixels, including turning them off entirely to create extreme contrast. These are becoming highly popular in gaming monitors, in particular. You should think about what's most important to you (great color? thin form factor? max brightness?) to choose the best panel type for your needs.
Nvidia G-Sync/AMD FreeSync support: A gamer-specific criterion, these two features let monitors adjust their frame rates based on the games they're playing. This reduces screen tearing without affecting performance. G-Sync is made by Nvidia and FreeSync comes from AMD, and while FreeSync monitors can usually work with most modern Nvidia graphics cards, G-Sync doesn't work with AMD cards, so make sure everything you have is compatible when buying.
HDR support: This isn't crucial for productivity, but if you watch a lot of media or play games, it's increasingly nice to have. Just like on TVs, HDR dramatically expands the range of colors a screen can reproduce, as well as leading to more vivid pictures. But you have to be careful, as many monitors will claim to have HDR; displays need to have extremely high contrast and be very bright to create the HDR effect strong enough to notice. The DisplayHDR 400 certification, for example, means the display only goes up to 400 nits. That's not bright enough to create any meaningful sense of HDR. In almost all cases, the display needs to use Mini-LED or OLED. Mini-LED can get very bright, well over 1,000 nits in HDR. The catch is that you need to ensure it has enough dimming zones, preferably over 2,000; a few hundred dimming zones won't do. OLED doesn't tend to get as bright as Mini-LED, but OLED has the benefit of each pixel being individually lit, which dramatically increases contrast. They still need to get bright, though, preferably up to at least 1,000 nits in HDR.
Port availability: A crucial but easy-to-overlook factor is what kind of ports the monitor has for connecting your devices. Most typically come with one or two HDMI inputs and a DisplayPort input, which will cover most needs, but it's always a good idea to check what your setup requires. More expensive monitors can function as USB hubs, letting you connect all your peripherals and accessories directly to your monitor. Conversely, check out our Best USB Hubs guide if you need to expand your computer's port options without paying for a more expensive monitor.
Built-in KVM switch: A KVM (Keyboard, Video, Mouse) switch is a device that helps you easily switch your monitor, keyboard, and mouse between two different computers or source inputs (like a gaming console). If you have one monitor setup for both a work and a personal computer, or a computer and a gaming console, having a KVM switch built into the monitor means you can easily shift peripherals between your two devices without needing an external KVM switch.
Should You Worry About Burn-In on OLED Monitors?
Probably not. You'll see a few OLED monitors on the list here, and that's for good reason. They're the best monitors you can buy, and they're increasingly affordable. It's pretty incredible how quickly they've dropped in price.
But burn-in was always the biggest concern with the technology. After all, it's an inherent flaw with the panels, and it can't be erased once the damage is done. While it's still possible to see burn-in on your monitor over many years, it's just not as much of a justifiable fear as it used to be. Modern OLED panels are significantly better at reducing burn-in, and the latest year-long testing results are pretty promising. On top of that, most OLED monitor manufacturers now offer software to protect against damage and three-year warranties that include burn-in protection.
What Do You Need to Set Up Your Monitor?
Once you've picked out the best monitor, you'll need a way to set it up on your workstation. Most models come completely assembled or require you to connect the base to the stand and the stand to the back of the screen.
Monitor stands: Most monitors come with a stand (and sometimes a separate base), and the flexibility of these stands can go a long way toward reducing neck strain and/or back pain. Ideal stands let you adjust the height, tilt, and rotation of a screen so you can position it exactly where you need it. Higher-end models can even adjust orientation from landscape to portrait. If your monitor doesn't come with a height-adjustable stand, you may want to consider a monitor shelf, which elevates the screen to a more ergonomically sound height.
Mounting brackets: If you're using multiple monitors, connecting them to monitor arms is a good solution. Monitor arms clamp to the side of your desk and free up lots of space that would otherwise be taken up by stands. However, the type of mount the display uses is crucial. Most monitors and monitor arms use the VESA standard, though you'll want to double-check. You should examine the size and type of mount on the equipment you have before buying anything new.
Ports and cables: Once you have your monitor set up, you'll need to connect it to your desktop or laptop using one of the available ports. If your computer has an HDMI port, it's as easy as using the HDMI cable that came with the monitor and connecting it to the back of the display. If your monitor has USB-C, that's also a good option, especially if your laptop doesn't have HDMI anyway; a nice perk is if it can provide ample wattage to power the computer (USB Power Delivery, or PD). And lastly, you'll often get the fastest refresh rates if you use DisplayPort and hook it directly into your desktop's graphics card.
Speakers: A lot of monitors come with built-in speakers, but I wouldn't put much stock into them. They usually sound poor and don't get very loud. You're much better off getting a dedicated set of desk speakers. Check out our Best Computer Speakers guide.
How Does WIRED Test Monitors?
We never recommend products we haven't tested, so we get these monitors in and set them up on our desks at home. We integrate them into our workspaces and get a feel for what it's like to use them. That means we consider the ease of setup, adjustability, design, ports, and on-screen display (menu system).
But you can't talk about the quality of a monitor without testing the quality of the panel. So, using a colorimeter, we test and report on the brightness, contrast, color saturation, and color accuracy. We compare that data to how other products we've tested, across different prices and use cases. That testing is especially important for displays that are designed to be used for specific tasks, such as content creation or gaming.
Our goal is to give our readers the best possible monitor recommendations, and to do that honestly, we have to test a lot of different displays. We're constantly getting in the latest and greatest displays to test—directly from the biggest monitor manufacturers in the world. Like many of the other products we test, these products are most often offered to us as review units with no promise of positive coverage. We do not prioritize products from companies that send us products to test. Though most of the products listed above were provided for review by the manufacturers, there are some exceptions in which products were purchased for personal use, which are noted.
Beyond that, I try to test monitors throughout the price spectrum and from as many different brands as possible.
Can You Use a TV As a Monitor?
Yes. Since TVs have HDMI ports, you can connect a laptop or PC directly to a television without a problem. In a pinch, it's a decent solution if you don't have a monitor. As TVs have increasingly become more similar to PC monitors, there's less and less of a problem with using them interchangeably.
However, there are lots of reasons why people don't typically do this. The size of televisions is a problem for desk use. You probably wouldn't want to put anything larger than a 43-inch display on your desk for practical reasons, but even at that size, the pixel density can be a problem. If you're at a desk, you're likely sitting much closer to the screen than you would be in a living room, and you'll really notice those pixels when doing computer work, even if the TV is 4K. There are other concerns if you plan on playing games on your TV, such as the refresh rate or input delay.
How Do You Set Up Dual Monitors?
The simplest way to connect two monitors to your laptop or PC is to use different ports and cables for each device. For example, you could connect your desktop PC to one display via HDMI and another via DisplayPort to the graphics card. It can be trickier with a laptop, which may not have all the ports you need to connect two displays. Some monitors and laptops have USB-C, allowing for an additional one to be connected. But some laptops, like the M1, M2, or M3 MacBook Air, can only support one external display on their own.
Fortunately, if your laptop doesn't have support for more displays, you can use a laptop docking station. The other option is to daisy chain them together using USB-C that supports at least Thunderbolt 3 (which includes Thunderbolt 4 or Thunderbolt 5) for both the laptop and the monitor. This lets you connect to two displays through just one cable coming out of your laptop. Make sure you use a USB-C cable that supports Thunderbolt.

Rescuers search for survivors of powerful Indonesia earthquake
- Published
Rescue teams in Indonesia have been searching for survivors of Saturday's major earthquake which left at least 47 people dead.
The magnitude 7.7 quake struck the island of Flores shortly before 05:00 (22:00 GMT on Friday) and had a depth of 15km, Indonesia's meteorology and geophysics agency stated.
Preliminary reports indicate hundreds of buildings have been severely damaged by the quake and the dozens of aftershocks that followed.
However, the full scale of the disaster is still unclear, and news of a second earthquake of magnitude 6.9 at the other end of Indonesia served as a reminder of why they call this region the ring of fire.
Tremors from Saturday's powerful earthquake were reportedly felt by residents as far west as Bima Regency and City, the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) agency said, but the Manggarai province is among the most affected.
Preliminary data shows that 24 fatalities had been recorded there, meanwhile 17 deaths were recorded in East Manggarai province, three in Sikka province, and at least one in each of the Ngada, Ende and West Manggarai provinces.
At least two others had been seriously injured and 11 slightly injured.
The BNPB said aid was being sent to the affected areas with 10,500 packages arriving at the base operations so far.
It will take time to assess the full extent of the destruction in the region, which is remote and mountainous.
However, early reports indicate more than 150 houses had been severely damaged, as well as dozens of educational institutions, a number of healthcare facilities, places of worship, offices, and several other public facilities.
Video taken at the port in Maumere - the largest town in Flores - showed large chunks of concrete breaking off the terminal building onto passengers waiting to board an inter-island ferry. Some were thrown into the sea when the gangway to a ship collapsed.
Emanuel Melkiades Laka Lena, governor of East Nusa Tenggara province, told a news conference that they were killed in their sleep by collapsing rubble.
Others, like Arnold Welianto, who lives in Talibura, a village near the coastline in Sikka, East Nusa Tenggara, were shaken out of their beds.
"I was startled awake and immediately went to my child's room." He said.
He also told the BBC that many people had already fled into the hills because the sea had also receded.
While a tsunami warning was initially issued - leading some 2,000 people to self-evacuate - it was lifted around three hours after the initial jolt, when no significant sea level rise was detected.
Landslides, however, did block access to some villages but the experienced rescue teams worked tirelessly through the day to free those trapped under the rubble.
In Ruteng, a temporary medical tent was also assembled outside of a hospital to treat earthquake victims.
The ongoing advice from BNPB is for people to remain calm and to stay away from coastal areas and structures showing signs of damage.
Indonesia is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity, lying along the meeting point of three major tectonic plates.

A parliamentary committee has recommended a review and the rationalisation of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) limits governing the operation and acquisition of existing private hospitals, warning that aggressive corporatisation and the influx of foreign capital could push up healthcare costs and undermine the affordability of medical care.
The growing presence of foreign capital in private hospital chains was facilitating the acquisition of cost-effective, mid-sized hospitals by larger corporate entities, the committee said, and warned that such “aggressive corporatisation” was transforming healthcare from a public service into a “purely capitalistic enterprise”, with the potential to inflate the cost of medical procedures and trigger price increases across the healthcare ecosystem.
Foreign investment in private hospitals will make treatment unaffordable: RJD
The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare, headed by Samajwadi Party (SP) Rajya Sabha MP Ram Gopal Yadav, presented the 176th report on ‘Affordability and Accessibility of Healthcare Facilities in Public and Private Sector’, which distinguishes between foreign investment in hospital operations and investment in healthcare manufacturing.
Foreign capital should be encouraged in the manufacture of medical devices, consumables and specialised medicines for rare diseases, the report said, while its application in the direct operation and acquisition of hospitals needed greater scrutiny.
The report recommended that the government strictly review and rationalise FDI limits concerning the operational management and acquisition of existing healthcare facilities, while creating incentives to redirect foreign investment towards domestic manufacturing of medical technologies and pharmaceuticals.
The committee also argued that a strong public healthcare system could act as a market regulator by providing an affordable alternative to private care. Efficiently managed public hospitals, it said, could exert competitive pressure on private providers and help bring down healthcare costs.
It has recommended the establishment of autonomous, efficiently managed public multi-speciality hospitals in every revenue division to reduce patients’ dependence on major cities, and minimise travel for tertiary care.
The panel’s recommendations come against the backdrop of a widening public-private cost gap. Citing the 80th round of the National Sample Survey, the committee said the average cost of hospitalisation was ₹50,508 in private hospitals, compared with ₹6,631 in government hospitals. It has separately called for mechanisms to standardise and cap the cost of essential treatments, diagnostics, and routine procedures in private hospitals.
The committee has simultaneously proposed incentives — including tax holidays, soft loans, subsidised land and concessional electricity — to attract private investment in multi-speciality hospitals in tier-2, tier-3 and rural areas. It has suggested that public-private partnerships be used to extend advanced medical technologies and specialised services to underserved regions.
Private hospitals receiving government incentives should also consider cross-subsidisation, with revenues from higher-paying patients, including international patients, helping subsidise treatment for poorer patients, the committee said.
It has further recommended raising the mandatory reservation of beds for Below Poverty Line (BPL), Economically Weaker Section (EWS), and AB-PMJAY (Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana) beneficiaries from 10% to 20%, citing weak enforcement of existing obligations on private hospitals.
The committee has also called for hospital-level ethics committees to examine professional fees and for stronger regulatory oversight of public-private partnerships to ensure that commitments to provide affordable care are honoured.
It has proposed a single-window mechanism to ease regulatory approvals for healthcare facilities in smaller cities and called for greater empanelment of private hospitals in aspirational and remote districts under AB-PMJAY.
The thrust of the recommendations is that private and foreign capital should supplement rather than substitute public investment in healthcare, with incentives linked to affordability, geographical access, and services for vulnerable populations.

A Disney convention might be the only place where it's acceptable to wear a luxury wrist watch and Mickey Mouse ears in the same outfit.
Those accessories and more were on display over the weekend at D23, Disney's massive fan convention hosted every two years in Anaheim, California.
Disney fanatics strolled through the Anaheim Convention Center wearing character cosplays and theme-park-inspired costumes, while A-listers at the nearby Honda Center appeared onstage in designer ensembles.
Here's what some of the latter wore.
New Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro seemingly took some fashion cues from tech CEOs.
On the first day of D23, D'Amaro took the stage wearing dark skinny jeans, white sneakers, a light blue button-up shirt, and a black quarter-zip jacket.
His outfit resembled the casual yet elevated uniforms worn by tech leaders. It featured no logos or prints, and he wore no accessories.
Anne Hathaway looked like a princess in a pleated gown.
The "Princess Diaries" star took the stage to accept a Disney Legends Award, which is the highest honor given by the company.
She wore cobalt blue for the occasion in the form of the $970 Celestial gown from Aflalo. The dress had cape sleeves, all-over pleats, and a floor-length skirt.
The outfit was regal and made for one of Hathaway's best maternity looks.
Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson let his diamond watch do most of the talking.
The "Moana" actor attended the third day of the convention wearing a form-fitting white set. The outfit included pleated trousers and a button-up shirt worn open.
It was his accessories, though, that really stood out.
He wore an assortment of bracelets, rings, and metal-rimmed glasses, as well as the Jacob & Co. billionaire double tourbillon watch, which costs around $3.3 million.
It's the same timepiece Johnson wore to the 2026 Met Gala.
Sadie Sink kept things simple, but it worked for her.
The "Spider-Man" actor has undergone a massive fashion evolution since the early days of her career. The look she wore to D23 proves it.
She wore a vintage Alexander McQueen dress made by the designer in 2004.
The semi-sheer piece had a patchwork-style bodice, thin straps, and a ruffled skirt. She wore it with clear pumps banded with silver at the toes.
The Jonas Brothers mixed elegant eveningwear with theme-park fashion.
When they hit the stage to be recognized as Disney Legends, all three brothers wore some form of pinstripes.
Kevin Jonas wore a gray, striped shirt and tie, Nick Jonas donned a pinstriped gray suit, and Joe Jonas wore a similar style in black.
During their speech, though, the musicians added another key wardrobe piece: Mickey Mouse ear hats. The accessory was fun, festive, and a perfect nod to their history with the company.
Former Disney CEO Bob Iger kept his Rolex on while getting a cement handprint.
Iger was photographed putting his handprints in cement after being named a Disney Legend over the weekend.
No accessory was too expensive or precious for the occasion. Iger wore his "Pepsi" variant of the Rolex GMT-Master II watch.
It retails for around $30,000 on the secondhand watch market.
