Queensland's Crime and Corruption Commission (CCC) has taken issue with the interpretation of a recent court decision by the Queensland Police Service (QPS).
CCC chair Bruce Barbour told a parliamentary committee the watchdog was "in disagreement with the interpretation".
The QPS declined to respond to questions from the ABC.
It is of "enormous concern" Queensland police officers found guilty of a crime who do not have a conviction recorded can not be disciplined, the corruption watchdog says.
The Crime and Corruption Commission (CCC) has taken issue with the interpretation of a recent court decision by the Queensland Police Service (QPS).
CCC chair Bruce Barbour told a parliamentary committee the watchdog was "in disagreement with the interpretation".
"Any conduct of a police officer which is so extreme in its nature that there is a criminal conviction ought to be able to be the subject of review during the course of any subsequent disciplinary process," he said.
"To not be able to have regard to it means that you have an incomplete history, effectively.
"We see that as presenting an enormous risk not only to QPS but also to the community."
Shadow women's minister Shannon Fentiman questioned if the interpretation extended to domestic and family violence convictions.
CCC senior executive officer Craig Capper confirmed it would.
"The QPS can't take into account that DV information in deciding whether or not to take disciplinary action against an officer," he told the committee.
He noted the police commissioner had access to all DV matters but could not then use that if it related to an officer who didn't have a conviction recorded.
"The Commissioner, in one hand, can have that information for a DV purpose, but not if it relates to a police officer's discipline. Again, a matter that we're challenging."
Mr Capper said the CCC was challenging 19 matters where a police officer had escaped punishment.
"We say that the conduct of the officer is still liable to review and is still liable to discipline. That's where the disconnect occurs."
The CCC has been previously critical of a three-year delay in establishing a police integrity unit, an independent body to bolster accountability and trust in the QPS.
The unit was a key recommendation from the commission of inquiry into how the QPS responds to domestic and family violence.
The QPS declined to respond to questions from the ABC. Police Minister Dan Purdie has been contacted for comment.

Don’t Expect Russians to Protest the War
Ukraine may have hoped that deeper drone attacks would cause Russians to rise up, but mass demonstrations don’t look likely.
This summer, Ukraine began one of the most ambitious campaigns of its war with Russia. It launched drones deep into Russian territory, hitting some of the country’s biggest oil refineries and causing a nationwide fuel shortage. In some areas, Russians have waited for gas for as long as 69 hours, in lines stretching miles. Impatient drivers have beaten and stabbed one another. Even state-controlled media have acknowledged the problem.
Ukraine and its allies seemed to hope that frustrated Russians would rise up in protest. After more than four years, the war had finally “come home.” Now that more citizens were feeling its effects, one might assume, they would demand its end and apply pressure to President Vladimir Putin ahead of parliamentary elections in the fall. But so far, no mass uprising appears likely, now or anytime soon.
Russians are used to inconveniences. Under Soviet rule, they lived with shortages of just about everything. Lines were so ubiquitous that academics theorized about Russian identity being shaped by waiting. Books were published with chapter titles such as “The Queue as a Form of Soviet Life.” The newspaper Socialist Industry estimated that Soviet citizens spent 30 billion working hours a year waiting in line for essential goods.
In the late 1980s, at the peak of Soviet scarcity, my family lived on the outskirts of Gorky, a city east of Moscow. Sometimes my mother would send me shopping. I hated it. At a small, gray store called Vegetables, I would wait in line to pick through boxes of rotting produce, hoping to find an acceptable carrot or beetroot for borscht. Then I went to Bread, where I waited some more. Shelves were half empty. The only item that never seemed to run out was margarine; enterprising salespeople tried to make it more appealing by sculpting it into hedgehogs, which they put in display cases. Lines got even longer on the rare days when cheese or butter were delivered. Meat hardly ever came.
Still, nobody protested. We waved away the deprivation and delays. Everyone lives this way, we told ourselves. After all, Soviets knew the cost of complaining. In 1962, thousands of demonstrators gathered to protest wage cuts and government-imposed price increases. In response, Premier Nikita Khrushchev’s government deployed thousands of troops, who killed roughly two dozen demonstrators in what became known as the Novocherkassk massacre.
Russians continue to fear their government. I recently called my former neighbor in St. Petersburg, an art teacher and activist whom I’ll call Svetlana. When I asked whether she had witnessed any street protests, she laughed. “Are you guys living on the moon out there?” she asked me. “Don’t you get how dangerous it is here?”
“It’s even worse than in the Soviet days,” Svetlana continued. “One guy bragged to me the other day that he’d reported his neighbor to the FSB”—the successor of the KGB—simply for listening to anti-war music. She also told me about an acquaintance who had spent two years in prison for leaving a poem and flowers at a monument to a Ukrainian poet. In most households, gripes about the regime don’t leave the kitchen.
At the start of the war, demonstrations were more common. In 2022, police arrested nearly 19,000 anti-war activists, according to OVD-Info, an independent human-rights group. Since then, protests have all but disappeared. This year, one of the most notable critics of the regime was a veteran named Alexander Lunin. In June, Lunin put on his military uniform and recorded a speech denouncing Putin and the war. He posted it on social media, where it received more than 12 million views in 24 hours. The police jailed him, and Lunin publicly apologized for “giving in to emotions due to fatigue.”
Earlier this week, the only anti-war party was banned from parliamentary elections. Far-right politicians had sued the party, named Yabloko, alleging that it had received foreign funding, violated copyright law, and promoted “extremism.” The supreme court ruled in the far right’s favor, removing Yabloko from the ballot. Only a few hundred Russians protested outside the court.
Most Russians seem to have inherited the long-suffering mentality of the generations who grew up under Soviet rule. Rather than tiring of the war, “Russians realize that they are under attack, and that it’s time to stand together and tighten their belts,” Irina Borogan, a journalist who has studied Russian dissidents, told me. When the BBC asked a middle-aged man living in Crimea about the fuel shortages, he shrugged them off: “We are humans. We’ll adapt.”
Last month, I called Konstantin Sonin, an economist and a professor at the University of Chicago who left Russia in 2015. He told me that his friends in Moscow have made only the barest wartime accommodations—such as sending their kids to summer camp in Gelendzhik, a town on the Black Sea coast, instead of one in the heavily shelled Crimea, even though both areas are well within range of Ukrainian drones. He sounded astonished by his friends’ comfort with risk. “We’ve seen what Ukrainians have been capable of coping with,” Sonin told me. “Russians can endlessly adapt to this crisis too.”
I heard a similar message from Vladislav Inozemtsev, a Russian economist and political scientist who lives in the United States. Inozemtsev told me that his friends in Moscow have used their contacts to circumvent the fuel shortage and get gas delivered to their door. “It’s twice the normal price, but they can afford it; the middle class quickly adapts to difficulties,” he said, while acknowledging that Russians in rural areas will likely have a harder time.
By some accounts, Moscow hardly looks like the capital of a country fighting a war of attrition. Denis Volkov, the director of the Levada Center, an independent polling organization, described his walk to work to me. The city center, he told me, is filled with decorations that the government has put up: an oversized samovar, an inflatable elephant, sprawling flower beds. Volkov said that he sees no sign of a public revolt. “I would say that the expectations of a revolution in Russia are not based on any real facts,” he said. “All our data proves the opposite.”
A few months before the war, Levada found that Putin’s approval rating was 63 percent. In June, it was 74 percent, although it has been dropping since the start of the year. A majority of Russians—52 percent—said that their country was moving in the right direction. “People blame mainly the West and Washington for all their troubles” instead of Putin, Volkov said. These findings undoubtedly reflect the reluctance of citizens in an authoritarian country to complain to pollsters about their government. Nonetheless, according to Volkov, Levada found that 16 percent of Russians said that they would participate in street protests, up from 11 percent in 2024. Last year, 16 percent of respondents said they felt fear or sadness. This summer, that figure was 29 percent.
Even though there have been no signs of mass protest, Putin is preparing. This year, the Kremlin increased the budget for the national guard and other law-enforcement agencies to a record high of more than $47 billion. Just like Russians who fear the reprise of Soviet-era government violence, Putin also has a precedent to worry about. In 1991, after years of keeping Russians off the streets, the Soviet regime was unable to stop a rally of hundreds of thousands in Moscow, which accelerated its end. Putin may not have much reason to fear such a protest in the near future, but he can’t be too careful.

Jeanie Buss, the Los Angeles Lakers owner who has been the face of the team since the death of her father Jerry Buss in 2013, is reportedly contesting the plan approved by her siblings to sell the family’s remaining 18% stake in the storied NBA franchise to investors Bob Iger and Josh Kushner.
ESPN and numerous outlets reported Monday that Buss is challenging her siblings’ right to approve the sale of the team to the former Disney CEO and Kushner, an investor who founded Thrive Capital in 2010 at age 24.
Jeanie Buss and her five siblings — Jesse, Jim, Johnny, Janie and Joey — have had complicated legal maneuvering around the management of the team. In 2017, following a litigation process, Jeanie was designated the controlling owner of the team through 2030. Jeanie Buss’ attorneys indicated that she asserts that she has the right to approve any sale of the team. Iger reportedly had met with Jeanie and vowed to honor the agreement she had with Mark Walter to remain at the helm through 2030.
Popular on Variety
Walter, the CEO of Guggenheim Partners, acquired the Lakers from the Buss family in June 2025. The deal was finalized in October 2025, when the NBA distributed a photo of Walter sitting next to a smiling Jeanie Buss.
A representative for Iger and Kushner did not immediately respond to a request for comment late Monday.
Per ESPN, Jeanie Buss’ lawyer, Adam Streisand, has sent correspondence to the five Buss siblings who voted to sell that “a court had ruled in 2017 that no sale could be “effectuated without approval by the co-trustees, i.e. Jeanie, Janie and Joey Buss,” as reported by ESPN’s Ramona Shelburne.
Iger and Kushner surprised the industry and the sports world on Aug. 12 with their deal to acquire the Lakers from Walter for $12.5 billion — a premium from the $10 billion that Walter paid just a year ago. Since then, the New York Times, Wall Street Journal and other outlets have reported that Walter is now the focus of a federal probe into how he has handled some of his sports investments in recent years.

Nishinomiya, Hyogo Pref. – A siren blares, cutting through the sticky August air as two teams bow in a show of respect before the biggest game of their young lives.
As the air raid-like alarm begins to fade, players from Hachiman Commercial High School and Kendai Takasaki High School part and the typical sounds of Koshien Stadium become audible once again: vendors advertising sales of beer and snacks, the murmur of the crowd, the thud of baseballs hitting leather and the fluttering of thousands of hand fans as spectators desperately try to keep cool under the unrelenting afternoon sun.
The mercury at 1:30 p.m., the time of the game’s first pitch on Day 3 of the National High School Baseball Championship, reads 36 degrees Celsius. A thermometer placed in direct sunlight just above one of the concrete stadium’s plastic outfield seats, however, shows the extent of the danger: 45 C and climbing.
Experienced fans bring a cushion to sit on — not for a softer seat, but to avoid burning their rear ends on the historic ballpark’s scorching dark-green bleachers.
As human-caused climate change makes Japan’s summers ever hotter, one of the country’s most cherished summer traditions is under threat.
While organizers have enacted a number of measures in a bid to improve the safety of players and fans, some observers are now raising a question that once seemed unthinkable: Is Summer Koshien, as the tournament is commonly known, compatible with a rapidly warming world?
Summer tradition
It’s a stage unlike any other.
Each summer, 49 high school teams from across Japan do battle over 2½ weeks in a bid for baseball immortality and it all happens inside a 102-year-old ballpark that is as revered as the nation’s thousands of shrines and temples.
The tournament has a unique power to draw in even nonbaseball fans by evoking images of youth through the exuberance and innocence of the players, who give it their all in what serves as the high point of their high school athletic careers.
Games are televised nationally and top players become household names before they ever suit up for a pro team. The tournament’s place within the fabric of Japanese society is such that one could argue it sits right alongside fireworks shows, yukata and Bon odori (dance festivals to honor ancestors) in the realms of summer traditions.
Osaka Prefecture native Tatsuki Tanaka is a former high school player who follows the Spring and Summer Koshien tournaments religiously. He carries fond memories of his time playing youth baseball and says that helps fuel his fandom for the high school game even now.
“You can learn teamwork and things like that through baseball, and it makes for three incredibly fulfilling years,” he said.
Taking place during summer vacation and over the Bon holiday period, fans regularly pack Koshien Stadium, located a short train ride away from Osaka in Nishinomiya, Hyogo Prefecture, filling in the seats not already occupied by each team’s boisterous cheering sections.
“Of course, there are errors since it’s amateur compared to the pros … but that’s part of the charm,” Tanaka said. “There are a lot of come-from-behind wins and moments like that, so I think it’s fun to watch.”
After a team is eliminated, teary-eyed players fill up bags with dirt from Koshien’s hallowed infield to bring home as a final souvenir of their time in the spotlight, highlighting the stadium’s leading role in making the tournament special.
But for the players, coaches, cheering squads and thousands of fans who attend each year, one unsettling truth is becoming increasingly clear: soaring temperatures caused by climate change are making Koshien increasingly uncomfortable and, at times, downright dangerous.
“We brought plenty of frozen drinks and cold towels,” mother Eri Ishijima said as she fed shaved ice to her children on Day 3 of the tournament.
Like many fans, Ishijima and her three children left their seats to take shelter in the concourse, where large air conditioning units were a popular spot for people to get some relief from the heat.
“It’s too hot so we can’t watch now. … The little one just stays here,” she said, pointing to her 4-year-old.
Growing safety concerns
Japan endured its hottest summer on record in 2025, rewriting the record books for a third consecutive year.
This year, a later end to the rainy season meant cooler temperatures in early to mid-July, but temperatures in the high 30s and even “brutally hot” days — declared on days in which the mercury hits 40 C or higher — arrived in many parts of the country by late July.
The danger is clear: Japan marked an average of more than 1,500 heatstroke deaths per year in the five years through 2024.
While the large majority of deaths are elderly patients who are more susceptible to the worst outcomes of heat-related illnesses, young people, even in-shape athletes, are far from immune.
The recent death from suspected heatstroke of professional rugby player Saimoni Vunilagi, a 26-year-old from Fiji who played with Fukuoka-based Kyushu Electric Power Kyuden Voltex, served as a grim reminder of the dangers of physical activity in high temperatures.
“When something bad really occurs and we look back, there are so many obvious points, like ‘why did you host this to begin with?’” said Yuri Hosokawa, an associate professor at Waseda University’s Faculty of Sport Sciences and an expert on heatstroke, during an interview a day before Vunilagi’s death. “It’s not just Koshien. There are a lot of (youth sports) contexts in Japan … where some of those obvious risks are already there, but the adults, the organizers aren’t swift enough to make the decision.”
While baseball is not as grueling as rugby or soccer, Hosokawa highlights the fact that players tend to spend a prolonged period of time in direct sunlight as a cause for concern. And in high temperatures, any physical activity carries a certain degree of risk.
Case in point, Nippon Professional Baseball teams largely avoid day games in outdoor stadiums during the summer, while earlier this month the Korea Baseball Organization went on a six-day hiatus amid a record-breaking heat wave in South Korea.
In the case of Koshien, Hosokawa also highlights the player’s youthful exuberance as an obstacle for heatstroke safety.
“Because they are giving all that they have … they’re not gonna say, ‘Oh, I give up,’ right? Because there is no second chance for them,” she said. “It could be their last day for their entire high school baseball career. So all that motivation too is also putting a lot of strain on them, both physically and mentally.”
Essentially, with all that’s at stake on the field, players can hardly be expected to protect themselves from heatstroke — and that’s where the Japan High School Baseball Federation comes in.
Mitigating measures
Traditionally a daytime tournament, the 2024 edition of Summer Koshien saw the introduction of a limited split schedule as an anti-heat measure, with two games scheduled for the morning and two more scheduled from late afternoon into the evening in order to avoid the hottest part of the day.
The split schedule was expanded for 2025 and then modified for 2026, marking a fairly significant shift for a tournament that had long scheduled early-round matches to run back-to-back for a nearly continuous day of action. In fact, before technology made it somewhat obsolete, the stadium’s famous siren was traditionally used to notify players and fans outside the stadium when a game was either starting or ending.
Despite this momentum, the sheer number of games means it’s unlikely that organizers can avoid 35 C heat altogether through scheduling tweaks alone. This year, games have regularly taken place between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., when temperatures typically peak and the sun is at its highest point, meaning shade provided by the stadium is scarce.
Cooling breaks after the fifth inning have been the norm since the 2023 season, while stadium improvements could soon serve to protect more fans and student cheering sections from the sun. Koshien Stadium’s partial roof, which currently covers the infield seats, is due to be extended down the foul lines by 2028.
The biggest change under consideration — shortening games to seven innings — has garnered significant opposition from baseball purists and some of the sport’s biggest names, including Ichiro Suzuki.
But that shouldn’t stop the federation from doing what’s needed to safeguard against heat, former Samurai Japan manager Hideki Kuriyama said during a panel discussion earlier this year.
“If you think about protecting the kids, you have to consider their physical well-being,” he said, adding that decision-makers should listen carefully to people not involved in baseball.
“By taking proper precautions in advance and showing what we’ve done … sending a message to society might actually be a positive thing. We should discuss these issues together, do everything we can, and do it for the sake of the kids.”
Hosokawa gives Summer Koshien, which is co-organized by the Asahi Shimbun newspaper, credit for taking the heat issue seriously, but questions whether any of it is enough to avoid an even bigger debate: In its current location and timing, can the tournament as it looks in 2026 remain viable at all?
“In the past few years they’ve made substantial changes in making sure that these athletes have means to cool their body, take rest,” she said. “I think they are making a lot of progress. But the next step, I think, needs to be drastic. It can’t be this little prevention added here and there. It needs to be a total change in scheduling or shift in location.”
Long-term future
Like the proposal for shorter games, moving Summer Koshien to a different season or location would almost certainly be met with strong opposition from baseball traditionalists, but it’s a conversation that may become inevitable.
The tournament is intrinsically linked with the stadium, which was built specifically to host the high school tournament. The importance of having it at Koshien Stadium is such that the ballpark’s primary tenant, the uber-popular Hanshin Tigers, are evicted from their home every August in order to prioritize the high school players.
“Of course it sucks that it’s so hot, but this stadium has history,” said Naoki Kato, a Tigers fan who attended Day 3 of the high school tournament. “I want them to keep playing at Koshien if possible.”
Finances also play a key role in keeping the tournament at Koshien. According to a report by the Nikkei daily, the federation uses the historic stadium free of charge. And because the organization doesn’t collect broadcast fees, it is heavily reliant on ticket sales for its funding, which helps subsidize travel costs for participating schools. Of the federation’s ¥1.6 billion in revenue in fiscal 2024, ticket sales at the Spring and Summer Koshien tournaments accounted for ¥1.4 billion.
Hosokawa notes the prefectural tournaments that immediately precede Summer Koshien and determine its participants are equally problematic, so simply moving the main tournament indoors wouldn’t solve all of high school baseball’s problems, either.
Moving the tournament to another time of the year might seem like an easier solution, but that would create other problems given these are student athletes and the current tournament conveniently falls during summer break.
With those obstacles in mind, momentum could remain on the side of the status quo for some time yet.
“The one thing that I fear the most is that they won’t (act) until they see an actual catastrophic case,” Hosokawa said. “They have all the successes. … They know that they can host it and they know that they haven’t had a true catastrophic, fatal outcome. But do we need to have that to realize it’s dangerous?”
Back at Koshien, cloud cover provides some welcome relief for the latter half of Kendai Takasaki’s 7-1 win over Hachiman Commercial.
As the two teams line up to pay their respects after a hard-fought contest, the sun re-emerges, blasting the stadium with another dose of heat.
Then the players bow and the familiar siren blares, marking the end of one game and, soon, the start of another.
At least for now, Summer Koshien’s daily rhythm is just the same as it’s always been.

After Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi and Congress leader Sandeep Dikshit took a jibe at Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s customary hugs with foreign leaders and his public camaraderie with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Thursday, August 13, a statement purportedly issued by the Italian Embassy in New Delhi began circulating on social media.
Speaking at the Rachnatmak Congress national convention, Gandhi gave Dikshit a big hug. Dikshit quipped, “You weren’t hugging me thinking I was Meloni?” Gandhi replied, “I haven’t reached that stage yet,” drawing laughter from the gathering. The exchange triggered outrage among Bharatiya Janata Party leaders and its supporters.
The purported statement was posted on X by an account named ‘Italy in India’ (@AINga5f). It claimed that the embassy had expressed “deep concern and strong disapproval” over the “derogatory remarks” attributed to Gandhi.
“We respect India’s democratic institutions and political discourse, and we expect the same respect for Italy and its democratically elected leadership,” the purported statement read.
Media outlets Republic and Gujarat Samachar published reports based on the purported letter.
Several other influential and verified X handles, including Right-wing influencer Ajeet Bharti, K S Radhakrishnan, International Business Times, CNN News 18 journalist Vaibhav Singh, Saravanaprasad Balasubramanian (Modi ka Pariwar) and Damodar Singh amplified the purported letter on X.
The purported statement is also viral on Facebook and Instagram.
Fact Check
It is pertinent to note that the X handle that released the letter, @AINga5f, is a troll account and not the official handle of the Italian Embassy in India. The account has since been taken down from X.
The bio of the handle clearly stated that it was a satire account. Here is an archive.
The real handle of the Italian embassy in India is called @ItalyinIndia which also has a grey verification badge which is given to government or multilateral organization accounts.
We checked the website of the embassy and found no such statement. We also discovered that the last update on their website was on July 24, about a ministry of foreign affairs and international cooperation (MAECI) scholarship.
Thus, it can be conclusively stated that the letter circulating online is fake and was not released by the official handle of the Italian Embassy in India. The letter was first shared by a troll account that has since been taken down.

Who are the Chawinga sisters leading Malawi's bid for Wafcon glory?
- Published
Malawi have been the surprise package of the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon), but the source of the goals which have fired the tournament debutants into Sunday's final against Cameroon (19:00 GMT) has been less of a shock.
Sisters Tabitha and Temwa Chawinga are the undoubted stars of the show, scoring nine of Malawi's 12 goals - with Temwa leading the golden boot race with fives strikes alongside Zambia's Barbra Banda.
And while the Scorchers are the lowest-ranked side at the finals in Morocco, at 153rd in the world, the siblings have already won silverware for some of football's biggest clubs.
Who is Tabitha Chawinga?
Born on 22 May 1996 in the northern district of Rumphi, Tabitha is the older sister.
The 30-year-old began playing football as a child with boys in her village, with a ball made out of plastic or paper.
"Growing up, I never saw myself as different from boys," she told the BBC. "Whatever they did I believed I could."
However, her mother did not approve.
"My mum beat me because she was embarrassed," Chawinga told Africa Daily in 2023.
"People would provoke my mum: 'Look at your daughter - maybe she will not be married in the future. Your daughter, she doesn't want to go to school.'
"Even my friends said: 'No women can play football in this world'."
Tabitha persisted and her journey to international stardom began when she moved to join DD Sunshine in the capital Lilongwe.
Tabitha draws strongly on her Christian faith, paying tribute to God during many of her media engagements.
Where has Tabitha Chawinga played?
A switch to Europe came in 2014 after an American working for a non-governmental organisation had a spell at DD Sunshine before relocating to Sweden.
The NGO worker joined third-tier side Krokom Dvarsatts, and DD Sunshine owner David Dube then suggested the Swedes try out Tabitha as well.
"When Krokom Dvarsatts hesitated, Mr Dube offered to pay visa and flight costs for me to travel to Sweden for trials," said Tabitha.
"I joined the team and they were immediately impressed with my strength, dribbling, shooting from far and scoring skills."
She had to wait until after her 18th birthday to make her debut, then became the first Malawian woman to play in Europe and scored 39 times in 14 games.
Tabitha continued her exploits at second-tier Kvarnsveden, netting 43 goals to help them win promotion, and was then leading scorer in the Swedish top flight in 2017.
A six-year spell in China followed, which saw her win three league titles, three golden boots and two player of the season awards.
A successful loan with Inter Milan in 2022-23 also saw her win the Serie A golden boot.
"My goal is to achieve for African people," she said after that feat.
"I need to play for the girls in Africa. They need to see there are women in this world that can play football like men."
It was Paris St-Germain next for the striker, and another landmark as the first woman from Malawi to play and score in the Uefa Champions League in 2023.
France's most decorated female side, Lyon, came calling and Tabitha has helped them to back-to-back domestic titles.
She played in last season's Champions League final defeat by Barcelona.
Who is Temwa Chawinga?
Born on 20 September 1998, Temwa - whose name means 'love' in her native Tumbuka language - followed the path trodden by her elder sister.
She acknowledges that Tabitha has been "instrumental" in her career, with the two playing together for both DD Sunshine and Kvarnsveden after Tabitha recommended that the Swedes sign her younger sister.
"She made connections for me to leave Malawi to play abroad, but most importantly has always advised me to fight hard, to know what I want and to pursue it without listening to distracting people," Temwa told BBC Sport Africa.
The 27-year-old impressed in Sweden, scoring 35 league goals in 2019.
With agents in China asking Tabitha how to find a well-rounded player like her, the response was once again to recommend Temwa.
Wuhan Jianghan pounced and the forward helped the club win four consecutive league titles - including the 2021 edition alongside her sister.
Temwa Chawinga – world record goalscorer
In 2023 she was the world's top goalscorer of the calendar year, outscoring the likes of Erling Haaland, Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi with 51 strikes for her Chinese club and 12 for Malawi.
"When I found out I was so happy. I didn't believe it, but it was so amazing," she said.
Kansas City Current of America's National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) swooped and Temwa was the division's top scorer in her debut season in 2024 with 20 goals.
She bagged another 15 last year as the Current ended the regular campaign with the best record in the NWSL before being beaten in the play-offs.
She was named league MVP in both campaigns.
Despite their roll of achievements, neither sister has yet been named as African Women's Footballer of the Year.
A stunning impact for Malawi
Both have been prolific at international level since making their Malawi debuts in 2011 and 2016 respectively.
Tabitha usually captains the Scorchers, but it was Temwa who skippered the side to their first piece of silverware, the regional Council of Southern Africa Football Associations Women's Championship title in 2023.
"I was waiting to qualify for the [Women's] Africa Cup of Nations [for] a long time," Tabitha said before this tournament began.
"I've been playing big games in Europe, but I tell the girls 'Don't be shy, don't be scared'."
Those words proved invaluable as Malawi upset 10-time champions Nigeria in their Wafcon opener and also finished above 2022 semi-finalists Zambia in Group C.
The Scorchers came from behind to beat Ghana 2-1 in the quarter-finals - sealing qualification for next year's Fifa Women's World Cup - before both sisters scored in the semi-final win over Algeria.
"I'm so happy because a lot of people didn't give us a chance at this level, but we showed the world that we have a good team," Temwa said.
Malawi FA boss Fleetwood Haiya says funds received from world governing body Fifa have helped stoke the success of the women's side, but both sisters have called for more investment.
"If we can put money in Malawi to support girls' football I think there can be so many like me and Tabitha," Temwa said.
Should Malawi become just the fourth side to win the Wafcon title, after Nigeria, Equatorial Guinea and South Africa, they will be indebted to two sisters from humble beginnings.

US diesel crack surpasses US$100 a barrel for the first time on supply disruptions
Supplies are under strain from wars in Iran and Ukraine, and US threats against Chinese imports of Iranian oil could make matters worse
The US diesel crack, a key measure of refining profitability, hit an all-time high of US$102.20 a barrel on Monday as global supply disruptions from the wars in Iran and Ukraine run into peak agricultural consumption season.
Measured as the premium of US diesel futures over US West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures, the US diesel crack was trading at US$99.82 a barrel, up 2.4 per cent from Friday.
The crack has hit new intraday record highs in five of the last six sessions, reflecting growing concerns about fuel availability as fresh attacks on Middle Eastern refineries added to existing supply disruptions.
Global refinery crude throughput averaged 80.9 million barrels per day in July, down about 5 million bpd from a year ago, the International Energy Agency said in a monthly report last week.
The most immediate hit from surging diesel cracks is to farmers who need the fuel to power tractors, harvesters and other equipment, during the harvest season in the northern hemisphere and the planting season in the southern hemisphere.
Longer-term, it could hit most other sectors of the global economy as the fuel has wide-ranging uses from manufacturing to heavy transport and power generation in parts of the world.
Global diesel stockpiles have been under immense pressure due to the continuing wars, with both Russia and the Middle East among key suppliers of the fuel.

How to get the best audio out of your PC
For when your laptop speakers just aren't cutting it.
Modern desktop PCs and laptops aren't typically known for having the best sound systems right out of the box. Desktop manufacturers spend money on graphics cards and central processors instead of high-end audio components, as that's what consumers pay attention to.
But laptop makers have been making serious strides with audio. HP has teamed up with Bang & Olufsen, and Samsung owns several high-profile audio brands, including Harman Kardon. Newer Apple MacBook speakers sound pretty good, especially when compared to stuff that was coming out a decade or so ago. However, laptops are hobbled by the form factor. There's only so much room for speaker parts.
These factors have left consumers looking for external solutions. Luckily, there are plenty to choose from. Here are some ways to get the best audio out of your desktop PC or laptop.
Pair some external speakers
External speakers are the obvious choice here. This is a tried-and-true solution, though there are some caveats worth considering. The tech here has come a long way since the days of tinny-sounding bookshelf speakers, but that means there are hundreds of options to choose from. Some have built-in digital audio converters (DACs), and others offer wireless sound. Some are part of larger systems that include subwoofers, while others are passive and require an external power source.
In other words, go with something that sounds great and meets your budget. Speakers with integrated DACs tend to sound a bit better, due to higher-quality decoding, but an external DAC also gets the job done. Wireless setups are more convenient than wired systems, for obvious reasons, but tend to sound a bit thinner. High-end Wi-Fi speakers perform better than Bluetooth speakers, as Wi-Fi has a higher bandwidth than Bluetooth.
A system with a standalone subwoofer is also a great choice. These speakers accentuate the bass response and can typically be tucked away underneath a desk or entertainment table.
Don't forget about headphones
Headphones are always a great option, especially if you don't have the space for a real-deal speaker setup. A high-end pair of cans will sound decent out of the box, as most laptops and desktops have a built-in DAC of some kind. However, there are a couple of ways to increase the sound quality, which is important if you like to listen to hi-res audio.
For wired headphones, consider a portable DAC. These are usually about as small as a USB stick and plug into a USB port. They tend to sound better than a computer's built-in DAC. This can be coupled with a standalone headphone amp and a good pair of wired headphones for the ultimate in sound quality. Go for some open-back or closed-back studio monitors here. A standard gaming headset will technically get the job done, but this isn't the best option for top-tier audio.
Modern wireless headphones have gotten much more impressive, and many users likely won't be able to spot the difference in sound. They also have built-in DACs and amps, removing the need for multiple purchases.
Connect the computer to a home audio system
You could always connect the computer or laptop to a pre-existing home audio system. That way, you can listen to stuff in the same manner you normally do. This is fairly simple. Just plug a 3.5mm-to-RCA cable into the computer's headphone jack and the aux input of your receiver. For better audio, pop a standalone DAC into a USB port and then plug the cable into that. Many DACs actually have an RCA port, so you won't need that specialized adapter cable.
There are a couple of ways to do this wirelessly. There are plenty of Bluetooth-enabled home sound systems out there, allowing folks to just connect and stream. There are also wireless USB DACs, with a wireless transmitter and an analog signal receiver. The transmitter connects to your computer, and the signal receiver connects to the stereo or speakers.
Download loudness and EQ apps
Computers and laptops have access to tools that can impact every aspect of the audio signal, and many are worth considering. There are various EQ and loudness apps out there. EQ apps can help you tune the sound, which can help account for room acoustics. For instance, if your living room tends to accentuate the bass a bit too much, simply turn down the bass on the EQ.
Loudness apps are great for people who have run into a volume limit with their PC. They'll push a computer's built-in speakers to their absolute limit, so just be careful. A little goes a long way here. Too much loudness can cause harsh audio distortion, which will damage the speaker over time.
There are plenty of dedicated AI tools, but these are more for cleaning up or enhancing bad audio. These are a good choice if you plan on listening to an old cassette recording from 1988, but not that useful when streaming hi-res audio or any standard digital audio file. There are some tools that use algorithms to measure and adjust audio to accommodate a room's acoustics, which can be useful, but these tend to require (at least) a decent microphone.
Tips for great PC audio
There are some fairly easy ways to increase PC audio quality, beyond the listening platform and EQ software.
Spend some time optimizing your operating system. Delete unused files and, most importantly, try to not have too many things running at the same time when listening to audio. It can also help to partition your drive, separating the OS from audio files.
Pay attention to the actual audio files. It doesn't matter how much hardware you have going if the file is heavily compressed and was encoded at a low bitrate. If possible, download or stream hi-res audio. This refers to uncompressed or lossless digital formats that typically exceed CD quality. These file types include FLAC, WAV, AIFF and ALAC. The only downside? They tend to be much larger than MP3s, so a music library is going to take up a lot more space.
You want to minimize unwanted vibrations, as this could impact the audio signal. Use acoustic absorption if speakers are too close to a wall, and make sure to raise the speakers a bit from the computer desk. Some audiophiles go even further, placing the actual PC on a server, rack or anti-vibration platform. Acoustic treatment can also help.
Shut down the computer's display during playback, unless you're actively using it. LCD screens are notoriously noisy, and the high-frequency noise they emit isn't exactly pleasant. Another overlooked culprit of bad audio? Cables and cords. Make sure all of the cables running to and from the PC and any integrated audio gear are in good working order.
If you're primarily streaming hi-res audio, consider a wired Ethernet connection instead of relying on Wi-Fi. This will ensure uninterrupted streaming of large audio files without any jitter or lag.

On a pitch where the ball did not quite hurry, T. Natarajan had decided that perhaps the best way to hurry the batter was not to hurry the ball.
There was the slower bouncer, worked on for two years. There was the yorker, the old companion. There was the new ball, which was not quite new in behaviour, holding in the surface and denying the batter the easy pleasure of playing on the rise. And there was, above all, the need to adjust.
Natarajan did that rather well against Vida Kovai Kings, producing his best figures of this TNPL season so far. The iDream Tiruppur Tamizhans left-arm pacer finished with two for 24 in four overs, both wickets coming from slower bouncers at the death. R.S. Ambrish pulled one to hole out at deep midwicket, while skipper Shahrukh Khan couldn’t put it past short third man.
The spell helped Tiruppur Tamizhans restrict Kovai Kings to a moderate 166 for eight. The target was chased down with four wickets to spare, but Natarajan’s satisfaction was less about the figures than about seeing a plan come to life.
“When we first bowled, the wicket was holding up and stopping a bit. With the new ball, it was holding up, so it wasn’t that easy. The speed wasn’t there to hit on the rise from a good length. The wicket became slow for batting.
“So, we adapted to the wicket. Whether it was the spinners or the fast bowlers, whatever plan we had, we executed that. Especially, whatever I thought, whether with the new ball or at the death, I tried to execute that,” he said after the match at the NPR College Ground.
The slower bouncer was particularly satisfying. It had been two years in the making, and on that pitch it found a natural home.
The work behind that ball has been less visible. For the last three years, Natarajan has been working with former India and Karnataka left-arm pacer Sreenath Aravind.
“I worked with him even before going to the IPL this year. In modern cricket, batters easily start hitting whatever you bowl at the death. It’s very difficult for us to survive with just one type of ball.
“So, I felt that having a slower bouncer would be useful. I have worked on it for two years, and it is better now,” he said.
ALSO READ: Kovai Kings routs Trichy Grand Cholas for timely win
Their association goes back around seven years to Natarajan’s first Ranji Trophy match on this very ground.
Aravind was then a bowler Natarajan admired and sought advice from. He told Natarajan he could call him anytime.
“From then on, we communicated a lot. That’s how we got acquainted,” Natarajan said.
Their work together is rooted in the small details of fast bowling: creating angles for right-hand and left-hand batters, correcting technical errors, and spotting things a bowler cannot always see in himself.
“Even if I’m coming back from an injury, there may be some small technical mistake that I don’t notice, but he does. That can make a big difference.
“I had a shoulder injury (collarbone fracture) last year, so I worked with him during that time. I’ll tell him what I feel is wrong, and he’ll make a lot of small corrections. He even came to my ground (in Chinnappampatti, Salem) last year and worked with me for around four days. It is very convenient and easy for me to work with him since there is good communication between us,” Natarajan said.
The same practicality that informs his thinking at the death overs also shapes Natarajan’s thoughts about his larger ambitions. An India comeback is the obvious question for a bowler who has played for the country. Natarajan, though, is looking no further than the tournament in front of him.
“This is my identity - this TNPL. It is through this that everyone came to know me as Natarajan. Many youngsters like me are coming up, and it is a big opportunity for everyone.
“I don’t have any big goals as such. I have to play for the team, and the team has to win. My contribution is for the team. If we think of something big, we will miss out on what is here now,” he said.
Natarajan has become a source of information for young players around him, much as Aravind continues to be for him.
“There are a lot of young players coming into our team. I share my experiences with them and they learn a lot of things. It’s nice. Our team bonding is also good,” he said.
He helps even when the question comes from outside his own dressing room. “Even if someone from another team asks me, I do it. That makes me very happy.”
Perhaps, then, there is a certain symmetry to the journey. A young Natarajan once turned to an accomplished bowler for advice on this ground. Years later, he is the experienced bowler answering questions from younger players.
The larger ambitions can wait. The Indian team can wait. Even the next tournament can wait. For now, there is only the next ball.

Nasdaq is preparing for a major overhaul of its trading schedule, with plans to keep its US stock market open for nearly 23 hours a day, five days a week.
The move is aimed at catering to rising global demand for US equities and giving investors more opportunities to trade outside conventional US market hours.
Under the proposed schedule, Nasdaq would introduce an overnight trading session running from 9 pm to 4 am ET, bridging the gap between its existing after-hours and pre-market sessions.
The expanded trading week would begin at 9 pm on Sunday and continue until 8 pm on Friday, with a one-hour daily break between 8 pm and 9 pm ET for processing and the transition between trading dates.
Nasdaq's New Overnight Trading Session
Nasdaq said the new session is expected to start on December 6, 2026, although the launch remains subject to approval from the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and readiness of the securities information processor.
The exchange currently permits trading between 4 am and 8 pm ET, with the regular market operating from 9:30 am to 4 pm. These existing trading hours will remain unchanged under the proposed system.
Nasdaq said the regular session will continue to be the primary reference point for price discovery, while the overnight window will offer investors greater flexibility to trade US stocks across different time zones.
However, overnight trading will come with certain restrictions. Market participants will require new ports to place orders, while market orders and some opening and closing order types will not be available.
New Safeguards for Extended Trading
Orders that remain active when the overnight session ends at 4 am ET will be cancelled and will need to be re-entered when the following session begins.
Nasdaq also plans to introduce safeguards, including static price bands designed to reject orders placed outside specified limits, subject to regulatory approval.
Trading information from the overnight session will be provided through a separate market-data feed. The exchange also plans to introduce additional products to expand market coverage.
The proposed 23-hour schedule will apply specifically to the Nasdaq Stock Market. Nasdaq Texas, PSX and Nasdaq's options exchanges will continue operating under their existing schedules.
Nasdaq said the industry's transition to a 23-hour trading day is currently targeted for December 6, 2026, pending SEC approvals and the readiness of market infrastructure.

Kushner meets with Hamas on the Gaza road map ahead of talks with Netanyahu
CAIRO — U.S. negotiator and President Donald Trump 's son-in-law Jared Kushner held a rare meeting with the Hamas chief on Sunday in a new diplomatic effort to make progress in the stalled Gaza ceasefire. Kushner will meet with Israel's prime minister on Monday.
The talks aim to salvage the new 15-point, U.S.-backed road map for Hamas to disarm in Gaza and Israel to withdraw from the Palestinian territory shattered by war.
At stake are the lives of some 2 million people in Gaza and the reconstruction of the crowded enclave now largely controlled by Israeli forces, more than 10 months since the ceasefire ended major military operations. A meeting between Kushner, fellow envoy Steve Witkoff and Hamas leaders in Egypt last year helped clinch the ceasefire, whose progress until now had been stalled over the key issue of Hamas' disarmament.
The rare meeting in Egypt with Hamas' Khalil al-Hayya was confirmed by a regional official and a Hamas official, both speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to reporters. Kushner was one of a trio of envoys meeting with al-Hayya, with officials from mediating countries Egypt, Qatar and Turkey also there.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last week rejected the 15-point plan in a rare public show of defiance against the Trump administration, Israel's closest ally.
Now Kushner, former British prime minister Tony Blair and the director of the U.S.-created Board of Peace overseeing the ceasefire, Nickolay Mladenov, are set to meet with Netanyahu on Monday, according to a source familiar with the plans and a diplomatic source. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting.
Regional powers accuse Israel of obstructing peace effortsAhead of Monday's meeting, several regional powers including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates issued a statement condemning Israel's rejection of the road map, saying that "Israel now bears responsibility for obstructing the efforts to bring peace in Gaza." Other signers included Jordan, Pakistan, Indonesia and the ceasefire mediators.
The statement by foreign ministers also called on the Board of Peace and the U.S. to take "immediate and concrete measures" to keep any party from obstructing the plan's implementation.
Kushner's meeting with the Hamas leader aimed at ensuring the militant group's commitment to the road map, particularly disarmament, before his meeting with Netanyahu, the regional official said.
The Hamas official said the group is committed and waiting for mediators to start the 14-day negotiation period to work out a timetable for implementation. That period requires all parties' approval of the road map to begin.
The Hamas official also said the Hamas leader demanded that Israel halt its attacks on Gaza and withdraw to the so-called "yellow line" dividing the territory before beginning implementation. The yellow line was never precisely defined. Israeli forces have moved beyond it and now control about 60% of Gaza.
In May, Netanyahu said the next step was to move to 70% control, with Israel "tightening the grip" on Hamas "from every direction."
The White House had no comment on the talksThe White House referred questions about Kushner's meetings to the Board of Peace, which did not immediately comment. The Tony Blair Institute did not comment.
Under the road map, Hamas would hand over weapons to the Palestinian technocratic committee meant to oversee daily operations in the territory. The committee has not yet entered Gaza. But Hamas has linked the surrender of its heaviest weapons to the creation of a Palestinian state, something Israel's current government rejects.
The road map involves Hamas gradually giving up its weapons while Israeli forces halt attacks and begin withdrawing from Gaza. But Netanyahu says Israel will not retreat from any position in Gaza until Hamas has been completely disarmed.
That stance leaves other elements of the ceasefire, including reconstruction and the deployment of international forces to separate Israeli forces from committee-controlled areas, on hold.
Netanyahu faces a challenging election on Oct. 27 as he tries to hold on to power with a coalition that includes ministers taking a harsh line on Gaza, and it's not clear whether he will take decisive steps on the ceasefire before then. Also coming up is the anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel that sparked the war.
Netanyahu's Likud party on Sunday responded to the statement by regional powers by claiming that "Arab states want to topple" Netanyahu so that centrist challenger Gadi Eisenkot and center-left party leader Yair Golan "will give them everything they want. That will not happen."

Artificial intelligence (AI) could help India identify people at risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) earlier and enable more personalised prevention, but the technology is not yet ready to guide routine clinical decisions, according to a recent systematic review by researchers from the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), M.S. Ramaiah University of Applied Sciences, and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.
Published in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making, an open-access journal, the review assessed 30 studies published since 2017 on AI-based models developed to predict future cardiovascular disease among adults without established heart disease.
The researchers identified the studies through a systematic search of more than 6,700 records across major scientific databases. Most of the models were developed using datasets from the U.S., the U.K., and South Korea, and relied on routinely collected clinical information and machine learning algorithms such as Random Forests, Support Vector Machines, and neural networks.
Relevance for India
The findings are particularly relevant for India, where cardiovascular disease accounts for nearly one-third of all deaths and often affects people at younger ages than in many other countries.
Denny John, faculty of life and allied health sciences, M.S. Ramaiah University of Applied Sciences, and one of the authors of the review, said AI could potentially make cardiovascular risk assessment more precise, but the evidence was not yet adequate for widespread clinical use.
“AI offers an opportunity to make cardiovascular risk prediction more precise and more personalised. But our review shows that the evidence is still incomplete,” he said.
Several Indian institutions have already developed AI-based cardiovascular risk prediction models incorporating locally relevant factors such as smokeless tobacco use, psychosocial stress, and physical inactivity. However, Dr. John said such tools needed rigorous independent validation before they were used in primary care or public health programmes.
“Many models demonstrate good discrimination, but very few studies examine whether the predicted risks correspond to what actually happens in different populations,” he said.
He said that robust external validation, calibration, and assessment of clinical usefulness were necessary before AI tools could guide long-term treatment decisions, such as starting blood pressure- or cholesterol-lowering therapies.
Comparable with conventional risk scores
Twelve of the studies reviewed directly compared AI models with established cardiovascular risk calculators, including the Framingham Risk Score, which estimates a person’s 10-year risk of cardiovascular events such as a heart attack or stroke.
The review found that AI models generally performed as well as, and in some cases slightly better than, conventional tools in distinguishing people at higher risk of cardiovascular events from those at lower risk over five to 10 years.
However, the researchers cautioned that better statistical performance by itself did not establish that an AI model would improve patient care.
Major validation gaps
A key concern identified in the review was the lack of evidence showing whether the predicted risk accurately reflected what happened in real-world populations.
Almost all the studies assessed discrimination — the ability of a model to distinguish high-risk individuals from low-risk individuals. None assessed calibration — which determines whether the predicted probability of disease corresponds to the actual number of cardiovascular events observed.
Only seven studies validated their models using independent patient populations. Sensitivity — the ability to correctly identify people who subsequently develop cardiovascular disease — was reported in only four studies. None conducted decision-curve analyses to establish whether using the AI models would lead to better clinical decisions than existing approaches.
For India, this gap is particularly important because a model developed using populations in the U.S., U.K., or South Korea may not perform similarly in Indian populations with different risk factors and patterns of disease, Dr. John said.
Need for independent testing
The researchers have called for prospective validation of AI-based cardiovascular risk models across diverse populations, including Indian populations, before their integration into routine healthcare.
They have also recommended that future studies follow international reporting and assessment frameworks such as TRIPOD+AI and PROBAST+AI to improve transparency, reduce bias, and enable independent evaluation.

YouTube is the world's biggest video platform. Now it has figured out how to become bigger.
Even better: Google's video site is going to pull this off without spending a dime.
It's going to change the way it counts.
That's the upshot from a new policy the company announced Monday. The details won't make much sense to you unless you're a professional YouTube watcher, but the gist is YouTube is going to be more permissive about the way it counts views — which means view counts are going to go up.
Crucially, this won't affect the way YouTube counts views when it comes to Things That Involve Money — things like figuring out how it shares ad revenue with creators, or totaling up how much exposure an advertiser's video received. This change only affects "public views" — a purely cosmetic metric.
So why bother? YouTube says it's doing this on behalf of video creators who complain that YouTube's old system causes "confusion." But that doesn't fully explain it.
A slightly more useful answer is that other video platforms, like TikTok and Reels, already use a view-count system like the one YouTube is moving to, so this brings YouTube in sync with that.
But the most useful answer is that this will boost YouTube's numbers. Same platform, bigger metrics.
And that's most important to video creators that YouTube is always courting: It gives them the ability to tell a potential advertiser that a YouTube video that previously had 100,000 views now has, say, 150,000.
Again: Any remotely savvy advertiser will know the video didn't magically get more popular. But they'll also know that YouTube is counting views the same way TikTok does, so they no longer have to do extra math to understand a clip's reach or a creator's potential.
The change should help creators when they're trying to do "brand deals," as Rene Ritchie, a video maker who's now head of editorial at YouTube, tells me. "It will give them a better sense of how many people are reaching."
One more bit of translation: I think this move is another acknowledgment from YouTube that it no longer owns video.
That's been obvious for years, of course. It was certainly obvious when YouTube rolled out Shorts, its TikTok clone — you only copy the competition if the competition is working.
This tell is a bit more subtle: It tells creators "we know you're working with other people, and that's fine. Really! We just want to make sure you keep working with us. So maybe this will help."
I also don't think it's the most meaningful thing YouTube has told creators this month.
The fact that's going to make it more difficult for new creators to make money on YouTube, by raising the hurdles to get into its main revenue-sharing program, is a pretty big deal. And one that directly affects the dollars for future would-be YouTubers.
Monday's news is for YouTubers who've already made it — and for YouTube's own bragging rights.

MUMBAI: The process to start the trial in absentia against six Pakistani accused in the 26/11 terror attack on the city, including banned outfit Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) handlers Haafiz Saeed and Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, has been initiated.
It will be the first trial in absentia in a terror case since the introduction of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, said special public prosecutor 
Ujjwal Nikam
. Section 356 of the BNSS allows the trial of absconding offenders in their absence to prevent delays in justice.
26/11 Mumbai terror attack 
The special court conducting the 26/11 trial issued the proclamation against Saeed, Lakhvi, Sajid Mir, Abu Alqama, Asim alias Abu Qahafa, and Major Abdur Rehman Pasha.
Police commissioner Deven Bharti sent a letter to Nikam to initiate the trial in absentia for these accused.
“The 26/11 trial is very sensitive and we have enough evidence against the absconding terrorists who are accused in one of the most heinous crimes. They must be tried as per the law of the land and we want to utilise Section 356 of BNSS so that terrorists could be brought to justice. Hence, I have written to the special PP [public prosecutor] for an expeditious trial in absentia,” Bharti said.
Nikam told TOI they had filed an application in the special court and submitted that these were wanted accused in the 26/11 terror attack cases. “Ajmal Kasab had disclosed their role during the probe. So, it is a request to run a trial in absentia,” he said.
Nikam said he has also applied for issuing proclamation in the name of the wanted accused through Interpol. “The court issued a proclamation against the six wanted accused. It has asked these accused to remain present in the court on August 18,” Nikam said.
The proclamation was sent to the ministry of home affairs (MHA) to publish it through Interpol.
Special judge S R Navander issued the proclamation. The court directed the wanted accused to appear on or before August 18, Tuesday, to answer the complaint.
While Saeed is accused of engineering and executing the 26/11 attacks, Lakhvi, Qahafa and Alqama were present in a control room set up in Malir, Karachi, during the attacks. They are also accused of supervising the training of the terrorists. In the control room, they were accompanied by Sayyed Zabihudin alias Abu Jundal, an Indian who is accused of teaching the 10 terrorists Hindi and the local language of the city during a 10-day session.
In the November 26-29, 2008, attacks, 166 people were killed at Hotel Taj Mahal Palace and Towers, Hotel Trident, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, the Jewish centre Nariman House, in and around Cama hospital, Cafe Leopold, and other places.
Among those killed were several citizens of the UK, US and Israel. The police killed nine terrorists and caught one of them, Ajmal Kasab, alive.
On the days of the attack, seven persons, including Jundal, Lakhvi, Alqama and Qahafa, are said to have watched the terrorist operation unfold on TV while sitting in their control room, and Jundal even talked to Fahadullah and Abu Akasha, two terrorists who attacked one of the attack sites, from the control room.
On November 30, 2008, all the seven persons who were present in the control room in Karachi reached Baitul Mujahideen, Muzaffarabad. There, they came to know that Kasab was arrested instead of Ismail.
The crime branch through the Interpol got red corner notices issued against Saeed, a resident of Johar Town, Lahore, Lakhvi, a resident of Markaz LeT, Bait-ul-Mujahideen Camp, Muzaffarabad (PoK), Mir alias Vasi alias Khalid alias Vasibhai, a resident of Lahore, Pakisitani Punjab, and Major Pasha, a resident of Pakistan, and a blue corner notice was issued against Qahafa and Alqama alias Amjad, residents of Bait-ul-Mujahideen, Muzaffarabad (PoK).

Photos show Trump relying on cheat card for White House event – something Republicans lambasted Biden for
The card included photographs and biographical information of meeting participants
President Donald Trump used a cheat sheet during a White House event — a practice that Republicans sharply criticized when former President Joe Biden was in office.
On Monday, Trump met in the Oval Office with Ryder Williams, a 16-year-old California lifeguard, and Nathaniel Rai, 10, whom Williams rescued from drowning at a Santa Cruz beach in July.
Williams received a certificate of commendation signed by Trump, and the White House hailed him as a “young American hero.”
During the meeting, Trump clutched a curled card in his left hand. A close-up photograph shows the card included photos of the two boys — identified as external participants — as well as biographical information.
The card also contained the president’s schedule, including the entries “1:15 p.m. Photo Opportunity” and “1:30 p.m. POTUS concludes.”
Similar use of staff-prepared notes — which have been used by most recent presidents — drew conservative backlash during Biden’s presidency.
At a March 2021 news conference, Biden was photographed with a cheat sheet listing the names and outlets of reporters that he planned to call on. The document also included factual bullet points, including: "China spends 3 times more on infrastructure than the U.S.,” according to Newsweek.
“Joe Biden had a cheat sheet with the names and faces marked of which journalists to call on, and he knew EXACTLY what questions would be asked of him,” right-wing podcaster Candace Owens wrote on X at the time. “That was not a press conference—that was a play put on by bad faith actors in a pseudo-democracy.”
“It was not very reassuring today that Biden relied so heavily on generic notes from staff to discuss the growing threat from China,” Stephen Miller, then a senior advisor to Trump, told Newsweek.
During an interview with Fox News, Trump himself described the news conference as “very sad” and “ridiculous.”
The following year, Biden, then 79, briefly displayed a staff-prepared cheat sheet containing directives including: “YOU take YOUR seat”, “YOU give brief comments”, and “YOU depart.”
The specificity of those instructions prompted another wave of criticism from Republicans.
“HOLY SHEET! Biden’s Presidential Cheat Sheet Leaks Online, Reminds Him to Sit Down,” Fox News host Sean Hannity wrote on X.
“Next time someone tries to tell you Joe Biden isn’t a geriatric nursing home patient trapped in the White House, show them this,” right-wing commentator Benny Johnson wrote on X. “He needs a notecard with step by step directions telling him what to do, including ‘YOU take YOUR seat.’”
Those incidents, among many others, fueled a relentless stream of questions about Biden’s fitness for office. An ABC News poll released in February 2022 found that 54 percent of Americans believed he did not have the “mental sharpness it takes to serve effectively as president.”
Biden ultimately announced in July 2024 that he would not seek reelection.
Since returning to office, Trump has also faced scrutiny over his health and fitness for office, including over frequent bruising on his hands and apparent drowsiness at some official events.
In a May ABC News survey, 59 percent of respondents said Trump did not have the mental sharpness it takes to lead the country.
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

Reddit is experimenting with video and audio versions of posts
The company wants users to be able to watch and listen to conversations.
Reddit is known for not really changing much about its core features. It even maintains (for now) a 21-year-old version of its site for longtime users who want everything to always look the same. But now the company is testing whether people want to experience posts and comments without having to read walls of text.
Reddit is beginning to experiment with new audio and video features that make its text posts and comments more interactive, the company tells Engadget. With the test, which is starting to roll out now, users can choose to listen to posts or watch them as shortform videos.The company describes the test as a "limited experiment" affecting "a sample of posts across select communities" on the platform. The new audio and video formats will still link back to the original text posts and comments, which will "remain unchanged," according to a Reddit spokesperson.
It's not yet clear what exactly these new audio and video posts will look like, but the company has recently added more video features elsewhere in the app. In June, the platform introduced video comments, which allow Redditors to post videos in comment threads that can then be watched in a full-screen player.
The latest test is part of a broader effort from Reddit to draw more new users to the platform and keep casual lurkers coming back. CEO Steve Huffman previewed the change last month during the company's earnings call. "There's an emerging content type elsewhere on the internet of basically podcasts where people read Reddit content, and so I think this version of like listened-to or spoken-Reddit can be really engaging as well," he said.

For the past year or so, booksellers have suspected that AI firms are buying up huge lots of rare books, then destroying them after scanning them to train AI. But this was hard to prove until now, as 404 Media reports that an Airtag hidden in a rare book shows that at least one tech giant, in the race to advance its frontier models, is behind some of the bulk orders: Amazon.
On Monday, 404 Media revealed that it had connected with a bookseller who agreed to plant an Airtag in a rare book that was part of a bulk order. That Airtag was then tracked to an Amazon AI training facility in Las Vegas that housed a team focused on tearing books from their spines and scanning pages, 404 Media reported. Apparently tone-deaf to the escalating backlash over destructive book scanning, a logo on the door of that team’s warehouse, VGT3, showed a Tyrannosaurus rex preparing to devour a book, 404 Media documented.
Amazon deflects
Amazon declined to comment on 404 Media’s findings, only providing Ars with the same statement it gave to 404 Media, which does not mention AI training specifically.
“Amazon purchases books through commercial channels to help develop and improve the products and services our customers use,” Amazon’s statement said.
However, Amazon is developing what it considers frontier AI models, which require a massive amount of unique training data to stay competitive with leading firms like Google, OpenAI, or Anthropic. Right now, firms carefully guard their training data to avoid losing an edge. And training models on text from rare books that are difficult to find would seemingly offer an advantage for Amazon, especially since rivals like Anthropic and xAI have publicly stated that they are not training on rare or antique books.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US envoy Jared Kushner have agreed that an American general will oversee the disarmament of Hamas in Gaza, an Israeli official said on Monday, as Israel insisted that no troop withdrawal or reconstruction would begin until the militant group gives up its weapons.
The agreement followed hours of talks in Jerusalem between Netanyahu and Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and a key US negotiator on the Gaza ceasefire plan. Former British Prime Minister Tony Blair and other members of Trump’s US-created Board of Peace also participated in the discussions.
The meeting came a day after Kushner held rare direct talks with Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt as Washington pushes to revive a 15-point roadmap for ending the Gaza war.
Quick answers to key questions
Israel insists that Hamas must completely disarm before any troop withdrawal or reconstruction efforts can begin, as a security measure to ensure the safety of the region.
An American general will oversee the disarmament process of Hamas in Gaza, as part of a broader initiative aimed at the demilitarization of the territory.
The US-backed roadmap includes Hamas's disarmament, the establishment of a Palestinian governing structure, and steps toward Israeli troop withdrawal and reconstruction in Gaza.
Hamas has agreed in principle to hand over its weapons to a Palestinian technocratic committee and has expressed readiness to transfer governance in Gaza, provided Israel meets its commitments.
Netanyahu faces increasing regional pressure to accept the US-backed ceasefire plan, especially from countries condemning Israel's rejection of the proposal, as he prepares for upcoming elections.
Under the understanding reached on Monday, Hamas would hand over its weapons for decommissioning under the supervision of an American general. The process would be part of a broader effort to demilitarise Gaza.
“The first step toward the demilitarisation of the Strip would be to require Hamas to hand over its weapons for decommissioning under the supervision of an American general,” a senior Israeli official told AFP.
The International Stabilization Force, which is expected to deploy to Gaza if security conditions improve, is led by US Major General Jasper Jeffers. A roadmap agreed to by Hamas on July 30 had called for the force to supervise the decommissioning of weapons.
Netanyahu's office said Israel and the Board of Peace had agreed to establish two working groups — one focused on Hamas' disarmament and the demilitarisation of Gaza and another on public health.
The demilitarisation process “should be prompt and completed before any reconstruction,” Netanyahu's office said.
The position highlights a key disagreement over the US-backed roadmap. Hamas says it has accepted the plan, which includes disarmament and the creation of a new Palestinian governing structure. Israel, however, says Hamas must be completely disarmed before Israeli forces withdraw from Gaza.
Israeli troops currently control about 60% of the Gaza Strip. Hamas has demanded that Israel stop military operations and withdraw to the so-called “yellow line” before implementation of the plan begins.
The line has not been precisely defined, while Israeli forces have moved beyond it in several areas.
During his meeting with Kushner in Cairo, Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya reportedly reaffirmed the group's commitment to the US-backed roadmap and urged Washington and other mediators to pressure Netanyahu to accept it.
Hamas has agreed in principle to hand over its weapons to a Palestinian technocratic committee that would oversee the territory's day-to-day administration. However, the group has linked the surrender of its heavier weapons to progress toward the creation of a Palestinian state.
The US plan calls for a “credible pathway” toward Palestinian self-determination and statehood, a prospect rejected by Netanyahu's current government.
The disagreement has left several elements of the ceasefire arrangement on hold, including reconstruction and the deployment of international forces intended to separate Israeli troops from areas administered by the Palestinian committee.
Pressure on Israel to accept the roadmap has also increased across the region.
Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Pakistan, Indonesia and the countries involved in mediating the ceasefire issued a joint statement on Sunday condemning Israel's rejection of the proposal.
The countries said Israel now bears responsibility for obstructing efforts to establish peace in Gaza and called on the US and the Board of Peace to take “immediate and concrete measures” to prevent any party from blocking implementation.
The negotiations are taking place as Netanyahu faces a difficult political battle ahead of Israel's October 27 election.
The prime minister has increasingly shown a willingness to challenge Trump, despite previously highlighting his close relationship with the US president. Netanyahu has also expressed dissatisfaction with Trump's decision to halt the US-Israeli war against Iran and pursue diplomacy with Tehran.
