Lindsay Clancy Was Mentally Ill. But Was She Legally Insane?
A jury will soon decide whether the evident suffering that moved her to violence also mitigates it.
These are the facts that no one disputes: On January 24, 2023, Lindsay Clancy strangled her three young children to death, then she attempted suicide by cutting her wrists and neck and jumping out of a second-story window in her Massachusetts home, which left her paralyzed from the waist down. The point of contention, as her trial has progressed, is whether Clancy should be held criminally responsible for her actions.
Clancy has entered a plea of not guilty by reason of insanity. A jury will soon decide whether she was sufficiently mentally ill at the time of the murders to spare her a mandatory sentence of life without parole in a state prison. The problem for Clancy and her defense team is that although she appears to have been extremely sick in the months leading up to the tragedy, the jury may still find her legally sane. This is because the legal standard for insanity diverges from the clinical understanding of mental illness.
Insanity defenses, which are premised on the idea that people are not fully blameworthy for criminal acts that could be seen as outside their control, have existed since ancient Greece and Rome and have been a feature of jurisprudence for hundreds of years. The legal definition of guilt typically requires both action and intention, which means committing a crime while in a reckless, negligent, purposeful, or knowing state of mind. An insanity plea is premised on the assumption that people who are insane at the time of their crimes do not have the capacity for criminal intent, so they cannot be considered entirely guilty.
Christopher Slobogin, a professor of law and psychiatry at Vanderbilt Law School, told me that courts have applied different tests for establishing insanity over time, though none has overlapped fully with clinical descriptions of mental illness. In the Victorian era, courts seeking to determine whether a defendant could be excused from criminal liability by reason of insanity began relying on something called the M’Naghten rule, named for Daniel M’Naghten, a Scottish artisan whose paranoid delusions about a grand conspiracy moved him to shoot and kill a senior British civil servant in 1843. M’Naghten’s case inspired a rule that designated defendants legally insane if they did not understand the nature of their criminal acts or that their actions were wrong. This rule remains in use in roughly half of the United States.
According to Michael Perlin, an attorney and a professor emeritus at New York Law School, the insanity defense became controversial in the United States after the acquittal of John Hinckley Jr., whose defense attorneys had argued that his attempted assassination of President Ronald Reagan in 1981 was a consequence of his schizophrenia and delusional obsession with the actress Jodie Foster, whom he wanted to impress. Outrage swiftly followed the 1982 verdict, stoked by politicians who called trial-jury members before a Senate subcommittee to interrogate them about their decision. Idaho’s legislature promptly eliminated the insanity defense that year, followed by Utah in 1983 and Kansas in 1995. Congress passed the Insanity Defense Reform Act in 1984, which narrowed the application of insanity defenses in federal cases.
In states that kept the insanity defense, views on how to apply it have continued to evolve. The closures of mental-health institutions across the country in the 1960s and ’70s increased the number of mentally ill people in the criminal-justice system, which created some urgency for establishing an adequate standard for legal insanity.
By defining insanity in terms of what a defendant knew at the time of the crime, the M’Naghten rule excluded defendants who had understood their conduct was wrong but nonetheless had been unable to resist or control their impulses. Some states addressed that limitation by expanding insanity defenses to include defendants who had acted under an irresistible impulse caused by mental illness or who had been otherwise unable to abide by the law. In Massachusetts, defendants may be found not criminally responsible if a mental illness left them unable to appreciate the wrongfulness of their conduct or unable to conform their conduct to the requirements of law.
In the months prior to what Clancy’s defense team has described as a psychotic break, she had repeatedly sought psychiatric help. She was briefly hospitalized and had prescriptions for 13 medications to treat her intense anxiety, depression, racing thoughts, insomnia, and confusion. Her lawyers have argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric condition that occurs after 0.1 to 0.2 percent of deliveries in women who don’t have a history of mental illness. At the time of their death, her children were eight months to 5 years old.
According to Veerle Bergink, the director of Mount Sinai’s Women’s Mental Health Center, postpartum psychosis is an acute episode of psychosis, mania, or psychotic depression in the months following childbirth. Symptoms include severe mood disturbances, delusions, hallucinations, confusion, and catatonia, and patients generally lose touch with reality. Bergink told me that a woman may come to believe that all the wars in the world are her fault, or that her child is possessed by an evil spirit. Because mothers diagnosed with postpartum psychosis are at heightened risk of suicide and infanticide, the condition is considered a psychiatric emergency.
Clancy’s desperate diary entries dated from the days and weeks before the murders recount such symptoms. She described feeling “incredibly sad and guilty” about not breastfeeding and suffering from “crazy brain fog.” She wrote that she was living “moment to moment waiting for the next nap time,” terrified that her infant son was becoming overtired, “because I feel I can’t help him.” She admitted to contemplating suicide. “I feel like I’m drowning every day,” she wrote. She told medical staffers that she was suffering from “intrusive thoughts,” and she checked herself into a psychiatric hospital on New Year’s Eve and spent several days there before being discharged.
Clancy, her ex-husband, and their attorneys have filed a medical-malpractice lawsuit against the psychiatrists who treated her during the months she spent spiraling. But regardless of whether a timely and accurate diagnosis could have saved Clancy and her children, she was plainly suffering from severe mental illness at the time of her crimes. Still, the jury may deny her insanity plea because the clinical understanding of postpartum psychosis—like those of a host of disorders—does not fit squarely within the legal definition of insanity.
Massachusetts prosecutors have argued that Clancy acted rationally and with clear intent, noting that she seemed organized, reasonable, and communicative in the days leading up to the murders, according to witnesses. Clancy’s diary entries and help-seeking indicate that she knew that her desire to harm herself and others was wrong, yet on the day that she apparently intended to kill her children, Clancy asked her then-husband to run an errand that would keep him out of the house. But the symptoms of postpartum psychosis, like those of bipolar disorder and schizoaffective disorder, are known to involve sudden and dramatic fluctuations, meaning that Clancy’s moods and cognition could have changed rapidly in the run-up to the murders—in defiance of most legal tests of insanity.
Regardless of the evidence, judges and juries regularly treat such defenses with skepticism. Although lawyers present this defense in only 1 percent of felony cases, Perlin told me that many people assume insanity defenses are overused—and suspect that defendants who plead insanity are faking their illnesses. Some are certainly trying to sell a story, but studies have found evidence that defendants falsified mental illness in fewer than 10 percent of cases.
For this reason and others, claims of mental illness at trial can be a “double-edged sword,” Slobogin, the professor at Vanderbilt, told me. He explained that juries regularly treat evidence of insanity as a sign that a defendant is inherently dangerous, best managed by being locked away—or put to death. In 1995, Scott Panetti was put on trial for the 1992 murders of his in-laws in Texas and was allowed to represent himself despite his history of schizophrenia. Panetti conducted his trial defense in a cowboy outfit and attempted to call more than 200 witnesses, including the pope, John F. Kennedy, and Jesus Christ. Nevertheless, Panetti’s jury found him guilty and sentenced him to death.
Panetti remained on death row until he died from natural causes in 2025, about two years after a U.S. District Court judge ruled that Panetti “lacks a rational understanding of the connection between his offense and his sentence of death and that his execution would therefore violate the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment.” Yet his case and others have made defense attorneys wary of touting a client’s mental illness, even when it is overwhelmingly obvious and crucial to making sense of their crimes.
Another problem with an insanity plea is that many jurors are under the mistaken impression that the penalties for such verdicts are too soft. If Clancy is found guilty of murdering her children, she faces a mandatory sentence of life without parole. If she is found not criminally responsible, she will be admitted to a state psychiatric facility for observation, after which state officials can petition for her continued commitment, subject to periodic review. But this does not mean that Clancy will eventually be freed: Andrea Yates, a Texas mother who drowned her children while suffering from postpartum psychosis, was found not guilty by reason of insanity and remains in a state psychiatric facility to this day. (She received this verdict after a retrial was prompted by the discovery that the prosecution’s psychiatric expert had provided false testimony in her original trial.) Perlin told me that, in general, people who successfully plea insanity spend more time in state custody than if they had been found guilty.
Whether Clancy is committed to a psychiatric hospital or locked up in prison, her story is harrowing not only because of the abject horror of her actions, but also because of the eerie familiarity of her struggle with new motherhood. I can remember my earliest days with my second child—the restless hours, the boundless needs, the sudden doubling of diapers, the endless laundry rotation in our small apartment, the struggle to care for both a toddler and a newborn. But I also remember the sunshine, my daughter’s delight in her brand-new baby sister, the newborn’s tiny arms in a triumphant stretch fresh out of the swaddle, those first precious smiles.
Clancy’s illness caused her to drown in the overwhelming chaos of mothering, beyond the reach of such buoying joys. Although she survived her suicide attempt, her life was in many ways already over. Regardless of what the jury decides, she is already in hell, and has been for some time.

Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
- Published
Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.
But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.
Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.
Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.
There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.
The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.
The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.
We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.
Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".
We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.
It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.
In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting.
One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers - the case that Mathipa had been investigating.
After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police.

The case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.
It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.
Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks.
Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.
We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.
Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.
Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.
The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.
We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.
When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.
He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.
He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.
The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.
The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.
The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover.
At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment.
Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military.
So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court.
Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise.
They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them.
Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency.
We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment.
When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved.
When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer.
"When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC.
On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time.
Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria.
When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway.
He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police.
And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi.
This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add.
New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division.
Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them".
Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case.
The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction.
All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody.
Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder.
The military has refused to hand them over.
In July, their lawyers cited mental health treatment for their absence. Three years after Mathipa's killing, no trial date has been set.
Meanwhile, Abadigga's body has never been found.
"[Mathipa] was barking up the right tree. He was taking on the right lion," Vreugdenburg says of the late detective.
Mathipa's daughter Basetsana puts it starkly: "We need justice. I'm never going to see my dad anymore... Why my dad? Because he was doing his job."

Palestinian American returns to his West Bank home, under siege by Israeli settlers
QUSRA, West Bank — The Palestinian American whose home in the occupied West Bank has been besieged by Israeli settlers for over a week traveled to his property on Monday to join other family members who have been defending it.
The standoff, in the village of Qusra, has seen groups of settlers surround several Palestinian houses and prevent residents from leaving. The United States has condemned the siege and the Israeli military has deployed troops it says are there to maintain order.
The siege of Palestinian homes by Israeli settlers comes as violence in the West Bank has soared in recent months. The settlers, emboldened by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government, have ramped up attacks on Palestinian towns and villages, harassing residents and setting homes, mosques and fields ablaze.
Israeli soldiers and settlers have killed 87 Palestinians so far this year, according to Palestinian health officials. Palestinians have killed three Israelis, including two who were killed during clashes in the West Bank village of Tell last month.
As Loui Ridi, an Ohio-based owner of one of the houses, landed in Israel, settlers were still roaming near Qusra, according to video footage taken by his brother. It showed settlers driving ATVs and speaking with soldiers.
Ridi had also watched the scenes unfold from afar through his home security cameras.
"I've been watching this live for many days and now this is the second week. I can't sleep," he told reporters at Israel's main international airport. "I can't let the settlers steal my house while I was watching."
He finally arrived in Qusra on Monday evening, where he first reunited with his mother and sister before moving on to his house. Ridi's brother, Qusai Abu Rida, and his teenage son had stayed inside the home to protect the property.
As Ridi waited for Israel's military to escort him to the house, he said he believed little had changed since early last week, when the siege began.
Israel has since declared the neighborhood where Ridi's home is located a closed military zone. But on Monday, his brother's footage still showed soldiers interacting amicably with settlers.

For 28 days, Keshav had a new item on his daily to-do list: masturbate for research purposes.
Both before and after self-pleasuring, he logged his mood, energy levels, cravings for various vices, and whether he was procrastinating.
Keshav was taking part in AI companion company Joi AI’s experiment assessing what happens if erotic self-stimulation becomes “an AI-guided wellness ritual.” Throughout July, 10 “masturbation consultants” were instructed to masturbate every day except Sundays, enlisting Joi AI’s sultry digital companions twice a week and using their own preferred methods the rest of the time. “It's almost like you are chatting with a real person,” says Keshav, a single, 38-year-old Indonesian trader, who did not want to use his surname for professional reasons.
Joi AI invites users, for a fee, to chat and play with premade characters or to create their own companions, including with X-rated kinks such as blackmail fantasy, gangbangs, and emotional dependency, and capabilities and functions like squirting and roleplay.
During five-minute video calls with the digitized characters, Keshav explains, his female companions opened and closed their nude legs to reveal their genitals and would “do blowjobs and handjobs” while talking dirty. Some of the companions were “quite pushy and extroverted,” whereas others were more reserved and required a degree of courtship before the relationship became sexual—even soliciting gifts like handbags and lipstick, which cost up to $5 in the platform’s internal currency.
After ejaculating, Keshav’s “energy levels [were] a little bit down, but focus was a little bit up,” he says.
Keshav and his nine fellow masturbation consultants will receive $2,000 each for the qualitative, in-house research project run by Joi AI, which is promoting a daily guided “jerk off with purpose” masturbation tool combining “sound [and] ritual” as part of its professed goal to “solve male loneliness.” Of the 10, six completed the study. The website costs a minimum of $3.99 a month to access, but users are likely to spend far more on the platform, with 10,000 “Joi neuron” coins costing $99.99 and private videos from companions costing 1,000 neurons.
Joi AI surveyed 2,500 adults before launching the study, finding that 75 percent masturbate to reduce stress and anxiety and that 43 percent self-pleasure before “a big event,” like a date, exam, or difficult conversation. The company sought to discover how masturbation affects sleep, stress, craving intensity, focus, and ease of arousal—and how masturbating with AI held up versus other methods.
“You get this boost of dopamine when you ejaculate,” says Julie Levin, head of brand and communications at Joi AI. “We wanted our consultants to track whether their cravings [for vices] are worse or better and how it affects their self-discipline.”
Preliminary analysis of 134 masturbation session reports, seen by WIRED, suggests that participants' stress levels reduced by 25 percent and focus increased by 17 percent. The pre-research survey suggested that 37 percent of respondents are open to AI-guided masturbation or are already practicing it. In the masturbation experiment, AI-guided self-pleasure produced comparable satisfaction scores to the established methods. “The study found no significant differences between the methods; so there is no one best way to masturbate,” the company said in the report.
It also indicated that the study group’s self-reported cravings for nicotine, alcohol, junk food, and doomscrolling reduced by 44 percent after they had masturbated. “Masturbation may be the most accessible tool people have for managing addictions,” the report said—a claim that is not based in science.
“The fact that their unhealthy cravings decreased feels like a genuine breakthrough to me: What if this is an unexpected way to tackle addictions?” Levin says. “Masturbation is obviously way healthier than alcohol or nicotine.”
But Nicole Prause, a neuroscientist studying human sexuality and addiction, says “this is a gross overstatement from the evidence they claim to have.” Prause is not aware of any scientific evidence that masturbation reduces vulnerability to substance abuse, and she was critical of the research methodology.
“Since masturbation can never be placebo—people always know if they masturbated—it is important to use markers that are less subject to bias than self-report,” she says. “They use none. Someone saying ‘I feel focused’ is just that. There are dozens of cognitive tests that could be used to support a self-report. I do not see any.”
However, Prause, who is working on a large laboratory study of male orgasms, says masturbation to orgasm is a potent method of mood management. She adds that the most “dramatic shifts” among her study cohort come from people who report decreased anxiety and increased relaxation after climaxing.
Keshav, having recently completed the 28 days, looks back fondly on the experience. He says he was more clear-minded after masturbating and believes he is now better equipped to approach women. “Because I'm an introvert, it's difficult for me just to open myself to people,” he says. “This kind of helps me ... [with] what to expect, how to speak [to], or how to get a partner.”
He defied extraordinary odds to get the gig. More than 150,000 people applied for the 10 places in the monthlong experiment, with five handpicked by the company and another five chosen through public competitions, including one judged by porn stars—“may the best hands win,” the company posted on X—and another in which Joi AI made a call out for the “most unhinged” fetish. The winner had a balloon fetish.
Chloé Locatelli, a sex-tech researcher at King’s College London, was one of those invited to participate in the study because she is undertaking a collaborative project with Joi AI to see how different demographics build intimate and erotic relationships with the platform’s characters. “When they asked me to be a masturbation consultant, it was a bit of a no-brainer,” because of her research interests, says Locatelli, who recently split from her long-term partner.
“Masturbation is definitely something that I do to release stress,” says Locatelli, who was already a “daily girlie” with regards to her masturbation frequency. “I think there's a lot of physical and well-being benefits from self-pleasure.” She was less enamored with the AI companions than Keshav was: “I would engage with it and then be like, ‘OK, this has done it a little bit for me in terms of arousal, but there's more to be had.’”
She is acutely aware of the potential downsides of having a highly sexual AI companion. “I don't want to yuck anyone's yum as long as things are safe and consensual,” she says. But as AI companions become increasingly sophisticated, Locatelli is concerned about “the level of interactivity and personalization” they can give you: “If it becomes a bit of a crutch [and] your only form of sexual exploration, then that's not something that I would necessarily encourage.”
Despite the ubiquity of masturbating, surprisingly little research has tested what happens when healthy men and women do it every day. A 2024 review of 22 studies found masturbation tended to be negatively associated with sexual satisfaction among men, though the findings for women were mixed.
One interpretation is reverse causation: particularly among men, people dissatisfied with their sex lives may masturbate more, possibly increasing their discontent. A 2017 study published in Archives of Sexual Behavior found evidence that masturbation is often compensatory for men—a substitute for when partnered sex is not available—whereas for women it is more complementary, accompanying rather than replacing partnered sex.
Yet masturbation has documented benefits, too, such as stress relief through endorphin and oxytocin release and improved sleep, as well as providing the opportunity for connection with oneself. Public discussions about self-pleasuring, however, remain decidedly uncommon.
“We wanted to fight the taboo and stigma around masturbation and highlight that it's a normal part of a wellness routine, especially if you're single,” says Levin. “It's not some kind of a shameful habit.”
Locatelli says she is going to take her best friend on holiday to Spain, while Keshav says he will use the money from his gig to help fund purchases of stocks. But for Joi AI, which claims to offer men respite from isolation, the more consequential question is whether users will become so accustomed to its artificial companions that they retreat further from real-world connection.

Dancing with Shakira at World Cup was 'very, very, very, very, very good' - Ghetto Kids
- Published
Ugandan dance group Ghetto Kids are celebrating another milestone after appearing at the football World Cup final half-time show on Sunday - a life-changing experience summed up by 10-year-old Sierra as "very, very, very, very, very good".
Despite critics bemoaning the addition of a Superbowl-style show, external to the beautiful game's biggest event, the children's performance alongside global stars Burna Boy and Shakira was viewed by many millions around the world.
Speaking to the BBC's Newsday programme, members of the dance troupe and their manager say that rising from humble beginnings in Uganda's capital, Kampala, then finding fame while balancing it all with schoolwork has taken perseverance.
"Never give up... pray to God. Listen to your parents, education is first, that's all," says Sierra.
She and 11-year-old Josephine are still on a high, after their World Cup appearance midway through the game that saw Spain beat Argentina at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.
"I saw Messi and Lamine Yamal!" says Josephine about the two team's stars - Argentinian captain Lionel Messi and Spain's teenage winger Yamal.
"I was so happy to see Messi and people watching us. I felt so excited and I was smiling, and a little bit nervous," she recalls.
"Shakira, she's very kind," chimes in Sierra.
The children gave Colombian pop star Shakira and Nigerian musician Burna Boy a big hug on stage as their performance ended - a moment their manager, Dauda Kavuma, insists was a natural show of affection, rather than clever choreography.
Learning they had been picked to perform was a dream come true. The children "ran around in a circle, banging and shouting" when they learned the news, says Kavuma.
"They had already danced to Waka Waka, external in Britain's Got Talent," he explains about Shakira's remake of the 1980s Cameroonian classic Zangaléwa by Golden Sounds, external.
"But it was now a great moment to see that Shakira invited us... to perform with her.
"It means a lot and it's life-changing."
Kavuma's philosophy is that there is so much talent in the ghetto, you just have to polish it.
As a child he lived on the streets of Uganda's capital before the kindness of a teacher changed his life.
He wanted to give back and later became a teacher himself before creating the Ghetto Kids dance troupe - formed of homeless children and those who could not afford school fees.
Combining a multitude of African dance styles, comedy and pure joy, they soon caught the attention of Ugandan musicians including Eddy Kenzo, who asked them to feature in some of his videos.
The group's strategy has involved harnessing the viral-making powers of the internet, and their biggest break followed in 2017 when they appeared in the music video for French Montana's song Unforgettable - which at the time of writing has amassed more than 1.9 billion views on YouTube, external.
That recognition opened yet more doors, leading Ghetto Kids to the final of Britain's Got Talent in 2023, before also competing in America's Got Talent the following year.
It has also enabled Kavuma to expand his project offering housing, food and tuition to many children across Uganda.
This year's football World Cup final may have been the Ghetto Kids' biggest stage yet, but it was not their first major sporting event.
Back in 2023, the young dancers were thrilled to meet Kylian Mbappé and perform at a football half-time match in France between rivals Paris Saint-Germain and Reims.
Another recent career highlight was a film being made about their story, called Ghetto Kids Documentary: No Plan B.
Despite their fame, the children's parents and manager have instilled in them an "education-first" mentality.
Videos for their vast social media following are filmed at weekends, so that weekdays are largely kept free for school, Kavuma says.
If they have to travel for performances, the children connect online to their teachers while away and catch up on any missed work once back in Kampala.
Both Sierra and Josephine tell the BBC they plan to become doctors when they grow up but will never give up their passion for dance.
"Dancing changed my life - I went to school because of dance," says Sierra.
Josephine agrees: "Dance is what I know and that makes me happy because that's my talent."
So, what do they want to say to other children who, like them, might be talented but have not had the easiest start in life?
"To love themselves, believe in God, and pray. Be with their talents - don't deny them," answers Josephine.
"And we love them."

- Reports circulated that, in May 2025, a Texas sheriff's deputy searched a data pool of more than 83,000 license plate-scanning cameras made by surveillance tech company Flock Safety to find a woman whose partner alleged she performed a self-administered abortion. Public records confirm the officer did conduct such a search.
- We left this claim unrated because evidence for what motivated the search is mixed. While the deputy reportedly said they were attempting to locate the woman and her children to "check their welfare" (as they believed she may have been hurt by her partner), the investigation was, at that time, characterized as a "death investigation of a non-viable fetus" and the listed reason for the search was "had an abortion, search for female."
- Officers who arrived at the residence treated it as a potential crime scene, placing what the woman's partner told them was the frozen fetus in a "small body bag" and contacting the district attorney's office to ask whether the woman could be charged and "a civil lawsuit against the pharmaceutical company that supplied the pill" could be filed.
- It wasn't until five days after the death investigation was opened that the woman told authorities her side of the story and an aggravated assault case was opened against her partner. She told officers she ran from home, taking her child with her, after he threatened to kill her.
- Even if the woman performed an abortion on herself, Texas' anti-abortion penalties rarely apply to the person receiving the abortion.
- Flock has faced increasing scrutiny over its broad-reaching surveillance, which critics say infringes on personal privacy.
As public awareness of the spread of cameras made by surveillance company Flock Safety grew in August 2026, a claim resurfaced online that in May 2025, a Texas deputy pulled data from a network of 83,000 license plate identification cameras to track a woman who allegedly performed an abortion on herself.
The claim spread across several social media platforms, including Instagram and X. Another example of the claim had previously been posted on Facebook (archived) on July 8:
(Facebook user Feminist News)
After the U.S. Supreme Court overturned landmark abortion ruling Roe v. Wade in 2022, it became almost entirely illegal to have an abortion in Texas, though penalties rarely apply to the person receiving the abortion. The story above emerged amid growing concerns over police misuse of surveillance systems — including, reportedly, to stalk romantic interests.
We looked into the claim and found publicly available records confirm a Texas sheriff's deputy searched data across thousands of camera networks comprising more than 83,000 cameras made by Flock Safety, a company that uses automated license plate readers to identify cars.
According to an internal sheriff's office incident report obtained by Snopes, the deputy who made the search reported being concerned for the woman's welfare. "I began to believe the victim may have been hurt by [her partner] due to the call and it not making sense," the deputy wrote. "I wanted to use resources available to help find where the victim and her children could be to make sure they were okay."
Below, we analyze available evidence to understand how an officer used Flock data to track down a woman who went through a violent experience — and why.
Timeline of events
Incident reports and other documents reviewed by Snopes laid out a timeline of what occurred:
- April 23, 2025: The woman left her residence after her partner allegedly assaulted her. The man later told authorities he confronted her after finding what he thought was evidence of an abortion, saying an argument led to her leaving with their son and not coming back. The evidence included packaging for an abortion pill and what he thought was an aborted fetus, which he then stored in his freezer.
- May 8, 2025: According to the man, he made contact with his lawyer, who advised him to report the incident.
- May 9, 2025: The man contacted the Johnson County Sheriff's Office, reporting an "abortion incident involving his girlfriend." Deputies arrived and put up crime-scene tape, took photographs, collected the "fetus" for evidence and sent officers to attempt to contact the woman for a welfare check. They opened a "death investigation of a non-viable fetus" and reportedly contacted the district attorney's office to ask whether the woman could be charged. At this time, a deputy submitted the Flock search for her license plate number, reportedly out of concern her partner may have hurt her, as the man's story was not making sense.
- May 14, 2025: The woman arrived at the sheriff's office to report the alleged assault. Authorities opened an assault case against her partner, who public records show had previously been convicted of aggravated robbery.
- May 22, 2025: The lead detective signed a warrant for the man's arrest.
- June 11, 2025: A medical examiner determined the "fetus" was a blood clot. A few hours later, the lead detective officially recommended the case be changed to "cleared by exception" for that reason.
Officer searched data from more than 83K cameras
According to data Snopes reviewed from MuckRock — a nonprofit, collaborative tool that allows users to share records acquired through the Freedom of Information Act — the Flock search log indicated that on May 9, 2025, a Johnson County deputy named "J. Smith" searched 6,809 camera networks, totaling 83,345 cameras, between April 9, 2025, and May 9, 2025, for "Case #2500002320." The deputy listed the reason as: "had an abortion, search for female."
(MuckRock.com)
In an internal incident report from January 2026, the officers involved gave their accounts of the situation. The officer who submitted the Flock search, J. Smith, used a "TLO" (most likely "TransUnion Locator Services" — a massive investigative data platform law enforcement officers often use to find background information on people) to find the color and make of the woman's car as well as the license plate number.
"I entered the vehicle into FLOCK to see if we could see where the victim and her children might be at due to multiple different locations being given for the victim and her children," the deputy wrote in the report. "Deputies had attempted to try and contact the female, but were unsuccessful. The FLOCK hit showed the victim had been in Dallas prior but nothing recent."
What motivated the Flock data search?
News media outlet 404 Media originally reported on the search data, which digital rights organization Electronic Frontier Foundation characterized as an "abortion investigation."
It's important to note that the internal report was dated Jan. 30, 2026 — more than eight months after the incident. Until the internal report emerged, there was no documented, primary evidence the officers were concerned for the woman's safety.
According to the internal report, the deputy who submitted the search was not present at the home but rather "just was assisting with trying to locate the victim and her children to check their welfare." The deputy wrote:
I began to believe the victim may have been hurt by the RP [reporting person] due to the call and it not making sense.
The RP who was in a relationship with the victim didn't know anything about the victim which also wasn't making sense of where she could have been with the children.
I wanted to use resources available to help find where the victim and her children could be to make sure they were okay.
A detective at the home also reportedly told the man he "did not understand why it took him over two weeks to process what happened or contact his family attorney," then sent officers in nearby cities to look for the woman at various addresses "for a welfare check."
Johnson County Sheriff Adam King told 404 Media that "her family was worried that she was going to bleed to death, and we were trying to find her to get her to a hospital." The incident had occurred more than two weeks before the sheriff's office got involved.
As part of the death investigation, officers photographed and placed a stainless steel tumbler containing what the woman's partner told them was the fetus in "a small body bag." While at the home on May 9, they treated the area as a potential crime scene, including filling out a crime-scene log and putting up crime-scene tape.
Deputies at the home also discussed options for criminal charges related to the alleged abortion, according to the report. It read:
Deputies discussed the legal implications of the situation, noting that while the girlfriend self-administered the abortion pill, there were no criminal charges applicable under current Texas law.
CSI and CID collected all relevant evidence, including photographs and printed materials provided by [the woman's partner].
Deputies also considered the possibility of a civil lawsuit against the pharmaceutical company that supplied the pill.
According to the arrest warrant affidavit for the man, as well as the internal police report, deputies contacted the district attorney's office on May 9 to ask whether the woman could be charged. They were informed that the state "could not statutorily charge the abortion or miscarriage of the non-viable fetus."
When the woman arrived at the station on May 14, the lead detective "was initially under the impression [she] came to the Sheriffs Office to tell her side of the story about the non-viable fetus," according to the arrest warrant affidavit. The internal report read:
Detective Miller started out the interview with [the woman] by explaining the State would not be statutorily charging her with anything at this time so if she came to report [her partner] assaulting her because she learned he called the Sheriff's Office about the non-viable fetus trying to get her in trouble, there was no need.
What were the legal implications?
After a medical examiner determined the blood tissue deputies originally thought was a fetus was, in fact, a blood clot, according to the internal report, the lead detective on the death investigation wrote on June 11:
Disposition recommend case be changed to cleared by exception due to the tissue collected on May 9th, 2025, from [the woman's partner], being that of a blood clot and not a viable fetus.
This death investigation is linked to JCSO case number 25-00002423.
Please refer to that case for further information.
According to the FBI, "cleared by exception" means that "elements beyond law enforcement's control prevent the agency from arresting and formally charging the offender."
It's unclear how the investigation would have proceeded had the blood clot been a fetus. The initial case opened by the sheriff's office did not name abortion as a criminal offense; rather, it was a death investigation — a routine action following deaths that take place outside of hospitals and similar settings.
Investigating why a pregnancy loss occurred is medical in nature — an investigation to determine what caused fetal death. However, in many states, law enforcement has investigated pregnancy loss as a criminal case. In April 2025, for example, a Georgia woman was arrested after a miscarriage when a witness claimed she placed the fetal remains in a dumpster.
According to the nonprofit Pregnancy Justice, Texas has fetal personhood language applicable to criminal law.
Flock's inconsistent messaging
A spokesperson for Flock told Snopes via email that "the woman was reportedly being searched for as a missing person in what appears to have been a domestic violence case, not as a suspect."
This is not entirely correct. When the officer conducted the Flock search on May 9, the investigation was, at that point, officially characterized as a "death investigation of a non-viable fetus" — not a domestic violence case — even though the investigators' reports compiled later did express concern for the woman's well-being. We also found no evidence a missing person report had been filed.
Flock has also been inconsistent in its messaging. On June 19, 2025, the company released a statement (archived) ostensibly correcting what it called a "Women's Healthcare Falsehood" that did not mention domestic violence.
The company claimed a "family called to ask for help" because they "feared she was hurt." There is no evidence of this in the documents reviewed by Snopes; the official record indicates the woman's partner — who later was charged with assaulting the woman — called authorities to report "an abortion incident involving his girlfriend" that occurred weeks earlier.
Although it's true no charges were filed against the woman, the search was performed as part of a death investigation and authorities listed both the woman and her partner as subjects in the investigation.
Access to Flock data raises privacy concerns
A Texas deputy did use Flock data from a network of more than 83,000 cameras to find a woman her partner told authorities had performed an abortion on herself.
While an internal report says the deputy claimed to have performed the Flock search out of concern for the woman's welfare, this does not detract from the fact that, regardless of an individual officer's intentions, law enforcement officials have unprecedented ability to track civilians without a warrant because of Flock's vast network of surveillance cameras.
DeFlock, a site used to track such cameras with a crowdsourced map, estimates that, as of this writing, there are 130,235 cameras in view across the U.S. — approximately 107,000 of which are Flock cameras.
Flock has marketed itself to local law enforcement agencies as a modern solution to fight crime across jurisdictional lines with 24/7 coverage, providing police departments with "indiscriminate evidence from fixed locations."
"When people ask whether police officers can misuse Flock systems, the honest answer is simple: Yes. And when they do, they should be held accountable," a Flock blog post from May 2025 read.
In the case of this police officer scanning a data pool of more than 83,000 cameras to find one woman, many details remain difficult to review and were made transparent only through the findings of records requests made by civilians and journalists.
The data pool the Texas officer searched also tapped into networks in states where abortion is not illegal, such as Washington and Illinois. Though in January 2026 Flock said it does not share data with federal agencies such as Immigration and Customs Enforcement, in August 2025 the company said it had "engaged in limited pilots with the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), to assist those agencies in combatting human trafficking and fentanyl distribution" before it said it had paused its operations with federal agencies.
The University of Washington's Center for Human Rights has documented multiple instances of federal collaboration with local Flock client agencies, leaving much unknown when it comes to how civilians could be tracked across the state lines for the purpose of criminalizing women who receive abortions or otherwise.
On Aug. 13, 2026, Flock announced several changes to its access policies in response to the backlash, including recommending cutting default data retention from 30 days to seven. We reached out to Flock seeking more information regarding what is meant by Flock would "recommend" cutting the retention period — including whether it was possible to bypass this recommendation. We will update this story if we receive a response.
Although the woman in Texas wasn't charged for anything related to an abortion, she was the subject of a death investigation and the case was "cleared by exception" only after a medical examiner determined the alleged fetus was a blood clot. Court records show her partner, as of this writing, awaits trial on one count of aggravated assault and one count of family-violence assault.

BJP Rajya Sabha member and former Indian cricketer Harbhajan Singh recently re-shared a video on his official X account. Originally posted by an X user, Arshdeep Singh Saini, the clip shows two young men standing by the roadside in a seemingly disoriented state with their bodies appearing limp and their movements unusual. Sharing the video in the context of Punjab’s drug abuse problem, Singh expressed anguish, and wrote, “Very sad to see the situation of Punjab…”
Very sad to see the situation of Punjab 💔💔 . Punjab and its youth deserve better. This issue needs honesty, accountability, and urgent action—not denial. https://t.co/Vb6si8eAaj
— Harbhajan Turbanator (@harbhajan_singh) August 10, 2026
The post, published on August 10, has been viewed over 100,000 times, and shared more than a 1,000 times. (Archive)
Drug abuse remains a major issue in Punjab, which is slated to go to assembly polls in 2027. Harbhajan Singh, who switched from the AAP to the BJP in April 2026, shared the video while raising questions about accountability and the incumbent AAP government’s handling of the crisis.
Several other social media users also posted the same video with similar captions, pointing to the growing drug abuse problem in Punjab.
Fact Check
To begin with, we noticed that Punjab Police had reshared Singh’s post mentioning that the viral video was from Sri Ganganagar, Rajasthan, and not from Punjab. The post from Punjab Police’s official handle urged users to verify facts before posting things online. (Archive)
The video being circulated is from Sri Ganganagar, Rajasthan—not Punjab—and has no connection with Punjab Police.
A Punjabi audio track does not make an incident a Punjab incident.
We urge users and social media accounts to verify the facts and location before posting… https://t.co/bNHwjXVXsC
— Punjab Police India (@PunjabPoliceInd) August 10, 2026
Mainstream news media outlets such as Times of India and India Today also fact-checked Singh’s viral claim. All the reports echoed the claim of Punjab Police and mentioned that the video was from Sri Ganganagar, Rajasthan, although no detail of the actual incident or the original video was shared.
To verify whether the video was indeed from Sri Ganganagar, we continued our investigation.
On August 13, around midnight, the Times of India published a story on its digital portal on the Sri Ganganagar zombie drug case. According to the article, Sri Ganganagar district police detained two persons who staged a scene pretending to be under the influence of the so-called “zombie drug.”
Quoting district police superintendent Hari Shankar, the Times of India article mentioned that the detained youths were Yogesh and Yoginder, who had filmed the video for Instagram.
Armed with this piece of evidence, we carried out another round of investigation and came across a Facebook post by SBT News or Sandhya Border Times News. According to this platform, the two youths were detained from Bhambhu Colony area of Sri Ganganagar city after they had filmed the video on August 7.
We then geolocated the spot to make sure the scene was indeed from Bhambhu Colony.
The viral video had three important markers which helped us to geolocate the exact spot where the 41-second-long clip was filmed.
In the video, the two youths are seen standing in front of an iron pillar with orange and black markings at its base. Such markings are commonly seen at Indian Oil petrol pumps, and the tiled flooring in the video is also typical of petrol pump premises. Tall iron pillars bearing the pump’s branding are also commonly found outside petrol stations.
The road in front of the petrol pump appears to be a two-way road, with a divider in the middle. Cars can be seen travelling on both sides of the divider, while two flags mounted on tall poles are visible on the divider. On the opposite side of the road, a vacant plot overgrown with vegetation can also be seen.
To geolocate the spot, we searched for Indian Oil petrol pumps near Bhambhu Colony in Sri Ganganagar, looking for one beside a two-way road and opposite a vacant plot with dense vegetation. We found a petrol pump that matched these features exactly.
Thus from these above findings, it is clear that the video which BJP MP Harbhajan Singh shared was not from Punjab. It is from Sri Ganganagar in Rajasthan. Besides, according to police, the two men in the video were enacting being under the influence of drugs for an Instagram reel.

A large number of electors with even slight name mismatches are going to be issued notices as part of the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Electoral Rolls in Telangana. Close to 93 lakh voters are set to get notices asking them to explain the discrepancies, to which they must reply to retain their name on the final rolls.
Chief Electoral Officer C. Sudharshan Reddy confirmed during the media briefing, that the difference between a full name along with surname and a name with only initial too will be considered an anomaly. He had earlier, during an interview with The Hindu, stated that his own name would come under anomalies, because of the discrepancy between surname and initial.
However, the anomalies/logical discrepancies already listed by the CEO’s office did not have the elector’s name mismatch as one of the 11 red flags.
The officially listed anomalies or discrepancies are less than 9 months gap between progeny, less than 15 years gap between parent and progeny, greater than 50 years age gap between progeny and parent, less than 40 years age gap between elector and grandparent, different parent name between current e-roll and last SIR, mapping with different relative type between both rolls, mapping with father in the current roll and husband in the last SIR, father’s name different between both rolls, and incorrect age difference between current and last SIR.
Having zero documents, and only Aadhaar too have been listed as anomalies, but since no documents were sought during the Enumeration Phase, they will crop up only during the verification process.

Kremlin critic jailed in Russia for 11 years for opposing the war in Ukraine
Lev Shlosberg is a senior member of the Yabloko party which Russia has barred from the ballot in next month’s parliamentary election
A Russian court on Monday convicted a prominent opposition politician for speaking out against the war in Ukraine and sentenced him to 11 years and one month in prison in the latest crackdown leading up to next month’s parliamentary election.
The verdict against Lev Shlosberg, a senior member of the Yabloko party, was another step by the Kremlin to stifle dissent since Russia invaded its neighbour in February 2022. Yabloko is the only official political party overtly opposing the war.
In a separate ruling on Monday, Russia’s Supreme Court upheld its earlier decision to bar Yabloko from the ballot in the September 18-20 parliamentary vote, denying an appeal by the party.
The moves against Shlosberg and Yabloko highlight the Kremlin’s intolerance towards any criticism of the war, now in its fifth year.
Shlosberg, 63, is Yabloko’s deputy chairman and served in the regional legislature of Pskov from 2016 to 2021. He stood trial in the city of Pskov, some 600km (370 miles) northwest of Moscow, on charges of “discrediting” and spreading “false information” about the Russian military.
The charges stemmed from a debate in which he called for ending the war and from posting on his Telegram channel a British tabloid front page featuring an image of a bloodied woman next to one of Russian President Vladimir Putin, with the headline: “Her blood … his hands.” Shlosberg has rejected the charges as unfounded.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): The recovery of Rs 3 crore from the house of Saurabh Ahirwar in Gopalganj area of Sagar on Sunday was not only a matter of huge surprise to the raiding cops but to Saurabh as well who ekes out a livelihood by working as a driver.
A senior cop of Sagar police connected with the investigation told Free Press that Saurabh's close relative had retired as a PWD official.
It was in the month of October that this relative kept an almirah at Saurabh's house by stating that it contained government files.
Saurabh and his family, including brother Ankit, were not having the faint idea that the almirah contained so much cash. "Otherwise, he and his family are impoverished and could have spent the money," said Sagar police.
When cops went to his home in connection with the probe of the social media reel in which Saurabh is seen brandishing a pistol-like firearm, they saw the almirah was not only locked but was wrapped with tape as well.
This made cops suspicious. When they opened the almirah, they found Rs 3 crore cash stashed in bags.
Meanwhile, Sagar police has written a letter to the Income Tax department, informing it about the seizure of Rs 3 crore.
Social media addiction lands Saurabh in trouble
It is from the last few years that criminal-minded youths are posting reels on their social media accounts in Sagar. It was two and a half years ago that Saurabh also posted such a reel, showing a pistol-like item.
Sagar police have closely followed the social media reels and nailed down many criminals so far. It was in this connection that cops went to the house of Saurabh and found Rs 3 crore cash.

Australia vs Bangladesh: Hosts drop opener Jake Weatherald but keep faith in Marnus Labuschagne for must-win second Test
Australia have replaced Jake Weatherald with Matt Renshaw in their 13-man squad for their must-win second Test with Bangladesh; Weatherald is the only change after their shock nine-wicket loss on home soil in the series opener
Tuesday 18 August 2026 07:13, UK
Australia have dropped opener Jake Weatherald after their shock home loss to Bangladesh but retained Marnus Labuschagne for the must-win second Test.
Weatherald is the only change in Australia's 13-man squad for the second Test in Mackay, beginning Saturday, where the hosts will look to level the two-Test series after a humbling nine-wicket defeat in Darwin.
Bangladesh's first-ever Test win in Australia put pressure on the national cricket selectors for an overhaul of their aging line-up, with Weatherald replaced by Matt Renshaw in a bid to stabilise the top order.

Weatherald was out for 23 in the first innings and did not score in the second innings of his hometown Test, leaving him averaging 20.36 in his 12 Test innings, with Renshaw a likely contender to replace him to open with Travis Head.

What's going on at Cadillac and Haas? F1 Q&A
- Published
After a four-week summer break, Formula 1 returns with the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend.
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli has a 50-point lead in the drivers' championship going into the race at Zandvoort.
There are 12 races remaining on the 2026 schedule, though uncertainty remains over whether Qatar and Abu Dhabi will go ahead because of the conflict in the Middle East.
Before the season resumes, our F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
Is the Cadillac reorganisation too hasty? Surely the team would have been better served by evaluating at the end of the debut season? - Tim
Cadillac chief executive officer Dan Towriss made it clear last week that he had always envisaged there would be a time when Graeme Lowdon would be replaced as team principal. But he said that time had come "sooner than expected".
Lowdon and Towriss have worked together to set up Cadillac over the past four years in quite demanding circumstances.
These included the fact Cadillac did not have an official entry until March 2025, only a year before their first race.
Towriss paid tribute to Lowdon's efforts in building a team from scratch while not knowing until the 11th hour when or even whether they would be racing.
But it's clear the American businessman was not happy with what he saw in the first 11 races of Cadillac's life as a competitive entrant. Hence his decision to sack Lowdon and replace him with the highly experienced Marcin Budkowski.
Lowdon was careful to manage expectations as to what could be expected of Cadillac in their first seasons. But it seems there has been a disconnect between what he believed was possible in a given timeframe and what Towriss expected.
The brutal realities of Cadillac's performance are that - if one leaves aside the catastrophe that was Aston Martin for the first 10 races - Cadillac were on average 1.2 seconds off the next slowest team, Williams, who are themselves having a bit of a nightmare season and lag 0.4secs behind the next slowest team, Haas.
And now Aston Martin have introduced their major upgrade, Cadillac face the prospect of spending the rest of the season well adrift of the rest of the field.
On top of that, there have been serious, and repeating, reliability problems, most notably with overheating brakes. It has become a familiar sight to see a Cadillac stopping with its brakes on fire - and quite often early in a race or session.
Towriss was questioned about "blame culture and people forming silos". And he admitted these were both a problem, describing them as "early stage business issues".
He has concluded Cadillac need what he described as "a model with a very strong technical team principal".
That is the model pursued with such success in the past three years by McLaren with Andrea Stella, and now Red Bull with Laurent Mekies.
Towriss said the decision was less based on the reliability issues and more "about just having a clear vision on what we're building in the future, the rate of progress, and making sure that matches the ambitions of ownership".
What would Aston Martin see as a good result at the next race, where Honda will be bringing a new motor? - John
The success of the Honda upgrade planned for the Dutch Grand Prix is less about specific results, and more about whether Honda can prove it is on the right track.
The team believe the engine had a performance deficit that amounted to about 1.5 seconds in lap time compared to the best in the first part of the season.
Honda have not put any numbers on the performance step expected in Zandvoort - either publicly, or within the team.
But the hope at Aston Martin is the new engine will close that gap by about a third.
So it's about seeing a genuine step forward from the engine - not least as proof Honda has understood its issues and has solutions for them as it works on its 2027 engine.
For no-one is this more important than Fernando Alonso. He is said to be waiting to see how the new Honda performs before deciding whether to stay in F1 with Aston Martin next year.
The first positive sign is all the former engineers who worked successful on the Honda when the company was winning championships with Red Bull are now back on the project.
But Alonso has previous experience from his time at McLaren of Honda both not accurately assessing where the performance level of its own engine was, and in upgrades not delivering what was promised.
Honda's reticence in predicting any specific performance step from its engine suggests it has learnt the first lesson.
Alonso will be looking for evidence that is also the case with the second.

What's happening at Haas? They're slipping down the pecking order and they're the only team not using the budget cap in full. They used to have such charisma but I feel that they're becoming F1's forgotten team. Have the owners lost interest in the project? - Steve
As F1's smallest team, both in terms of personnel and budget, Haas have some natural disadvantages that are hard to overcome.
Haas came into this season on the back of their highest-ever points score in 2025, and were bang on time with their new car at the start of the season.
That contrasted with some other high-profile names, who Haas have continued to outperform this year. Haas are unquestionably overachieving for their size - they are not even spending up to the budget-cap limit.
Haas had consecutive points finishes in the first three races, the high point of which was a fifth place for Oliver Bearman in China.
Essentially, the team started the season with a chassis advantage over some rivals and that allowed them to benefit as others were still finding their feet.
At that point, they were on average the sixth-fastest team in qualifying. Now, they are eighth, having slipped behind Racing Bulls and Audi.
Haas have fallen down the pecking order as other teams have introduced upgrades and begun to get on top of the new rules.
Nevertheless, Haas are still seeing the benefits of that strong start - they lie seventh in the constructors' championship at the mid-point of the season.
Haas did have their own upgrade, introduced in Canada, and featuring a new floor, bodywork and rear suspension. But team principal Ayao Komatsu has said it coincided with the team uncovering what he described as a "fundamental weakness" of the car with regard to a lack of high-speed downforce.
A reluctance by team owner Gene Haas to invest in upgrading the team's facilities has been a frustration over the years, but a new simulator - funded through Haas' new partnership with Toyota - is coming on stream shortly, which should give them a boost.
There are valid questions, however, as to what exactly Haas wants from his team. He doesn't seem interested in investing, but he's also not interested in selling. So they're a bit stuck, really.
How soon could a German Grand Prix return to the calendar and what races are likely to replace to Middle Eastern races in 2027 if the conflict continues? - Tom
Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali raised the possibility of the German Grand Prix returning to the calendar in a call with F1 media at the start of the summer break.
The race was last held in 2019, before falling off the calendar because race organisers could not make the event work financially.
Domenicali said: "Germany, for the first time, we are reconnecting with the possibility of having contact with the Hockenheim people to see if in the future, mid-term, not short term, they can have a race back."
When and if Germany comes to pass will depend whether organisers can put together a suitable financial package.
Right now, that's not the case, although things may change if Audi become competitive and that makes two German teams competing at the front.
Don't forget Domenicali has also said he does not want to have the schedule extend beyond 24 races, and there is pressure to have other new races, especially in Africa.
As for the start of next year in the context of the ongoing war in the Middle East, current plans are for the season start in the Middle East, as it last did in 2024.
Australia had the opener for the past two seasons because of where the Muslim holy month of Ramadan fell.
Domenicali said: "So far, the calendar that will be presented, let's say in autumn, will be as a sort of a normal plan.
"But of course, in case the situation in the Middle East will be not solved, we have options, [a] different plan. And the trigger for that is at the end of the year. So we have still a lot of time, if I may say, to adjust.
"We have different plans with different options ready in place that will accommodate the fact that we will keep, in any case, the target of 24 countries also for next year."
In the scenario that Bahrain and Saudi Arabia cannot open the championship in 2027, the obvious solution would be to do what happened this year - start in Australia before moving on to China and Japan.

Inside secret police warehouse as Germany targets small boats gangs
- Published
Germany has carried out its first raids under a new law to crack down on smugglers using the country as a staging post for small boat crossings on the English Channel, the BBC has learned.
More than 9,000 life jackets, dozens of dinghies and engines and 360 pumps were seized by police this spring during a joint operation involving the UK, France and Germany in the North Rhine-Westphalia region.
The dinghies and equipment are now being stored at a secret location that the BBC was given special access to.
The boats could have taken more than 2,000 migrants across the Channel illegally, according to the UK's National Crime Agency.
Gangs have long used garages or warehouses to store equipment in western Germany before transporting it to northern France, but Berlin passed a law last December making it a specific criminal offence to facilitate migrant smuggling to the UK.
Before that, key anti-smuggling laws in Germany only applied to nations within the EU's zone of free movement, not to third countries, which included the UK post-Brexit.
Raids have happened in Germany before, but often relied on French or Belgian warrants.
In 2024, Germany said it would tighten its laws to make it easier to prosecute those helping to ferry migrants to the UK, as part of a new plan agreed between the two countries.
It followed a BBC investigation which exposed the country's role in the small boat supply chain.
Germany's Interior Ministry confirmed that these raids marked the first time enforcement measures had been taken under the new law, but did not confirm if the law had been employed more than once.
The BBC was able to see the results at an undisclosed police storehouse in western Germany. The stash has been kept much as it was found. The dinghies, that officials say measure approximately 9m (29ft), are deflated and mainly packaged up in cardboard boxes.
In June, when the National Crime Agency first revealed the raids had happened, it was estimated that the equipment could have taken more than 2,000 people across the Channel - which would work out to about 65 people per dinghy.
That number is less than the so-called mega dinghies seen this summer but matches recent averages as well as the general trend of rising passenger numbers.
Oxford's Migration Observatory, external believes the emergence of these mega dinghies is likely connected to increased enforcement, as there is an "additional incentive for smugglers to fit as many people as possible into available boats".
Gangs are prone to adapt - rather than abandon - their money-making schemes when supply lines are disrupted.
The life jackets in the warehouse are tightly bundled and wrapped in plastic. Their bright orange covers are stuffed with little more than what feels like poly-foam -completely inadequate for the open and unpredictable waters of the English Channel.
The tag has Chinese lettering. Much of the equipment used for small boats is known to be produced there before being transported to Europe, often via Turkey.
A well-known entry point from Turkey into the EU is at the Bulgarian land border.
Customs officials recently found 20 undeclared inflatable dinghies hidden between mattress pads at a Turkish-Bulgarian border crossing. The truck driver had been heading for Germany.
British investigators believe Kurdish criminal networks hold a particularly controlling grip over the small boats business in western Germany - a region that has become a hub for migrants.
According to one German official, gangs operate out of Germany because many of them live there.
Western Germany is also close - but not too close - to the more heavily patrolled beaches of northern France from where migrant boats launch.
Local prosecutors warn that German's amended legal provision is, so far, largely untested.
Lawyer Bernhard Schmeilzl, who specialises in UK-German law, points out that the legal situation is essentially as it was before Brexit.
However, he believes it will make a difference, even if stretched German law enforcement agencies may be more likely to focus on domestic matters.
"This now enables the German police to go after these people," he says. "If they are being notified about such suspicious activity, they will have to investigate."
Enforcement and migrant sources have told the BBC that the gangs are coming under more pressure in Europe, including in Germany.
Channel crossings overall are on course to be lower this year, but illegal entries into Europe have also been falling.
The UK Home Office says its work with countries like Germany "is bearing fruit".
The UK government reports a drop of roughly 43% in the number of people who have made crossings between 1 January and 8 August this year, compared to the same period last year. It attributes this to efforts in disrupting the supply of boats to the gangs, and getting more law enforcement on French beaches.
But opposition politicians have said the decline is due to adverse conditions in the Channel, including wave height - not the direct result of action taken by the government.
