Demand for Canadian citizenship certificates soaring, fuelled by Americans
Archives swamped with requests for records, application backlog now tops 120,000
Applications from people around the world seeking Canadian citizenship certificates have been rising rapidly in recent months, fuelled by thousands of applications from the United States, CBC News has learned.
The number of people who have already received certificates as a result of Parliament’s adoption of “Lost Canadian” legislation late last year rose nearly 50 per cent between April 1 and May 31, according to new data obtained by CBC.
Bill C-3 allows citizenship for those who can prove they're descended from a Canadian ancestor, even if that ancestor left the country several generations back. It was adopted after the courts ruled that limiting citizenship to the first generation born outside of Canada was too restrictive.
Between mid-December — when Bill C-3 went into effect — and May 31, some 6,100 citizenship certificates were granted by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) to those who now qualify.
That is up from 4,075 certificates issued as a result of Bill C-3 from mid-December until March 31.
Another 17,390 people have received certificates as a result of having a Canadian parent. Prior to the bill's adoption, those who were born outside Canada had to have a Canadian parent to qualify for citizenship.
Tip of the iceberg
The certificates allow the 23,490 newly recognized Canadian citizens to apply for Canadian passports and live and work in Canada.
Elections Canada, however, says they can't vote in federal elections unless they've lived in Canada at some point in their life.
People born in the U.S. account for nearly half of those recognized between mid-December and the end of May. According to the data from IRCC, 3,110 Americans have qualified for Canadian citizenship certificates as a result of Bill C-3, while another 8,125 Americans have been granted certificates because one of their parents was born in Canada.
However, that’s just the tip of a very big iceberg.
The number of citizenship certificate applications waiting for a decision has exploded. In April, around 56,000 applications were waiting to be processed. That climbed to 70,400 in May.
Now, the IRCC’s website says 121,800 people are waiting for a decision. Those applications could be for anything from seeking recognition as a citizen under Bill C-3 to requesting a routine replacement of a lost or stolen certificate.
At the same time, the estimated wait time for a decision has doubled from 12 months in May to 25 months as of Aug. 10.
Estimates of just how many people could qualify for Canadian citizenship as a result of Bill C-3 vary widely.
Some point to a span of over 100 years in the 1800s and 1900s when hundreds of thousands of Canadians — particularly from Quebec — flowed over the border to jobs in the U.S.
The parliamentary budget officer has estimated that 115,000 people could be affected by the change in the law.
Last October, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab told the House of Commons immigration committee that she didn’t expect a flood of applications for citizenship certificates once Bill C-3 went into effect.
“We anticipate volumes in the tens of thousands over time," she said. "We do not expect any surge.”
Taous Ait, spokesperson for Metlege Diab, said IRCC took steps beforehand to prepare for the implementation of Bill C-3 and is working to process applications as quickly as possible while protecting the integrity of the citizenship program.
"We’re closely monitoring application volumes and trends and will adjust our operations as needed to manage demand as efficiently as possible," Ait said.
IRCC has not changed its requirements for documents, she added, but has taken steps to make the requirements clearer on its website and in other information for the public.
Demand soars for genealogical records
Meanwhile, Canada’s archivists are reporting a sharp rise in the number of requests for the genealogical records needed to prove someone seeking a Canadian citizenship certificate under Bill C-3 has an unbroken line of descent from a Canadian ancestor.
Alyssa Hyduk, president of the Association of Canadian Archivists, says her members are swamped, with some institutions seeing requests jump by 100 to 300 per cent.
Some are for documents that go back hundreds of years, she added.
“I think across the board there is this overwhelming feeling of just, of overwhelm and burnout …it’s really having an impact,” Hyduk explained.
“These requests are taking up so much of archivists' time that other reference requests — the [ones from the] rest of the public that we’re trying to still serve and do all our jobs — those are being set back too.”
Hyduk said the requests, most of which appear to be coming from the United States, are often complicated, as the records pre-date Confederation or are located in small church archives.
“We are at the point where [we're] going through boxes and boxes of material to find a single document sometimes,” she said. “You are going through reels of microfilm to find ship manifests with one name.”
“And these aren’t searchable documents,” she added. “We can’t go to Ctrl+F and find a last name. We have to read the handwriting. We have to figure it out.”
Archivists need more funding, says group
Mab Coates-Davies, executive director of the association, says the requests can also take an emotional toll on archivists.
“It is personal, it’s emotionally charged, it’s about family history,” she said. “There’s so many reasons that people, you know, might be looking to leave the States right now or planning for future moves.
“And so, there is that human element to it that archivists are feeling and experiencing, and frankly, IRCC isn’t on that front line in terms of the documentation.”
Another problem archivists are facing is the list of documents that IRCC will accept keeps evolving, said Hyduk. When the association met recently with the department, IRCC didn’t want to provide a definitive list of documents, saying it was likely to change.
The association is calling for more funding for archives across the country to keep up with the demand for records created by Bill C-3.
Coates-Davies said the flood of requests also began just as the Carney government’s budget cuts ended Library and Archives Canada’s $1.5-million-a-year Documentary Heritage Communities program, one that many small-and-medium-sized archives across the country have counted on for funding help.
“This funding package was just cut and then our workload skyrocketed," Coates-Davies said.
Another wave looms?
During an association meeting last week, some archivists were also bracing for a new wave of requests for genealogical records.
In June, IRCC suddenly suspended an estimated 100 certificates that had already been issued after flagging problems with the documents submitted with the applications. The concern from archivists is that some people who've already applied to IRCC will be sent back to archives to find more genealogical records.
The IRCC says 83 of the suspensions have been resolved and the certificates restored. It has sent procedural fairness letters to another 17 people whose certificates were suspended and given them 60 days to submit the documents necessary to prove their Canadian ancestry.
If they fail to provide acceptable proof, their citizenship certificates could be revoked.
New Democrat immigration critic Jenny Kwan said she has been getting letters and inquiries from people affected by the suspension letters and has written to Metlege Diab, calling for answers.
“It really makes no sense whatsoever, what’s going on," Kwan said. "And the minister is completely ignoring that reality right now.”

A US judge on Monday dismissed criminal charges against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, after the justice department said it had decided to abandon the fraud and bribery case.
The Brooklyn-based district judge Nicholas Garaufis’s decision to grant federal prosecutors’ rare attempt to toss the case came after he inquired into their reasons for doing so, including by asking Adani whether anything was promised in exchange for the dropping of the case. In November 2024, before the charges were unsealed, Adani had promised to invest $10bn in the United States.
Adani was charged in 2024 with agreeing to bribe Indian government officials so a subsidiary of his Adani Group could win approval to develop a solar energy plant, then misleading US investors by providing reassuring information about his company’s anti-corruption practices.
Adani Group has consistently denied wrongdoing. Adani himself has not appeared in US court to respond to the charges. On 18 May, the justice department announced it would no longer pursue the case. That marked the latest instance in which federal prosecutors had sought to drop a high-profile white-collar criminal prosecution during Donald Trump’s second term in the White House.
Legal experts say US judges have little discretion to compel prosecutors to continue with criminal cases they no longer wish to pursue, but the charges cannot be formally dismissed without a judge’s approval.
Garaufis asked the justice department to justify its decision to drop the charges, writing that its “bland and conclusory” announcement did not give him enough information.
In a 4 July court filing, Trent McCotter, a senior justice department official, said the case was primarily foreign, hard to prove and inconsistent with the agency’s current priorities.
In the filing, McCotter also denied as false what he called media stories suggesting he sought to dismiss the case in part because of a promise by Adani to invest money in the United States.
In response, Garaufis asked Adani whether he was “aware of any agreement exchanging anything for the dismissal of the indictment”.
In a sworn declaration filed in court on 15 July, Adani said he was not aware of any such agreement. He acknowledged having previously promised to invest $10bn in the US and said his lawyers told the justice department in meetings that the pledge “might be part of a resolution of these matters”. Robert Giuffra, a lawyer for Adani, said in a 15 July court filing that the justice department had told him that it would not consider the Adani Group’s willingness to invest in the US as part of any resolution.

No matter how hard we try, remembering anything that happened to us before the age of, say, 3 or 4 years old feels impossible. Even memories before 7 years old feel hazy and fragmented.
Why babies’ experiences matter (even if they can’t remember them)
How early childhood shapes us as adults.
Our brains just aren’t built to store specific memories from our first few years, something known as “infantile amnesia.”
And chances are, even the earliest memories we think we have might just be amalgamations of stories we’ve been told, images cribbed from old family snapshots and home videos, or scenes we’ve borrowed from movies or TV shows.
So does it really matter if it happened, if we can’t really remember it?
Yes, science says. Even if we don’t have a specific memory of what happened when we were babies, those experiences leave lasting impressions on us of being safe and being loved, which shapes how we form relationships later in life. But whether babies are able to encode and store permanent memories is still an open question.
Columbia University cognitive psychologist Tristan Yates put babies in MRI machines and showed them a series of images, and found that the babies tended to stare longer at an image they’d been shown before, suggesting that they remembered seeing the image the first time.
“We are showing that they’re able to form some memories,” Yates said. “The hippocampus is capable of forming specific memories over a few minutes, but now we need to start doing the research that can get us at longer durations, that can get at more complex memories.”
One theory for infantile amnesia is that an infant’s brain is prioritizing learning general skills, like how to walk or talk or eat, or learning to detect patterns like a bedtime routine, rather than storing specific memories that aren’t necessary for survival.
Noam Hassenfeld spoke with Yates and Dr. Dana Suskind, a professor of surgery and pediatrics at the University of Chicago, on the latest episode of Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Suskind studies early childhood development and the important role that parents and caregivers play, and she told Noam about how our early childhood experiences can shape us.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
You started out as a cochlear implant surgeon and now you’re working on childhood development. How did that happen? What’s the connection there?
It actually makes a whole lot of sense. When I first started our pediatric cochlear implant program at the University of Chicago, I started implanting cute little kids who all look like they had the same potential to thrive after implant surgery, and found very quickly that I could implant two children who looked very much the same, who had parents who loved them equally, with the same technology, but they would have very different outcomes, with one of them really thriving after surgery in terms of language learning and trajectories, and others barely able to communicate.
It was that experience and seeing these huge differences in outcomes after the same surgery that led me into this incredible world of childhood development and the importance of the early years and the importance of parents.
Humans come out with brains that are literally only one-third the size of adult brains. That’s very different than any other species. It’s why the puppy can start feeding itself pretty quickly and start walking, whereas the human infant is helpless. In those first three years of life, 85 percent of the physical brain is built during those periods of time.
A million new neural connections happen every second. The environmental input, the input from parents and caregivers — every serve and return, every touch, every gaze — literally is helping shape and strengthen the neural connections that happen in our brain.
The brain isn’t being just built for your child’s vocabulary development or their literacy ability. It’s building their social brain, their ability to relate to and connect to the rest of the world. The relationships and the expectations for relationships are built in those early years.
Tell me if this is maybe an oversimplification, but I’m a parent of a young son; he’s a little over 7 months old. And I feel like what I’m doing when I’m raising him is building the structure of his brain, or building the architecture, and all the other stuff, all the specific things, are going to fill in all the rooms of the big building that we’re constructing together. But he’s not going to start filling those in with specific ideas or specific memories until later on in his development.
The analogy you make is exactly right. I think of building the physical brain — if you were thinking about it through a computer lens — as building the hardware, the firmware, the memory, the RAM. I think of K-12 as really important, but I think of those as software updates. But these early years are building that infrastructure.
“I want you to not strive for perfection, because the one thing that AI has shown us is that humans don’t grow from perfection and frictionless existence.”
At the end of the day, it’s your attachment with him, being the perfectly imperfect parent. I want you to not strive for perfection, because the one thing that AI has shown us is that humans don’t grow from perfection and frictionless existence. So feel okay every time you misstep, misunderstand and repair, because that is, for him, building the understanding of, “I can be loved by another human who missteps but is able to repair.” He is starting to understand how to expect to be treated.
That’s why it’s almost like you’re building the relationship map for him that’s going to allow him in the future to have expectations of how he’s going to be treated and loved by an imperfect human: building that strong bond, showering him with rich language, that back and forth, looking at him as a conversational partner from day one.
It’s interesting you brought up AI and friction. What do you think this idea of a more frictionless existence is going to start meaning for kids?
I had a book that just came out on this called Human Raised, and that’s a lot of the argument of the book. Children learn from imperfect parenting through friction, through the productive struggle. And we’re seeing that friction that we’ve always looked at as a bug in the system — like, “Oh my gosh, I wish this was a more frictionless existence with the other humans in our world” — what we’re finding is that it is key for relationships development, learning to have relationships, and actually even learning.
That’s why, writing an essay with an LLM — you don’t remember it at the end of the day. There’s something about what happens in the brain that we’ve discounted on the friction side of things. So I actually think in some ways friction should be the word of the year, and we need to embrace it a little bit more. We don’t need to friction-max, but we do need to see the power of the friction.
It sounds like even if my son is going to forget all of this, maybe on a deep level it’ll stick with him. But should I still have a nice big 1-year-old birthday party?
Heck yes. Because you’re doing it partially for you — and the grandparents, let’s be clear. Those are wonderful moments that they do remember at some level. My son, who’s now 20-something in medical school, was obsessed with Thomas the choo-choo train. I still have the box of the Thomas the choo-choo train.
He may not remember exactly that birthday party and the cake that I worked very hard on, but it’s even fun to talk about it now in his twenties. So yes, do enjoy every moment. Don’t get obsessed, like everything has to be perfect, but those are memories for everyone.

Could South Sydney's Tallis Duncan be the answer to Australia's second row World Cup shortage?
The South Sydney backline might be an unusual place to find the answer to Australia's second-row shortage for this year's World Cup but regardless of position the form of Rabbitohs tyro Tallis Duncan is fast becoming impossible to deny.
Of the backrowers who played in this year's Origin series only Liam Martin can be considered an automatic selection for Kevin Walters's squad.
Hudson Young and Dylan Lucas are both out with injuries, Haumole Olakau'atu will represent Tonga, Briton Nikora is already tied to New Zealand and Angus Crichton's status is uncertain amid his impending move to rugby.
Duncan would have to beat out the likes of Canterbury's Jacob Preston and Warriors veteran Kurt Capewell, and Kulikefu Finefeuiaki, David Fifita and Heilum Luki will all be in the mix if they don't opt to represent Tonga and Samoa respectively, but the door is open for him to claim his first taste of higher honours.
The 24-year old has been a rare constant for South Sydney in a helter-skelter season, impressing at second row and in recent weeks at centre.
His effort against Canterbury last week, where Duncan scored a try, threw the final pass for another and ran for 182 metres from 23 carries, has become typical fare and with the Rabbitohs hitting form at just the right time, a strong finish to the season could well propel Duncan into a green and gold jersey.
"It's definitely something I've dreamed about my whole life. I haven't spoken about it too much publicly, that's not really the type I am," Duncan said.
"But that's a dream and if I was able to achieve that dream it would mean everything to me and my family. That's all I have to say about it now."
Injuries have forced Duncan to spend the last month at centre and while he's still just filling in out wide, that versatility would make him all the more valuable as part of Australia's squad.
That time out wide is only temporary but his success there is proof of Duncan's growing maturity.
He's improved out of sight compared to this time last year by leaning on the experience of players like Jack Wighton and the injured Latrell Mitchell, who have both played centre for New South Wales and Australia.
"I'm a second-rower, but being able to help the team in any way, I'll always put my hand up for that," Duncan said.
"I want to be part of an environment that's team first and for me to want that I have to live that. I believe we're doing that now.
"I've got a lot of good centres around me at training and I'm not too proud to ask for help."
Duncan also believes an increase in trust between himself, South Sydney's ageless wonder Cody Walker and Alex Johnston, who Duncan cites as key to identifying opposition shapes, as a key to his recent success.
At the time of writing he has as many tries this season as the Dolphins' Herbie Farnworth, the best centre in the league, and he's first in the league among backrowers for line breaks and second for tackle busts.
"I try to have intent in what I do and I pride myself on running hard lines," Duncan said.
"I know how hard it is to defend someone when they're running genuine leads, it just puts the defence under pressure.
"Everyone has a job to do and if I do mine then I'll get the ball because we've got quality ball-players like Cody and Duff (Matt Dufty)."
If the Rabbitohs' showing against Canterbury is anything to go by, Duncan will get more than a few chances to push his claims for an Australian jersey.
Wayne Bennett's side produced their best performance of the season to all but secure their top eight spot with a series of try-saving efforts the highlight of the 22-6 victory.
"I'm really proud of that one. We saved three tries before we scored one, that's what the good teams do," Duncan said.
"We might not seem like a team that prides themselves on defence but that's what we've been working on, so it's good to see the fruits of it.
"Good teams don't make errors in their own half, but when they do they defend them. We can be very proud of that."

Defence ministry inks ₹1.9 cr deal to lease 2 MQ-9B Sea Guardian drones for Navy
The contract is valued at approximately ₹1,943 crore, according to a ministry statement.
The Ministry of Defence on Monday signed a contract with General Atomics Aeronautical Systems to lease two MQ-9B Sea Guardian high-altitude long-endurance drones for the Indian Navy for 30 months.
The contract is valued at approximately ₹1,943 crore, according to a ministry statement.
"The Ministry of Defence has signed a contract with General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. (GA-ASI) for the leasing of two MQ-9B Sea Guardian High-Altitude Long-Endurance (HALE) Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS) for the Indian Navy for a period of 30 months," the statement said.
"The MQ-9B Sea Guardian HALE RPAS, equipped with advanced systems, state-of-the-art sensors and sophisticated payloads, will significantly enhance the Indian Navy's Maritime Domain Awareness capabilities," it added.
It also said “the systems will provide persistent intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance coverage over vast areas of the maritime domain, strengthening India's ability to monitor and respond to developments across the Indian Ocean Region.”

Peyush Bansal, the cofounder of eyewear retailer Lenskart Solutions, is the latest Indian to join the three-comma club. Shares of SoftBank-backed Lenskart, which went public nine months ago, hit an all-time high of nearly 627 rupees on the National Stock Exchange last week. Bansal’s close to 9% stake in the $11 billion market cap company plus the proceeds of shares he sold in the IPO, give him an estimated net worth of $1 billion.
The stock jumped after the company reported a four-fold rise in net profit to 2.28 billion rupees ($24 million) for the quarter ended June 30 amid surging sales in both domestic and overseas markets. Headquartered in the northern Indian city of Faridabad, Lenskart sells everything from glasses to sunglasses to eyewear accessories both online and through a network of stores.
It has a presence in 16 countries including Singapore, Japan and the UAE, apart from India where it has 2,725 stores across 157 cities. It added 132 stores in the latest quarter, of which 116 were in India and 16 overseas taking the company’s total store count to 3,459 stores.
Bansal, 42, started the business in 2010 with his sister Neha, who heads merchandising and two other cofounders, Amit Chaudhari, the sourcing chief and Sumeet Kapahi, who oversees the store network. The company got going initially as an online retailer offering customers a 3D feature to try on the glasses virtually. It later expanded offline opening its first store in New Delhi in 2013.
“Buying spectacles is not an easy decision,” says Arvind Singhal, chairman of Gurgaon-based retail consultancy, The Knowledge Company. “You want the opinion of a family member or a friend and you want to look at a wide assortment. It is good that Lenskart corrected course and opened physical stores.”
Bansal took the company public in November 2025, raising $821 million in an IPO that was oversubscribed 28 times. However, the stock listed at a 3% discount to its issue price.
SoftBank first invested in Lenskart in December 2019, leading a $275 million funding round that made Lenskart a unicorn. The Japanese investor sold a small stake during the IPO but offloaded a bigger 3.25% stake for $300 million in June after the mandatory six-month lock-in period had ended. It still remains the largest shareholder with a nearly 10% stake. Other marquee investors include Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, private equity giant KKR and TPG.
Bansal, who has an undergrad degree in electrical engineering from Canada’s McGill University, started his career with Microsoft in Redmond where he worked as a program manager for its MS Office product. He quit within a year to move back to India in 2007 and started Valyoo Technologies a year later. It operated a website called searchmycampus.com aimed at helping students find campus housing.
Reading an article about how India was an underserved market in eyecare and eyewear, gave him new direction: organized eyewear retailing was a ripe opportunity as the market was dominated by scores of small opticians across the country. He worked at one such shop in Delhi to get a better understanding of the business before he took the plunge.
An October 2025 report by Mumbai investment firm ICICI Direct pegs the size of the Indian eyewear market at $9.2 billion in fiscal 2025 and projects it will expand to $17.2 billion in fiscal 2030. Prescription glasses account for 75% of sales with sunglasses contributing $2 billion or just over a fifth and contact lenses the remainder. Sales of sunglasses is expected to nearly double to $4 billion by fiscal 2030 while the contact lenses segment is expected to expand to $730 million from $ 480 million over the same period.
Lenskart’s main rival is Titan Eye + , the eyewear division of Titan Company, part of the Tata conglomerate but its revenue of 9.16 billion rupees for fiscal 2026 and store count of less than 1,000 are both well behind Lenskart. Other legacy retailers such as Kolkata-based Himalaya Opticals and Delhi-based Bonton Opticians compete in the luxury and premium niche.
Analysts say that the eyewear market has enough room for all players. ICICI Direct estimates that as of 2020, 43% of the country’s population had weak eyes and by 2030, nearly two-thirds of Indians will need eyeglasses.
Foreseeing this trend, Bansal has been ramping up Lenskart’s brick and mortar presence. The store count crossed 1,000 in 2022 and 2,000 in 2025. The overseas expansion started off with opening a store in Singapore in 2019, which has since grown to 65 stores. Lenskart entered the UAE with a store in Dubai in 2022 and Saudi Arabia in 2023.
In June 2022, Bansal cast his gaze on a further horizon by acquiring a majority stake in Japanese eyewear brand Ownday for $400 million. Ownday now has 669 stores from 460 stores when Lenskart acquired it.
For the year ended March 31 Lenskart’s net profit jumped 148% to 5.3 billion rupees on revenue that was up nearly a third to 90 billion rupees. Analysts say the company is reaping the benefits of scale and backward integration. It makes lenses at a factory in Rajasthan state and has a joint venture for manufacturing frames at a Chinese factory in Zhengzhou. The company is building a a new factory on a 50-acre site in the southern India city of Hyderabad with the capacity to produce 50 million pairs per year,
“Lenskart’s business model is one of a kind,” says Singhal. “Even Titan has not been able to do what the company has done in terms of the scale of manufacturing and the range that they offer.”
That said, challenges lie ahead. “Lenskart’s ability to sustain its growth and profitability will depend on its resilience across four critical fronts - securing stable and cost-effective raw material supplies, maintaining uninterrupted manufacturing operations, attracting and retaining skilled vision-care talent, and navigating intensifying global competition in the eyewear industry,” says Amarjeet Maurya, deputy vice president for fundamental research at Mumbai-based Kotak Securities.
Bansal, who refused to comment when contacted, has outlined his vision for Lenskart in the company’s latest quarterly presentation. “We set out to sell eyeglasses,” he noted. “It was always a dream—to change how a billion people see and experience the world…Few companies get to attempt this. It is still Day Zero.”

White House denies Trump chief Susie Wiles’ phone was hacked again after UK Prime Minister falls victim to hoax
Denial comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham was taken in by a hoaxer who claimed to be Wiles in a text exchange
The White House was forced to deny on Monday that Chief of Staff Susie Wiles’ phone was hacked a second time after it emerged that British Prime Minister Andy Burnham received texts from a person he thought was President Donald Trump’s top aide.
Politico first reported that Burnham had briefly “engaged” with text messages purporting to be from Wiles, a veteran Florida political operative who is the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, before becoming concerned that the messages in question were not actually from Wiles.
The prime minister’s office said the “few messages” exchanged were “of no significance” and described the incident as a “national security matter” on which there would be no further comment.
But the incident was concerning enough that the British government contacted the White House about it through their embassy in Washington over fears that Wiles’ phone had been breached as it was a year ago, when business people and political figures began receiving texts from her that she had not actually sent.
Still, a White House official told The Independent the incident with Burnham is not related to that prior security breach.
“This incident had nothing to do with the Chief of Staff’s devices being hacked,” the official said.
The transatlantic contretemps over the inauthentic messages comes more than a year after the FBI and White House launched a probe into how a slew of political and business bigwigs began receiving texts and calls from someone purporting to be Wiles — after which she reportedly told people her phone had been breached.
According to The Wall Street Journal, FBI officials told the White House they did not believe a foreign adversary was to blame for the incidents.
Burnham is not the first British or American official to fall victim to a high-profile hoax in recent years.
In 2024, Lord David Cameron — then the British Foreign Minister — was duped by a hoaxer who had tricked him into texting and getting on the phone with someone pretending to be ex-Ukrainian president Petro Poroshenko.
And last year, Secretary of State Marco Rubio was impersonated by an individual who used AI to ape his voice and written communications in a series of voice and text messages to what The Washington Post described as “three foreign ministers, a U.S. governor, and a U.S. member of Congress.”
Unlike the incident with Burnham and Wiles, the Post said a State Department cable attributed the Rubio hoaxes to an actor who had the “goal of gaining access to information or accounts.”
Trump administration officials frequently flout record-keeping laws and long-established security practices by using their personal devices to conduct government business, often using the Signal encrypted messaging app.
Michael Waltz, the ex-Florida congressman who currently serves as the U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations, was sacked from his prior position as President Donald Trump’s national security adviser after he inadvertently included The Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg in a signal chat in which he, Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and other top administration officials discussed plans for airstrikes on Houthi rebels in Yemen last year.

Flipkart wanted to draw attention to the final day of its Freedom Sale. Instead, its obituary-style print advertisement has triggered a debate over dark humour and how far brands should go to grab eyeballs. The advertisement borrowed the visual language of obituary notices, placing photographs and personal details of individuals inside memorial-style boxes. However, it was Flipkart’s deals, and not the people featured, that were supposedly nearing their end. “We aren’t sad at all,” the advertisement said, adding that while the people featured would continue to live, Flipkart’s deals would soon disappear. The advertisement was released as Flipkart’s Freedom Sale, which began on August 8 after early access opened a day earlier, approached its conclusion on August 16. The sale offered discounts across smartphones, laptops, televisions, appliances, fashion, and household products. The creative quickly drew criticism online, with several users calling it insensitive and inappropriate. Author and columnist Shobhaa De described the campaign as “self-serving, disgusting and insensitive” and called for consumers to boycott Flipkart. Another user said, “We should leave normal people with dignity in death. This ad is insensitive and inhuman.” The criticism also prompted questions about whether the people featured in the advertisement were real or the images had been generated using AI. Flipkart has not clarified how the images were created. However, the reaction was not uniformly negative. Some users argued that the advertisement was clearly a parody and did not present an identifiable real person as having died. Others described it as a “non-obit” celebrating fictional people while they were alive. “These are AI-generated images, not real people. Personally, I didn’t find this insensitive at all,” one user said. The divided response raises a larger question for advertisers: does grabbing attention make a campaign effective if the controversy overshadows the product or proposition being promoted? Flipkart has not publicly responded to the criticism. Questions sent by Inc42 to the ecommerce major remained unanswered till the time of publishing. Attention Without Conversion? Harish Bijoor, founder of brand consultancy Harish Bijoor Consults, believes the campaign succeeded in generating awareness but questioned whether it could move consumers further down the advertising funnel. “The first (purpose of advertising) is to gain awareness, and I think this piece of advertising gets that awareness bang on right—100 on 100,” Bijoor said. However, he argued that the campaign’s reliance on dark humour could prevent that attention from translating into interest or sales. “After attention, nothing much happens. The prime purpose of good advertising is to convert into an actual sale. If your advertising isn’t doing this, then you’re failing,” he said. Although Bijoor does not believe the campaign warrants the scale of criticism it has received, he said Flipkart may have underestimated the sensitivity attached to obituary-style imagery. “When ads of this kind rub shoulders with real obituaries, if at all, it is insensitive to the dead, the grieving and the mourning,” Bijoor said. Communications consultant Karthik Srinivasan disagreed, arguing that the advertisement does not feature real people or attempt to pass itself off as a genuine obituary. According to Srinivasan, Flipkart’s branding is prominently displayed and the campaign uses what he described as imaginary, AI-generated characters who remain alive within the advertisement’s premise. He called the creative an example of “elementary subversion”, briefly leading viewers to interpret the advertisement one way before revealing its actual message. However, Srinivasan acknowledged that death remains a sensitive subject in Indian advertising and said brands should rigorously scrutinise such ideas internally before releasing them. Independent brand and digital advisor Ashok Lalla was more critical of the execution. Lalla noted that Flipkart has historically used unconventional advertising, including campaigns featuring children portraying adults and its “SASA LELE” campaign around the festive sale season. However, he said the latest campaign lacked the creative strength of Flipkart’s earlier work. “The current sale announcement using mock obituary-style callouts seemed very contrived and devoid of any real creative idea.” He added that the response to the advertisement may be better described as rejection than outrage, particularly among advertising and marketing professionals. Provocative campaigns can generate immediate reactions, he said, but may not necessarily build a brand favourably over the long term. When Attention Backfires Flipkart’s campaign is the latest example of an Indian consumer internet company using a provocative marketing device to cut through an increasingly crowded media environment. In 2024, home salon startup Yes Madam drew criticism after circulating a purported internal email claiming that employees who reported high stress levels in a survey had been fired. The company later said no employees had been dismissed and that the episode was part of a campaign intended to highlight workplace stress. The same year, actor and model Poonam Pandey staged a fake announcement of her death from cervical cancer as part of an awareness campaign. The stunt drew widespread criticism for using death and grief as marketing devices. These campaigns share an underlying strategy: creating something that audiences are unlikely to ignore. However, they also highlight the distinction between generating conversation and building trust. “Attention, memory and love are three different things,” said Dr Sanjay Arora, founder of Shells Advertising. Arora believes the insight behind Flipkart’s campaign – that people are often celebrated only after they die – had creative potential. However, he questioned the decision to express it using the visual language of an obituary. “An obituary is not merely another visual format. It is culturally associated with death, grief and the loss of a human being, a family member,” he said. Arora described the campaign as a blunder that generated visibility at the cost of civility. He added that provocative advertising can deliver diminishing returns if the controversy becomes more memorable than the product, sale, or brand proposition. “Being talked about is not the same as being liked, trusted or remembered for the right reason,” he said. Flipkart’s advertisement succeeded in making people stop, look, and argue. The question now is whether consumers remember the Freedom Sale or only the controversy surrounding its promotion.

A man has received threats from the Taliban after his work for the Afghan police was revealed by a Ministry of Defence leak and the UK refused his application for resettlement.
Hamid* worked for the Afghan national police special unit and received certificates for his work signed by senior British figures praising his “dedication, unparalleled service and leadership”. His details were also included in an accidental 2022 leak by an MoD official that identified 18,700 Afghans who had worked with or for the British government.
Hamid said he had received a number of threats from the Taliban, including a video he shared with the Guardian in which a man cradling a rifle and sitting below a Taliban flag threatens to pursue him and cites knowledge of his previous movements.
The MoD, however, has rejected his application for resettlement under the Afghan relocations and assistance policy (Arap) scheme. His most recent rejection, received on 31 July, stated that Hamid had not provided evidence of “working alongside, in partnership with or closely supporting a UK government department”. It gave him 28 days to appeal.
Hamid said: “This is extremely painful because I have already submitted every document available to me proving my service. Furthermore, many of my former colleagues who served in exactly the same department and performed the same duties have already been relocated to the UK through the Arap scheme.
“Despite this evidence, my case continues to be refused. I believe my case raises serious questions about how some former Afghan partners of the UK continue to be treated despite years of loyal service.”
Hamid’s plea for help comes five years after the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan on 15 August 2021 after the withdrawal of US and Nato forces. The UK government launched the Arap scheme on 1 April 2021 and closed it to new applications on 1 July last year. Pre-existing applications continue to be processed.
Under Arap, high risk of death or serious injury are only taken into account if the rest of the criteria are deemed to have been met, which they have not in Hamid’s case. “Must I wait until I am captured, tortured or killed by the Taliban before my service and the danger I face are finally recognised?” he said.
“Following the Ministry of Defence data breach, my personal information was exposed, placing me at even greater risk. Since then, my life has changed completely. I cannot safely leave my home to work. I live in constant fear of being recognised or targeted.”
After the leak, the then defence secretary, John Healey, said the dataset included people who had made speculative applications under Arap and had not worked with British forces. He said being included in the leak “doesn’t give them a right to claim access to Britain”.
“It doesn’t give them a right to claim asylum. It doesn’t make them eligible for the special [Arap] scheme that Britain put in place for those who’d worked alongside or served with our forces,” he said.
Hamid said that because he was in hiding he had no reliable income and relied on his wife, who supports the family by doing small jobs from home. “This is our family’s only source of income, and even then we struggle simply to survive,” he said.
“The emotional impact has been devastating. My wife and I have become deeply exhausted, depressed and hopeless after years of fear, uncertainty, repeated refusals and financial hardship.
“I am not asking for special treatment. I am only asking for a fair review based on the evidence I have already provided.”
An MoD spokesperson said: “Each application is considered on a case-by-case basis, assessed against the evidence provided, such as how they supported the UK mission in Afghanistan, and in line with the publicly available eligibility criteria.
“Since the Taliban takeover, the UK has resettled almost 39,000 Afghan men, women and children through Afghan resettlement schemes.”

Egypt’s Theban necropolis holds over 400 tombs, a rich resource for archaeologists eager to learn more about that region’s ancient history. A new paper published in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology outlines how Egyptian burial trends likely changed over the course of centuries, shifting from individual burials in elaborate coffins to reusing earlier burial sites for later interments, resulting in greater density and the occasional superposition of bodies.
There has been prior research on the reuse of tombs in Thebes. This latest paper focused on a Theban tomb known as 209 in the western necropolis, dating back to the early 25th Dynasty (754–656 BCE) and ultimately abandoned in the Ptolemaic period (305–30 BCE). The original owner was likely a high official of Nubian origin named Nisemro. Over the centuries, the tomb was prone to repeated flash flooding due to its location within an active drainage channel of the Wadi Hatasun, so it’s a complex site, archaeologically speaking.
That made it ideal for what the authors term an “integrated archaeothanatological approach,” incorporating collected data on body position, coffin use, superpositions of remains, and stratigraphic relationships with osteological analysis in order to reconstruct the chronological sequence of the burials. They focused on a site known as Side Chamber 3, one of the main secondary areas of the tomb that was largely undisrupted.
Their excavation resulted in the discovery of 16 mummified people (1,444 bones), one mummified dog, and one chamber containing the disarticulated remains (1,775 bone fragments) of at least four other individuals. “The detailed study of the bodies indicates neither chaotic accumulation nor a loss of the original ritual over time,” said co-author Jared Carballo-Perez of the University of La Laguna in Spain. “Rather, there was a spatial logic in which each new deposition was adapted to the presence of previous bodies—a kind of funerary memory in the processes of reuse.”

Death row inmates desperate to escape execution in Saudi Arabia call the BBC
- Published
There was desperation in the voice of the young Ethiopian man when he managed to get through to the BBC from a phone in his prison cell on death row in Saudi Arabia.
Habtom, whose name - like the other prisoner featured in this article - has been changed to protect his identity, has been held in a jail in the southern city of Khamis Mushait for more than three years.
Above the noise of cellmates shouting behind him, he pleaded for help and sounded angry that his government appeared to be doing little to change his fate.
"One prisoner cannot comfort another. We have no choice but to cry. We are waiting for our turn, even though we do not know when it will happen," said Habtom.
He and some of his fellow inmates had fled war and poverty at home in the hope of finding a better life.
But that quest, which took him through Djibouti and Yemen, led to his incarceration - joining a growing number of Ethiopians in Saudi prisons who face the prospect of execution for drug-smuggling offences.
Anxious to tell their story, some of the prisoners managed to get hold of the mobile phone number for the BBC's Tigrinya language service. In total we have spoken to seven of the dozens - perhaps as many as 200 - Ethiopians inside the prison who are waiting for a death sentence to be carried out.
Other foreigners, including Pakistanis, Sudanese and Jordanians, are in a similar position, but in the first seven months of this year 17 Ethiopians have been executed - the highest number among non-Saudis. Five of those executions happened on Monday.
Two years ago, according to research by Amnesty International, just two Ethiopians were executed, but 35 were put to death in 2025.
It is not clear exactly why there has been an uptick, but it could be linked to more people leaving the northern Ethiopian region of Tigray, where a brutal two-year civil war in Tigray ended in late 2022, leaving devastation in its wake.
"It may also be linked to Saudi Arabia's expanding use of the death penalty for drug-related offences in recent years," Amnesty International researcher Dana Ahmed tells the BBC.
Habtom, who like most of those the BBC spoke to is from Tigray, was found guilty of smuggling hashish, a type of cannabis. In Saudi Arabia, on the judge's discretion, a guilty verdict can result in a death sentence.
But rights groups - including Reprieve, Human Rights Watch (HRW) and Amnesty International - have said that in these kinds of cases due process is rarely followed.
Defendants are not given access to a lawyer or the court papers - while translation, when it is offered, can be inadequate, Amnesty's Ahmed says.
Although there is the theoretical right to appeal, without a lawyer they cannot submit one "and then the sentence is automatically upheld", she says.
"There is a near-total lack of transparency throughout the entire judicial process, from sentencing to Supreme Court review and ratification by the King. People on death row and their families are left in the dark about their fate."
Habtom alleged that he was not given the chance to speak to a lawyer or defend himself. He also said he was forced to sign a document in Arabic, which said he agreed to the sentence, without understanding what he was putting his name to.
Other prisoners that the BBC spoke to had similar stories about the legal system.
HRW has also contacted people close to the cases and learned about "mass sentences, mass trials that lacked any kind of due process and people detained then just waiting with no idea when the sentence would happen", Nadia Hardman, the organisation's senior adviser on refugee and migrant rights, said.
The Saudi authorities did not respond to a BBC request for comment on allegations that the legal process was not fair, but every execution is accompanied by a statement issued through the official press agency. It outlines a clear process: an investigation, a court case, an appeal, a Supreme Court ruling and then a royal decree.
The sentence reflects the commitment to protect citizens "from the scourge of drugs" and the damage they can cause, the statement adds.
Habtom said that although he manged to keep in occasional contact with his family via the wall-mounted phone in his prison cell, he refused to tell them he was on death row: "I would rather they be told after I die than now."
He had dreamt of finishing high school, graduating from college and getting a job to support his parents - but the Tigray war put paid to that.
"My goal was destroyed, so I decided to emigrate," he said.
After surviving the dangerous journey to Saudi Arabia in 2021, Habtom found low-paid work as a goatherder, but his employers offered him and others a chance to earn more money.
They were asked to deliver a package but were stopped by police on the way and were found with the narcotic leaf known as khat - a natural stimulant that is widely used in the Horn of Africa.
The official Saudi statements all refer to hashish smuggling but those the BBC spoke to talked about khat.
"I did not know what we were carrying. But later I was told it was khat. I don't even know what khat is," Habtom said, admitting that he was tempted into the work by the sum of money on offer.
Habtom acknowledged he had "made a mistake without knowing it" and hoped that his sentence could be commuted to prison time.
Three of his fellow Ethiopian detainees were executed in April - another nine were killed in June. The April killings sparked an outcry from rights groups and some leading Ethiopian figures, including the influential head of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.
Patriarch Abune Mathias urged the government to negotiate with the Saudi authorities and called the inmates "voiceless children" living "under the shadow of death".
In its April report, HRW called on the Saudi authorities to immediately halt executions of Ethiopian migrants and ensure all cases were handled in line with international law. It also asked Ethiopia's foreign ministry to intervene urgently and provide consular support.
The safety of Ethiopians in general in Saudi Arabia was raised at a meeting in Addis Ababa in May between Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos and Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Waleed Al-Khuraiji.
This was followed in June by a visit to the prison by Ethiopia's Ambassador Tafa Tulu Dadi, though the prisoners told the BBC that they were not given enough time to explain their situation to him.
It also appeared to have limited impact as in the following week more Ethiopians were executed.
The African Union's human rights commission has also urged Ethiopia to safeguard the lives of Ethiopians facing execution in Saudi Arabia.
The BBC has contacted Ethiopian officials in Saudi Arabia and the government in Addis Ababa for comment but has not received a response.
Without referring to the death penalty specifically, Ethiopia's foreign ministry did release a statement on 13 July saying it was in regular contact with the Saudi authorities "pursuing appropriate remedies for Ethiopian citizens facing difficult circumstances".
It added that "to date" nearly 2,000 Ethiopians had "benefited from royal amnesties" - without mentioning the crimes or sentences.
As they await the outcome of diplomatic manoeuvres, the prisoners who spoke to the BBC said they were enduring hardships in overcrowded facilities.
Desta, located in another part of the prison, said there were 200 men in his cell crammed into an area designed for 90 people, with 45 bunk beds arranged around the walls.
During the day, the prisoners sat on the floor in stifling conditions squeezed up next to one another; when the temperature dropped at night, they covered themselves with rubbish bags in lieu of bed sheets, he said.
"The stress of facing execution, combined with the overcrowded conditions, exposes us to illness and anxiety," Desta said.
"The guard only opens the door to bring food, covering his mouth and nose with a mask - that is the only time the door is opened. After he gives us the food, he quickly locks it and leaves.
"It is not possible to ask them any questions or speak to them. Even if you ask, there is severe beating."
He was arrested while trying to cross the border from Yemen more than three years ago and accused of smuggling drugs.
"We were four Ethiopians, and there was one Yemeni with us. He told us he could help us cross the border safely because he knew the safest route. In return, he asked us to carry packages containing khat and even promised to pay us some money.
"Unfortunately, shortly after we crossed, we were captured by police officers. They opened fire on us, and the Yemeni man ran away, but we couldn't. We were shocked and had no idea where to go."
Like all those interviewed by the BBC, Desta said he had never expected to be sentenced to death and believed he would eventually return home after serving time in prison.
Instead, he alleged that he was also forced to sign a document in Arabic that listed charges carrying capital punishment. Later, when he appeared in court, he said that he was denied the chance to challenge the charges and had no legal representation.
"When you appear before the judge on the first day, he asks: 'Do you accept the charges?' On the second appearance, he sentences you to death," Desta said.
As a brick-maker struggling to support his family, he had left Tigray during the war as the fighting edged closer to his home.
Now he worries for his life again - and he, Habtom and dozens of others on death row are begging for outside help.
"We are living in deep fear and cannot even eat the food we are given," said Habtom.

Chinese navy’s combat software guru Zhao Xiaozhe disappears from academy website
The vice-admiral is the latest prominent expert to be removed from the prestigious national engineering institution’s membership list
2-MIN READ2-MIN

Ling Xinin Ohio
A top naval software expert, whose work helped warships to process battlefield information and support combat decisions, has vanished from the Chinese Academy of Engineering’s online membership list.
Zhao Xiaozhe, 63, a vice-admiral in the PLA Navy, once headed the Central Military Commission’s top science and technology body, helping to shape research priorities across China’s armed forces.
He is the latest prominent defence expert to disappear from the academy’s website, following reporting in March of the unexplained removal of profiles belonging to a nuclear weapons scientist, a radar specialist and a missile designer, among others.
Zhao was reportedly absent from a high-level Communist Party study session on artificial intelligence chaired by President Xi Jinping in April last year, with his deputy attending instead.
His profile has also been removed from the academy’s separate online museum of academicians.
Zhao was elected to the academy in 2011 while at the Dalian Naval Academy, where he was a professor and doctoral supervisor. He also served as director of its Combat Software and Simulation Research Institute.

Thousands of angry young job-seekers clashed with police in Jharkhand, one of India’s poorest states, on Monday as a weeks-long protest over alleged irregularities in recruitment drives for coveted government jobs escalated into a march on the state legislature.
Police fired water cannon and teargas and swung batons as they tried to stop flag-waving demonstrators from clambering over barricades and surging towards the assembly in Ranchi, the state capital. Some of the protesters responded by dancing and cheering as jets of water drenched the crowd.
The unrest comes just weeks after the Cockroach movement, a youth-led protest campaign – which began as an online joke and grew into a nationwide outcry over leaks in a national medical entrance examination – put the BJP-led national government under heavy pressure and led to the resignation of the education minister.
Both protesters and police officers were injured in the Jharkhand clashes, local media reported, although no official figures were released.
“The baton charge was barbaric. We were protesting peacefully, but the government used batons against us,” protester Piyush Kumar Soni told the Press Trust of India.
The demonstrators are demanding an investigation by the CBI, India’s premier investigative force, saying only an independent inquiry can get to the bottom of alleged wrongdoing in government recruitment examinations.
They accuse authorities of failing to prevent irregularities in public service exams, including test paper leaks and cheating, and say the alleged scandals have deprived young people of a fair chance.
Jharkhand has long struggled with high unemployment, making government jobs highly sought after. Competition is intense for civil service and other public sector posts, which offer job security, health and pension benefits.
Government recruitment drives routinely attract hundreds of thousands of applicants, and many young people spend years preparing for examinations. In one recent Jharkhand recruitment exercise, nearly 640,000 applications were received for 2,025 posts. In another, more than 322,000 candidates competed for 510 vacancies.
The state government, led by a regional party allied with the opposition Congress, has sought to defuse the crisis through talks. Officials say most of the protesters’ demands have been accepted and that they are open to more negotiations.
The Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, condemned the use of force. “Students have a right to peaceful protest, and only dialogue can yield solutions,” he said.
The row has already toppled senior figures. The former Jharkhand public service commission chair was arrested over alleged exam irregularities, while three commission members have resigned.
The protests underscore mounting frustration among young Indians over corruption in public examinations and recruitment systems, a shortage of good jobs and fears that opportunities are being lost to cheating and political influence. Nearly two-thirds of Indians are under 35.
Official data shows unemployment fell to 9.9% last year, but a 2026 study by Azim Premji University found that nearly 40% of graduates aged 15 to 25 were unemployed.

Perhaps it’s the local summer diet of deep-fried cheese curds, corn on the cob, and Spotted Cow, but Wisconsin residents have been feeling pretty dyspeptic about Flock’s automated license plate cameras.
Over the past few months, a spate of Wisconsin towns and cities have withdrawn from Flock deals over privacy and trust concerns. As they did so, another issue revealed itself: With each city that leaves, the Flock network becomes less useful to the cities that remain. And cities are starting to notice.
Consider Dane County, which includes the city of Madison. It’s one of the most populous counties in Wisconsin. It was also a significant Flock user, with a contract for 24 license plate cameras. But after complaints from citizens and privacy experts, the Dane County Board of Supervisors on April 16 voted to cut the $80,000 in county funding for Flock cameras and banned “further expenditures on the system.”
“There are well-documented concerns about how this company operates and uses its technology to violate people’s Fourth Amendment rights [against unreasonable searches],” said County Board Chair Patrick Miles. “The board’s action supports protecting our community from a proven bad actor. We have full confidence in our Sheriff and deputies, and we are open to considering other companies that have stronger safeguards in place.”
The county’s Flock cameras soon went dark, cutting off Dane County data from the 140 other law enforcement agencies that had once accessed it. Many of these agencies were local, but they also included cops in Missouri, New York, and Tennessee.
(As for the city of Madison itself, it has avoided Flock cameras altogether. The city says it does not use any “automatic license plate readers, gunshot detection systems, or gait analysis software.”)
Monona, another Dane County city, in early May announced that its Flock contract was “under review.” The Monona police chief supports license plate cameras and said that Flock had helped solve “an enticement case involving a suspect who transported a vulnerable adult across state lines.” Still, local police were concerned about “privacy considerations” and “maintaining community trust and accountability.”

Of all the feedback she’s received on All Her Fault, there is one comment that sticks with creator and showrunner Megan Gallagher: “Those are two of the worst husbands I’ve ever seen on television, and neither one of them were having an affair.”
It certainly would’ve been easy (and predictable) to fuel audiences’ distaste for the spouses of Marissa Irvine (Sarah Snook) and Jenny Kaminski (Dakota Fanning), the two women at the center of the thriller who are brought together by the disappearance of the former’s son, by adding an extramarital relationship to the mix — particularly for Jenny’s husband, Richie (Thomas Cocquerel), whose sins amount to far less than Peter’s (Jake Lacy).
But, it also would’ve undercut the themes Gallagher wanted to drive home with the limited series, which explores the ways that women and mothers often shoulder the brunt of societal responsibility and therefore get the lion’s share of the blame as well.
Watch on Deadline
“I don’t think that that’s the worst thing that you can do to your spouse, necessarily. I really don’t,” Gallagher said during an All Her Fault x Women in Entertainment FYC screening at The London in West Hollywood on Sunday. “The truth is, if you are Jenny Kaminsky, and you are miserable every day and asking for help every day, and the person who’s supposed to love you and be your life partner is doing everything within their power to keep you miserable, that’s so much worse, I think, than having an affair. Like, I’d rather have you sleep with your secretary than do that. It meant something to be able to get that on the screen, that look at marriage.”
It also gave Gallagher an opportunity to dig into the complexities of a woman like Jenny, someone she says “might seem like [a] pushover” but is far from it.
“She’s a people pleaser by nature. She’s very clearly depicted that way, as somebody whose strength is in being empathic and being intuitive and kind of sensing what other people need,” she explained. “And I feel like I know so many people like that, men and women both, but I think that those people often have a very steely core down there.”
Gallagher describes the scene where Jenny finally puts her foot down with Richie as the character finally “finding that moment of no.”
Jenny’s realization is fueled not only by her husband’s actions throughout the series but also by the revelations about Marissa’s missing son and the part her own husband Peter played in his disappearance. At every turn, Marissa blames herself for Milo’s disappearance, as do others, and Peter lets her bear that undue weight for most of the series without explaining his part in any of it.
Ultimately, Marissa is a devoted mom who had nothing to do with her son’s disappearance and who was fooled by her own husband. Just like with Jenny, Gallagher says she wanted to challenge expectations for the kind of woman Marissa would be.
“I purposefully wrote Marissa as an incredibly accomplished career woman who wasn’t necessarily a lovey-dovey mom,” she said. “She’s got a real edge to her, in a good way, in a way that I find relatable. I’m not a wilting flower. She’s a really strong lady.”
Marissa’s devotion to both her son and her own sense of self was an important component to get on screen, Gallagher said, adding: “It’s one thing when society blames you or the media blames you and all that kind of stuff. It’s another thing when women internalize this guilt and we take it on ourselves. To me, that’s the most heartbreaking part.”

Aiming for her first World Championships medal in seven years, P. V. Sindhu arrives in New Delhi with renewed confidence following her Japan Open triumph. At a press conference ahead of the start of the tournament, the five-time world medallist spoke about the losses that shaped her, the evolution of her game, the pressure she feels before a major tournament, the importance of her new support team and what it means to finally compete for a world title on home soil.
Q: You must have renewed confidence after winning the Japan Open?
Definitely. Winning the Japan Open gave me a lot of confidence and a boost. I’m really looking forward to the World Championships, especially because it’s happening in India.
Q: You’ve won five World Championship medals. Looking back, which moments shaped your career and made you tougher?
Having five medals at the World Championships has been an amazing journey. Each medal gave me a different experience. I had bronze in 2013 and 2014, then silver (2017 and 2018) and eventually gold. That transition was wonderful.
But there were also difficult moments that made me stronger. One was losing the 2017 World Championships final to (Nozomi) Okuhara in Glasgow. It was a very hard-fought match, and I lost 22-20 in the deciding game. I was very hard on myself because I felt I was almost there and that it was just a matter of one or two points. That made me much stronger.
There were other moments too, like in 2018, when I was leading but lost the first game and eventually the gold. Those experiences, especially at the World Championships, made me stronger and taught me how to come back.
Q: How special would it be to win a medal here in India?
It would be very special. It’s happening in India after so many years. I won gold in 2019, and since then, it’s been almost seven years without a World Championships medal.
READ | ‘I kept believing that I could do it,’ says Sindhu after winning Japan Open
This time, the Japan Open win has given me a lot of confidence, so I hope I can carry that into this tournament. Everything is going well, but for me it’s about taking it one match at a time. I’ll get a lot of support from the Indian crowd, and I hope I can win a medal here.
Q: How have you changed over this seven-year period?
There have been quite a few changes, both in terms of my game and how I think and strategise. Badminton itself has changed. Earlier, women’s singles was more attacking and played at a faster pace. Now, there are longer rallies and you have to stay on court longer, so you need a lot of patience.
As a person, I’ve gained a lot of experience. I’m much more experienced in dealing with situations on court — whether there’s drift, how to control the shuttle, or how to adapt when things don’t go according to plan. Those are some of the things that have changed over this period.
Q: Are there still butterflies ahead of the first match?
I’ve had a lot of experience and played many first-round matches where there were butterflies and pressure. I won’t deny that there is pressure.
But at the same time, for me, there’s nothing to lose. I just want to give my best because I know I’ve trained hard and worked hard in my training sessions. I just have to go out on court and give my best, irrespective of the result.
The hunger for the game hasn’t changed. I know it’s still in me and that I can still do it. That hunger for the sport hasn’t changed.
Q: What do you think of the facilities here?
I really appreciate the effort that has gone into this. I’ve been here since yesterday and played today, and we’ve had really good sessions without feeling uncomfortable. Everything is comfortable and good.
From the washrooms to the people helping us, everyone has put in their effort day in and day out to make this happen. That itself shows that they’ve done a great job and that this can be one of the greatest World Championships.
As an Indian, I can proudly say that we’re fortunate to be playing here at home.
Q: Do you have any particular ways of staying focused?
Everyone has their own way. Some people might consider it superstition — trusting in God or praying that they do well. We all have our unique ways.
You can’t predict the result or know what’s going to happen tomorrow. Some players might have a particular racket, T-shirt, dress, hairstyle or shoes that they feel comfortable with.
For me, I just trust in God, go to the court and give my best.
Q: You’ve been pretty consistent since the Malaysia Open this year. What’s made the difference?
I’ve had a really good team around me, and it took some time to build that team. Once we got everyone together — the sports science team, physio and trainer — we sat down, discussed what was required and worked on those things with coach Irwansyah.
Everyone has played a major role. People see us when we play matches, but there’s a lot happening behind the scenes. We have to understand what is required and make smart decisions because sometimes your body doesn’t cooperate when you’re playing.
You need to know when to rest and make those decisions intelligently so that you’re at 100 per cent and peak at the right time. We’ve been doing that correctly, and that’s what has made the difference.
Q: You spoke about the changes you’ve made with the sports science team. How important has that been?
It was very important for me to have a sports science team around me. The coach is always there, but Dr Wayne Lombard heads the strength and conditioning, Hira is my physio and Shreyasi looks after the sports science.
It’s important to build that team around you because sometimes, your body isn’t at 100 per cent, but you still push yourself. Injuries can happen without warning, so you have to take precautions and make smart changes.
We now have gadgets and metrics that can tell us about strain, how tired you are and whether you can push yourself. Based on that, we can make changes — maybe doing a different kind of training the next day.
These small things have helped me. Physically and mentally, I’ve been quite good, and I’m able to see the changes in my game and movement. I’m happy that things are going in the right direction.
Q: India is hosting the World Championships after 17 years. Where were you the last time it was hosted in Hyderabad?
I was a very small girl. I used to come and watch matches from morning until evening. We would just play around and watch the matches. At that time, you just thought, “Okay, you get to see a lot of top players,” but you didn’t realise how serious it was.
Now when I look back, I feel I got to experience the best back then. And now, I’m here playing the World Championships in India 17 years later.
It’s really good to see how the whole journey has been so memorable. It’s always great to have the World Championships in India, and this time I’m hoping I can win a medal on home ground.
Q: We always speak about An Se Young, but you also have a rivalry with Wang Zhi Yi. How do you see that matchup?
I won against her at the last World Championships, but in our last match, I was leading and then lost. She’s doing well and she’s at the top.
With the top 10 players in the world, you just need to give your best. Everyone wants to play their best at the World Championships or any tournament.
We might know each other’s game, but you still have to make adjustments depending on the court and shuttle conditions and make sure you’re comfortable playing against them.
Every athlete has a different style. Whether it’s Wang Zhi Yi, (Akane) Yamaguchi or An Se Young, it won’t be easy. These will be tough matches and I need to be prepared.
Q: You were part of a golden generation that pushed the Chinese players, and now there’s another generation coming through. At the same time, there’s a new scoring system coming next year. How do you assess all these changes?
There is a younger generation coming up in badminton, especially in women’s singles, and there is some good talent.
The new scoring system will be very different and challenging. With 21 points, if you’re seven points down, you still have time to come back. With 15 points, if you’re seven points down, the match is almost done.
READ | “Format could wipe out some shuttlers” - Players, coaches weigh badminton’s scoring-system overhaul
You need to be on your feet from the first point. You can’t take it easy and think you can come back later. With the 15-point system, you have to be alert from the beginning and every single point will matter.
The game itself is constantly evolving. Earlier, it was a faster game, whereas now, there are comparatively longer rallies. With 15 points, it could become different again, with shorter and faster rallies, so you have to adapt.
I’m happy to see changes in the sport. Anything that is good for Indian sport is good. You have to get used to changes because that’s how sport works. The scoring changes, shuttles change, venues change — you don’t really have a choice but to adapt.
Q: How have you been able to strike a chord with Irwansyah? You previously worked with Mrs Kim and then coach Park.
It’s been good over the last one-and-a-half years. When you initially get a new coach, it takes some time for the athlete and coach to understand what each other needs.
But now, it’s working well. As I mentioned, it’s important for the coach and sports science team to come together, understand the requirements and work together.
I think that’s what we’re doing. It’s going well. You also need to keep making changes because the game keeps changing. Other athletes aren’t going to play the same game either; they keep changing their strategies. So, we need to make sure we’re adapting accordingly.
